nl6 is a single Go program that stands up thousands of simulated devices inside a dedicated Linux network namespace. Each simulated device has its own IP address on a TUN interface, its own SNMP listener, its own SSH server, a gNMI server, and, for storage devices, its own HTTPS REST endpoint.

The diagram is a C4 container view rendered as a Mermaid flowchart. It shows what lives inside the nl6 process, the host-side Linux infrastructure it depends on, and how operators and monitoring systems reach it. The namespace was opensim before the fork was renamed; see Network namespace for the one-time cleanup.

Choice Gained Given up sync.Map for OID lookups Lock-free O(1) reads under concurrent SNMP load Simple iteration; walks need the pre-computed next-OID map Pre-computed next-OID mappings GETNEXT and WALK without scanning the table Memory per loaded device type Buffer pool on the SNMP path Less GC pressure at high request rates Every handler path must return its buffer to the pool Shared SSH and TLS keys across all devices No per-device key generation, so 30,000 devices start in minutes Every device presents the same host key and certificate; nl6 does not model PKI Analytic IF-MIB counters Every ifTable and ifXTable counter is computed on demand from a per-direction sine wave, with no polling loop Traffic shapes other than the sine wave. See SNMP reference One counter dispatcher SNMP, gNMI, sFlow and YANG-Push read IfCounterCycler.GetDynamicAt, so every protocol reports the same number at the same instant A protocol cannot carry its own traffic model Network namespace isolation The nl6sim namespace keeps systemd-networkd off the TUN interfaces Linux only, and root is required Per-device flow egress A FORWARD -i veth-sim-host -j ACCEPT rule lets per-device exporters send out of the namespace on Docker hosts that default FORWARD to DROP An iptables dependency in the image; the rule is removed in NetNamespace.Close

nl6 does not currently ship a supported Kubernetes deployment. This page is the honest accounting of why. The simulator's design fights Kubernetes' isolation model in several places, and the workarounds shift the risk onto cluster operators rather than removing it. If you need to run the simulator today, use bare-metal or Docker on a single host. Both are documented and tested up to 30,000 devices.

The simulator behaves more like a hypervisor than an application. It owns host-level resources by name, mutates the host network stack, and has no horizontal scaling story. Kubernetes pods, by contrast, are designed to be isolated, replicable, and free to land on any node. The conflicts fall into four buckets.
documents.s: Why Kubernetes is out of scope

documents.t: Out of the box the simulator needs: CAP_NET_ADMIN for TUN device creation, link configuration and route installation. CAP_SYS_ADMIN for setns(CLONE_NEWNET) to enter the nl6sim namespace, plus the ip netns operations that depend on it. CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (or root) to bind UDP/161 and TCP/22 on every device IP. With -netconf-enable it also binds TCP/830 on cisco_catalyst_9500 and juniper_mx10004 devices. gNMI on TCP/9339, NETCONF over TLS on TCP/6513 and HTTPS REST on TCP/8443 are above 1024 and need no capability. Trap and syslog export bind an ephemeral source port; 162 and 514 are the collector's ports, not nl6's. NETCONF call home and gNMI dial-out also dial out from an ephemeral port and bind nothing. 4334 is the NETCONF client's port, not nl6's. /dev/net/tun mounted into the container. CAP_SYS_ADMIN is effectively the "new root". Restricted-profile PodSecurity admission will refuse this combination, so the namespace hosting the simulator must be labelled pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: privileged. On clusters where that label is centrally controlled (most shared clusters), the simulator cannot run.

The simulator does not stay inside a pod sandbox. It reaches out and edits the host's network stack: Creates and removes the nl6sim network namespace. Installs a veth pair (veth-sim-host / veth-sim-ns) with a hardcoded CIDR (10.254.0.0/30). Inserts an iptables rule: iptables -I FORWARD 1 -i veth-sim-host -j ACCEPT (and removes it on clean shutdown). Writes sysctls: net.ipv4.ip_forward=1, net.ipv4.conf.*.rp_filter=0, net.ipv4.conf.veth-sim-host.forwarding=1. Under hostNetwork: true (the only mode that makes device IPs reachable, as point 4 explains) those edits land on the node, not on a pod-local network stack. They co-exist with kube-proxy's iptables chains and the CNI's sysctls. The interaction is brittle: a CNI upgrade, a kube-proxy mode switch, or another DaemonSet that resets sysctls on the node can silently break per-device flow / trap / syslog egress without surfacing an error.

Several names and addresses are hardcoded: Network namespace name: nl6sim (the nl6sim namespace name is compiled in). veth pair names: veth-sim-host, veth-sim-ns. veth bridge CIDR: 10.254.0.0/30. Two simulator instances on the same node will collide on all three. There is no per-instance discriminator today, so a Deployment or StatefulSet with replicas: > 1 only works if every replica lands on a different node, and even then they share the FORWARD-rule global side-effect. That makes the workload effectively "this node is the simulator". That is at odds with the typical reason to use Kubernetes (workload density, reschedulability, replicas).

Each simulated device gets its own IP (-auto-start-ip sets the first one; 10.42.0.0/16 is the convention the examples use) on a TUN interface inside the nl6sim namespace on one node. From the host of that node, traffic to those IPs routes via veth into the namespace and reaches the device. From any other pod or node on the cluster, 10.42.0.0/16 is unknown and unreachable. The pollers and collectors that talk to simulated devices (your NMS, Prometheus, flow / trap / syslog receivers) usually live elsewhere on the cluster network. To make device IPs reachable from them you need one of: Pin the consumer to the same node with nodeAffinity and hostNetwork: true, so it shares the host's view. Works, but defeats most of the reason to put either workload in Kubernetes. Multus with a second pod NIC on a network that carries the device CIDR. Requires Multus installed and a bridge / VLAN configured at the node level. Calico BGP advertising the device CIDR from the simulator's node. Requires Calico in BGP mode, peering with the cluster's router, and cluster-admin coordination. All three are real network engineering on the cluster operator's side, not configuration the simulator can ship as a Helm chart. deploy/helm/nl6-minion/ exists despite this. It is a single-node lab chart that co-locates nl6 with an OpenNMS Minion in one hostNetwork pod (option one above), fixed at one replica. It is a convenience, not a supported deployment, and its own README says so.

For completeness, the work that would put Kubernetes back on the roadmap: Area Change Singleton names Make NETNS_NAME, veth pair names, and bridge CIDR configurable per instance, so multiple simulators can co-exist on a node. Host mutation Move iptables / sysctl / netns setup into a separate init phase that can be done by a host-DaemonSet (or skipped when the host is pre-prepared), so the runtime container does not need CAP_SYS_ADMIN. Routing story Ship a tested recipe for one of Multus / Calico-BGP / hostNetwork co-location, with worked examples and reachability tests. Lifecycle Reconcile terminationGracePeriodSeconds against the FORWARD-rule and netns cleanup so a pod evict does not leak host state. Manifest A Helm chart and / or Kustomize base that declares the privileges, sysctls, fd limits, and node taints needed. None of this is conceptually hard. It is several weeks of focused work and a non-trivial test surface. The value depends on whether anyone actually wants to run a hypervisor-shaped workload in Kubernetes rather than on a dedicated lab host.
documents.s: What it would take to make Kubernetes a first-class target

documents.t: Bare-metal Linux. The canonical environment. Quick start, Scaling. Docker on a single host. Same privileges, isolated filesystem. Docker. Both reach the documented 30k-device scale and exercise the same code paths as a Kubernetes deployment would.

nl6 can tell you what it put on the wire. It cannot tell you what your collector accepted. This page is the method for finding that second number, and for not fooling yourself while you do. The worked example uses OpenNMS Horizon syslog ingest. The method generalises to any push protocol nl6 exports.

A load generator reports what it sent. UDP has no failure signal, so "sent 60,000, failures 0" is true even when the collector received nothing at all. Every claim about capacity therefore needs a second measurement taken on the collector side, and the gap between the two has to be explained rather than assumed.
documents.s: Why a delivered number is not an answer

documents.t: One quantity travels under four names, and conflating them is the most common way this measurement goes wrong. term meaning here work unit whatever the collector processes as one indivisible chunk record, batch, dispatch the same thing, named by whichever layer you are looking at message one datagram nl6 emitted event one row the collector persisted A work unit usually holds several messages. One message does not necessarily become one event: a collector may coalesce or expand. Where the two differ, say so, or the identity check below will fail for a reason you never modelled. The OpenNMS example uses "Core" for the product component and "vCPU" for processor count, because "core" means both.

number what it means how you get it service rate how fast the pipeline drains a backlog offer a burst, then measure the drain sustained ceiling the highest rate the pipeline keeps up with ramp the offered rate, watch the queue slope The second is almost always the one an operator wants, because "can my collector keep up with 30,000 devices?" is a question about steady state. A result must state which one it measured. Define the sustained ceiling as the highest offered rate at which the collector's input queue depth stays bounded over a sustained window. Bounded, not zero: queue depth oscillates normally. The test is the slope. Sample queue depth at a fixed interval across a 15 minute window and fit a line. A slope that stays positive across the whole window means the offered rate is above the ceiling; a slope oscillating around zero means it is at or below. That makes the ceiling a search rather than a single run, and a cell is not finished until its final rate has held flat for the full window. A rate that holds for 60 seconds and degrades at 10 minutes is not a ceiling.
documents.s: Two different numbers, both called "the ceiling"

documents.t: Two measurement points cannot distinguish loss from slowness. Three can. (1) nl6 `sent` what reached the wire | gap = loss between generator and queue (2) queue input what arrived | gap = backlog, or drops inside the collector (3) persisted records what was accepted Point (1) is the report's sent field, which is in_window + drain. It is deliberately not emitted: that also counts send_failures, dropped and suppressed_pre_window, none of which reached the wire, so using it would charge nl6-side non-sends to the network. See the report schema, which names sent as the loss denominator. Report all three. A run that reports only (1) and (3) cannot tell a lossy pipeline from a slow one, and those have opposite fixes. The (1) to (2) gap covers everything between the generator and the queue: datagrams dropped in the network, a receiver whose buffer overran, and any loss inside the collector's own pre-queue path. The (2) to (3) gap is backlog or in-collector drops, and a consumer-side drop counter sits on this segment, not the first.

Loss instruments must read zero on runs that claim a rate: the loss-isolation control and every at-or-below-ceiling cell. They will not read zero while searching above the ceiling, and that is expected. Probing above the ceiling is how the search finds it, and on a UDP path an overrun receiver is the signal you are looking for. An above-ceiling probe with loss is a valid probe; it is not a result.
documents.s: When zero loss is required, and when it is not

documents.t: Run at roughly half the measured ceiling, sustained, with the queue flat throughout. There (1) and (3) must agree within the reconciliation tolerance nl6 itself uses (nl6-reconcile defaults to 0.5%), not bit-exactly: (3) is a database count and carries its own noise. If they do not agree, the pipeline is lossy at any rate. That invalidates the ceiling, rather than annotating it.

Find the collector's equivalents of these before running anything. Without them you are measuring a black box and guessing at the mechanism. you need OpenNMS Horizon equivalent arrival count, point (2) producer-side offset delta on the sink topic queue depth over time Kafka consumer-group LAG for the sink topic work-unit service time ..._sink_consumer_syslog_dispatchtime_* messages per work unit ..._sink_consumer_syslog_messagesize_*, plus offset delta versus messages sent drop counter ..._sink_consumer_syslog_dropped_count accepted count, point (3) windowed, filtered count of the run's events The OpenNMS names are one deployment's rendering, not canonical. The lowercase forms such as dispatchtime and messagesize appear only when the Prometheus JMX exporter runs with lowercaseOutputName: true. Check that setting first if the names do not match. Confirm them on your build before trusting a run, since a rename between versions invalidates a whole session silently. The accepted count must be windowed and filtered. An unqualified select count(*) from events is a lifetime total across every event source, including the collector's own internal events, so it can never match an offered rate. Take a delta across the run window and restrict it to the events the run produced.

throughput = (messages per work unit / service time per work unit) × concurrent workers The worker term matters: on a single-consumer pipeline it is 1 and disappears, but any run that varies parallelism must carry it or the identity under-predicts by exactly the worker count. Service time is wall clock, not CPU, and the difference decides how the identity scales. Where the per-message cost is dominated by waiting (database round trips, network), adding workers overlaps those waits and throughput rises without CPU rising with it. Expect sub-linear scaling. Treat a large gap between predicted and measured as a pointer to the next constraint rather than a broken model. State which statistic you used. The mean and the median give different answers, so a reader replicating your check needs to know which one you meant. If the identity does not reproduce the measured rate, something is missing from the picture, and the ceiling number is not yet understood.

Background emission inflates (3) without touching (1). It is the one failure mode three-point reconciliation cannot self-detect, because it makes the pipeline look like it is running ahead of the load. Start nl6 in fidelity mode, then verify the generator is actually silent before offering load: its sent counter must not move while idle. The report discloses the answer too, in metadata.fidelity. A measurement that skips this check is measuring its own background noise.
documents.s: Before any run: silence the generator

documents.t: Run the cheapest test that can invalidate the most work first. Each gate can end the investigation early, which is a successful outcome. G1 Is service time FIXED per work unit, or proportional to its contents? vary the work-unit size, plot service time |- proportional -> batching is not a lever, drop that axis '- mostly fixed -> batching is the lever G2 Does the collector parallelise when given more partitions? add partitions, re-read the consumer-group assignment |- consumer count unchanged -> that axis is inert, drop it '- consumer count rises -> the axis is real The matrix that follows is not a gate; it is the work these two gates decide the shape of. G2 has two traps, and the second one loses data. First, on Kafka num.partitions only affects newly created topics. Raising it without an explicit --alter on the existing topic changes nothing, which looks exactly like the collector failing to parallelise and would retire a live axis on no evidence. Second, and more serious: the producer starts using new partitions immediately, while a running consumer may never discover them. In the worked example's lab, records written to the new partitions sat unprocessed until the collector restarted. Restart the collector after altering, re-read the assignment, and only then judge the axis. Then confirm the added consumers are distinct instances doing real work rather than one consumer holding several partitions. Do not perform this on a production topic without planning for the restart. Partition counts also cannot be reduced, so the change is one-way. If both gates fail, the honest answer is "this collector's ceiling is X and only a code change moves it". That is worth knowing and costs about an hour.

An aggregate rate does not determine the work the collector sees. Where the collector aggregates per source and flushes on an interval, batch size follows the PER-DEVICE rate: batch size ~ per_device_rate x flush_interval The worked example shows this at a fixed aggregate rate. More devices at the same aggregate rate made the collector slower in that example. That is the opposite of the intuition that a fleet is only a rate. Smaller batches are one candidate cause, but not an established one. The measured service-time fit gives batching about 12 to 30 percent, against a 2.2x difference between the two rows. Two consequences for any result: A ceiling figure is meaningless without the device count and per-device rate that produced it. Report them beside the number, and carry them in the manifest as controls. Comparing two runs at the same aggregate rate but different fleet sizes compares two different workloads, not two configurations.
documents.s: Load shape is a variable, not a detail

documents.t: Declare exactly one independent variable per run. The axes are whichever gates survived, so the cell count follows from them. axis levels (OpenNMS example) survives if A work-unit size the sink's batch-size setting, at three levels G1 passed B consumer parallelism partitions and consumers: 1, 4 G2 passed Both axes gives six cells, one axis gives three, neither gives none. The baseline cell is the untouched configuration, and it is run twice: once first, once last, so drift across the session is visible rather than assumed absent. Discard any cell whose observed messages-per-work-unit drifted materially from its declared level. That cell is not the configuration it claims to be. Note that a queue's batch-size setting is often a soft target rather than a hard cap, so decide and record what "materially" means before running, instead of adjudicating it afterwards. Everything else is a control, and controls belong in the manifest so two runs can be compared: generator version and device count, protocol and message format, collector version, VM sizes, JVM and GC flags, database durability settings, and whether devices are provisioned as nodes. Two runs are comparable only when every control matches and exactly one axis differs.

Gather at run time, never reconstruct afterwards. It must be able to express the result the method demands, which means carrying the three reconciliation counts and the correctness check, not only the tuning: { "measured_quantity": "sustained_ceiling", "sut": { "queue": { "partitions": 1, "batch_setting": "<property>=<value>" }, "consumers": { "count": 1, "assignment": ["syslog-0"] } }, "controls": { "generator_version": "...", "devices": 500, "collector_version": "..." }, "reconciliation": { "sent": 0, "arrived": 0, "persisted": 0, "drop_counters": { "consumer_dropped": 0 }, "loss_isolation_run": { "sent": 0, "persisted": 0, "within_tolerance": true } }, "observed": { "service_time_ms": { "statistic_used": "mean", "p50": 0, "mean": 0, "min": 0, "max": 0 }, "work_unit_size_bytes": { "mean": 0, "max": 0 }, "messages_per_work_unit": 0, "concurrent_workers": 1, "queue_slope": "flat|positive", "ordering_preserved": true } } messages_per_work_unit and service_time_ms are derived controls. If a cell's observed values drifted from its declared level, that cell must be discarded rather than reported.

If a tuning change can alter the collector's output, throughput alone is not a result. Parallelism can reorder events. Message queues typically guarantee order only within a partition. Unless records are keyed by device, raising the partition count lets two messages from one device be processed out of order. For a monitoring system that is semantically loaded, not cosmetic. A linkDown and linkUp pair delivered inverted leaves an interface latched down that is actually up. So the parallelism axis carries a mandatory ordering check: emit a known-ordered per-device sequence and assert the order survives. Where the collector's persisted records cannot reconstruct that sequence, assert instead that all of one source's work units land on a single partition, which is sufficient because the ordering guarantee holds only within a partition. A result showing higher throughput with broken ordering is reported as a regression, not as a gain. Work-unit size changes alter packing rather than order, so that axis carries no equivalent confound, which is a further reason to test it first.

One syslog session against OpenNMS Horizon 36.0.3 shows each step. The lab was a single Minion, a 4 vCPU Core and a single-partition Kafka sink. It is not a tuned production deployment. The first run offered a burst far above capacity and measured the drain. So it reports a service rate, not a sustained ceiling. nl6 --UDP--> Minion --produce--> Kafka --consume--> Core --> Postgres service time p50 29.4 ms | mean 30.0 ms work unit ~4 messages per record model (4 messages / 0.030 s mean) x 1 worker = 133 msg/s measured ~130 events/s drained The identity reproduced the drain. One consumer thread handled about four messages per record at about 30 ms per dispatch. G1 found service time proportional to batch contents, at about 3 ms fixed plus 6.7 ms per message. So n / (3 + 6.7n) approaches 149/s, and batching buys about 12%. G2 at 4 partitions raised the drain to about 320/s. The ordering check then failed. Forty sequential messages from one device became seven work units spread across three partitions. That configuration is reported as a regression, so no tuning-level lever remained. Keying the records by source would be a code change. Load shape changed the work. At a fixed aggregate of about 3,000/s, 500 devices at 6/s gave 4 messages per work unit, and 63 devices at 47/s gave 24. On 500 devices at 4 partitions, the drain was about 144/s at 1.8/s per device and about 320/s at 6/s per device. The identity reproduces neither row, so that mechanism is not understood. Batching explains about 12 to 30 percent of the 2.2x gap by the G1 fit, so most of it has another cause. The shape is measured: capacity depends on per-device rate, not only on the fleet total. Size against what the busiest devices send during an incident, and report the device count and per-device rate beside any figure.

Runbooks for the scenario mechanics each run is built from, including how the offered rate is set Scenarios for the lifecycle and fidelity mode Report schema for sent versus emitted, and what nl6 reports about its own side of the measurement

How far can you trust a value nl6 serves? It depends on where its OID lives. Data Proven Not proven Standard MIB-2 leaves the type table types Encoded at the declared type, as well-formed BER, by three load rules Nothing further is needed: the MIB is public and the objects are standard Interface counters and state, and every metric nl6 computes Computed by the interface engine, the same value on SNMP, gNMI and sFlow at the same instant Traffic shapes other than the sine wave Vendor enterprise subtrees, 5 audited arcs Under the right vendor's number; values read against the vendor's MIB Access modes Vendor enterprise subtrees, 14 labelled arcs Under the right vendor's number Whether the objects below it exist, mean what their values suggest, or are readable. Treat them as plausible-looking test data, not as a model of the device The automatic rules prove only that nl6 will not emit a mistyped BER value. Whether an OID means what the vendor's MIB says is a question only a human reading that MIB can answer. This page explains both halves. The tables of rules, tests and arc dispositions are in SNMP data validation.

Find the OID in the SNMP reference. A standard leaf the type table types has passed the load rules, so its wire type is right. Interface counters and state come from the interface engine, not the file. For an OID under a vendor PEN, look the PEN up in the vendor arc disposition tables. Audited: the value was read against the MIB. Labelled: the resource file part says UNAUDITED-ARC(<pen>) and nobody has checked it. An OID that is wrong against its MIB is a data defect. Report it with the MIB name and the object.

validateSNMPResourceValues runs three rules over the snmp array of every resource file, in the order encodeTypedValue applies them, so the first diagnosis to fire is the one that matches what the wire would do. Rule Leaves Refuses Note 1. Exception sentinels All A value exactly equal to noSuchObject or endOfMibView nl6 carries SNMP exceptions internally as those strings. The match is exact: NoSuchObject or noSuchObject seen is ordinary data 2. OID values OID-typed leaves, today sysObjectID and entPhysicalVendorType A value the encoder cannot represent as an OID 3. Numeric types Counter32, Gauge32, TimeTicks, Counter64, IpAddress A value that does not encode at that type: whitespace, units, hex, fractions, out of range A negative value on a 32-bit unsigned leaf loads with a warning and goes out wrap-cast, so -1 becomes 4294967295. The same -1 on a Counter64 is refused, because that type has no signed fallback Rule 3 is the class that once shipped a real bug: a freeMem entry carrying the device's name went out as an OCTET STRING, and a collector that types the OID as a gauge logged a conversion error on every poll. The full outcome table is in SNMP data validation → Load rules. How the rules run: Every rule calls the production encoder and inspects what it emits. A second predicate would drift from the encoder, and then the loader would accept what the wire refuses, or the other way round. They run on every load path: startup, round-robin creation and REST device creation. A rejection at startup exits the process. Over REST it answers HTTP 400 with the file's base name, the OID and the value; the full path stays in the server log. Round-robin creation fails the call rather than skipping the offending type. See Web API → resource_file failures. What the rules do not reach: A leaf the type table does not type. It is served as INTEGER when the value parses as a number and as OCTET STRING otherwise. Both are legitimate encodings, so a mistyped value on an untyped leaf loads and is served. The OID key. The rules check the value, never whether the name is a legal instance of its table. Semantics. A value that encodes cleanly passes even when the object at that OID is a different object, or does not exist. Access modes. sysName and sysLocation, which are served outside the resource map. sysName derives from the device. sysLocation comes from the worldcities dataset, and a location spelled like an exception sentinel is replaced with Unknown Location. Each of those gaps is covered below by a corpus guard, a hand audit, or a label saying it is open.
documents.s: Resource values are validated at load

documents.t: A varbind name has to be an instance, with exactly as many trailing sub-identifiers as the table's INDEX clause says. Both ways of getting that wrong encode cleanly, so no load rule can see them. Shape Example Legal form Bare column, too few sub-identifiers 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.2.3.1.4, the hrStorageAllocationUnits column …1.4.<index> Over-specified instance, too many …1.2.2.1 under ciscoImageEntry, whose INDEX has one arc …1.2.2 A hand audit deleted 61 such entries from the shipped profiles: 57 bare columns and 4 over-specified instances. Some were vendor columns served by profiles of a different vendor, which the PEN guard below now refuses on its own. Two corpus tests keep the class from growing back: One reads the JSON and reports any shipped OID that another shipped OID extends. The other walks every profile and reports any bare column a walk would emit. Both scan across profiles, not within one, because legality is a property of the OID and not of the profile that carries it. What they cannot see: The detector is a heuristic. "Some other shipped OID extends it" stands in for "it is a column", and fails when the extending sibling is the malformed one. A hit is a candidate to check against the MIB, never a verdict. A bare column that nothing in the corpus extends, an over-specified instance whose legal prefix is absent, or a wrong INDEX arity in general. "The census reads zero" means no shipped entry is an interior node of the shipped set, not that every shipped name is a legal instance. Deleting rows can empty a table. Four profiles lost their only hrStorageTable row in that audit and now model no storage. That is the intended outcome: a collector getting nothing is better than one binding whose name is not a legal instance. Do not restore a row to make a table non-empty.

A trap catalog declares each varbind's ASN.1 type, and the resource snmp array separately determines the type a GET of the same OID answers. One Cisco power-supply description was once sent as a string by a trap and answered as an INTEGER by a poll. A corpus test joins the two surfaces on the OID, per profile, and requires the tag each production encoder emits to match. It reads the merged effective catalog, so the universal catalog and per-type overlays are compared as a device would fire them. A second rule requires one catalog never to declare the same OID at two types. The check is internal consistency only. It asks whether nl6 contradicts itself, never whether nl6 agrees with the vendor. Most trap varbinds name notification objects no profile serves, so the join compares only a handful of pairs.
documents.s: A trap and a poll must agree on type

documents.t: The three load rules answer "will nl6 put a mistyped BER value on the wire". They never answer "is this profile faithful to the MIB". The Palo Alto audit calibrates how much the guards prove: of the 11 Palo Alto enterprise OIDs palo_alto_pa3220 served, 8 were wrong or invalid, and every one passed all three rules. A collector keyed on panMgmtPanoramaConnected got 4194304 where a real PA-3220 answers connected. One keyed on panChassisType got 127 where the MIB defines a DisplayString such as PA-3220. The same audit found twelve profiles that are not Palo Alto devices serving that subtree. Those entries were deleted, not corrected: a vendor enterprise subtree is an identity claim, and a collector keyed on PAN-COMMON-MIB would read an Arista serving it as a firewall. So nl6 answers two separate questions about every vendor subtree. Whose number it sits under, which a guard enforces. Whether the objects under that number mean what the vendor says, which only a human reading the MIB can answer.

A corpus guard walks every shipped profile and requires each enterprise OID it serves to sit under the one IANA private enterprise number its device type belongs to. It reads both positions an enterprise OID can appear in: an OID name, and an OID-typed value such as sysObjectID.0 or entPhysicalVendorType. sysObjectID.0 is the field a collector reads for vendor detection, so a name-only scan would miss the most important case. It covers the dynamic metric OIDs served from Go code, and the compiled-in fallback a device gets when its named resource file is missing. That fallback answers the RFC 5612 documentation PEN instead of claiming to be Cisco hardware. The PEN is matched on a sub-identifier boundary, because PEN 2 is a string prefix of the Huawei, Check Point, Juniper and Palo Alto numbers. An entPhysicalVendorType with no known vendor type answers zeroDotZero (0.0), as RFC 4133 prescribes. A value under the reserved PEN 0 fails the guard like any other foreign arc. The map from device type to PEN is curated by hand from the IANA registry, never derived from name matching. Several correct pairs share no word with their type name: Device type PEN Registered to hpe_proliant_dl380 232 Compaq dell_emc_unity 1139 EMC nokia_7750_sr12 6527 Nokia netapp_ontap 789 Network Appliance ibm_power_s922 2 IBM aws_s3_storage 32473 Documentation PEN. The profile is a category of S3-compatible gateways, and AWS's own S3 has no SNMP surface, so naming Amazon would trade one misattribution for a more plausible one. The exception is allowed for this profile only What the guard does not cover: Whether the objects below a correct PEN mean what the vendor's MIB says, or are readable at all. That is the audit question below. An OID-typed value under the right PEN that resolves to no assignment. One sysObjectID that named no Arista product was found by audit and fixed. The class needs a MIB per arc. A missing identity. Nothing requires a profile to identify itself, only to identify itself truthfully. gNMI, the REST surface and trap catalog snmpTrapEnterprise values. The catalogs were checked by hand and are clean, but no test scans them.
documents.s: Every profile serves its own vendor's PEN and no other

documents.t: Five arcs have been audited by reading the vendor's MIB. Each audit is quoted as a miss rate: distinct OIDs found wrong or unresolvable, out of distinct OIDs read. Vendor PEN Wrong Palo Alto 25461 8 of 11 Cisco 9 11 of 13 Arista 30065 6 of 6 Ciena 1271 0 of 1 Juniper 2636 13 of 15 The pattern is the finding. Four of the five arcs were mostly or entirely wrong. The Ciena result keeps that from becoming a general claim: the corpus is split between data somebody read a MIB for and data nobody did. The errors fall into a few shapes, and an unaudited arc can contain any of them: A value of the wrong kind, such as a number where the MIB declares a DisplayString, or a percentage outside its declared range. An OID that is not a valid object at all, such as a child under a leaf scalar, or a value on an OBJECT-IDENTITY container. A wrong INDEX arity: a table served with a scalar .0 instance, or with too few index arcs. A sysObjectID that names the wrong product. One Juniper profile identified itself as a different chassis in the same family, so vendor detection succeeded and was wrong. An object that exists but is not readable, covered in Access modes are not modelled. A whole vendor subtree on the wrong vendor's device, which the PEN guard refuses. Audit fixes either correct a value against the MIB or delete the entry. An entry is deleted when no correct readable value exists, or when the right sub-identifiers could not be resolved from the MIB. Each audit is pinned by a test that records the reading. That is a record, not a live verification: no MIB file is checked in, and nothing in CI compares nl6 against a vendor MIB. NVIDIA's PEN 5703 is in the audited set for a different reason. NVIDIA publishes no SNMP GPU MIB, so every object below that PEN is nl6's own definition, documented in the GPU collector OID contract.
documents.s: Vendor arc audits and miss rates

documents.t: Every enterprise arc a shipped profile serves is exactly one of three things, and a test fails by name on any arc that is none of them. State Meaning Marker Audited Somebody read the vendor's MIB A test that records the reading Labelled Nobody has UNAUDITED-ARC(<pen>) in the _comment of every resource file part that carries the arc Excluded Not a vendor claim, such as the documentation PEN on aws_s3_storage A row in the excluded pairs table That is what stops the corpus regrowing silent, unchecked vendor data: a new device type that serves a vendor subtree and is none of the three fails the suite. Fourteen arcs are labelled rather than audited. Nothing in this repository reads them: no published polling rule, no trap varbind and no doc keys on any of them. At the observed miss rates, auditing them would be weeks of work whose main output is deleting data nothing reads. If you key a collector on one of them, that arc is a candidate for an audit. Each label states: that the objects under the PEN have not been read against any of the vendor's MIBs, that the PEN itself is checked, so what is unverified sits below the number, what "unverified" covers: whether each object is defined, whether the value matches its SYNTAX, and whether the object is readable, the audited miss rates, so a reader can calibrate. The marker is per file part and carries the PEN, so every file a reader might open says so, and a labelled arc does not excuse a second, unlabelled arc in the same file. git grep UNAUDITED-ARC lists every labelled part. A staleness check fails a marker naming a PEN its part no longer serves, and a marker on an arc that has since been audited. No test can check that a label is true, because no test can read a MIB. What the test refuses is the fourth state: a vendor subtree that reads as checked because nothing says otherwise.
documents.s: Every arc is audited, labelled, or explicitly excluded

documents.t: No nl6 rule models MAX-ACCESS. The load rules check encodability, the PEN guard checks vendor identity, and the audit tests check names, types and values. None of them can see that an object is write-only or not-accessible, because an access mode is a property of the MIB and nl6 has no MIB. One instance has been found and fixed. Two Cisco profiles served writeMem from OLD-CISCO-SYSTEM-MIB as a readable integer: the object exists, the arc is right and the value encoded, so every guard passed it. It is write-only, and a command rather than a datum: writing it saves the configuration, and writing 0 erases it. The entries were deleted, since a write-only object has no correct readable value. The class is open: any unaudited arc may still contain objects a real device would refuse to read. For how the agent answers a request, see the SNMP reference. For writing your own profiles, see resource files.

The labmonkeys.nl6 Ansible collection installs nl6 from its native package and runs it under systemd. Its one role, nl6, downloads the .deb or .rpm for the host from the GitHub release and verifies it against the release checksums.txt. It installs the package with apt or dnf, so ip, iptables and sysctl resolve as package dependencies. It then sets the sysctls, writes /etc/nl6/nl6.conf and enables the packaged nl6.service. Platform Package Package manager Debian 13, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS nl6_<version>_<arch>.deb apt CentOS Stream 10, Rocky Linux 10, AlmaLinux 10 nl6-<version>-1.<arch>.rpm dnf Both amd64 (x86_64) and arm64 (aarch64) are supported. Any other host fails before the role downloads anything. That includes other Debian and Ubuntu releases, interim Ubuntu releases such as 24.10, and derivatives such as Linux Mint and Oracle Linux. Install the package by hand there. It installs the same package as Install packages. It also sets the sysctls and runs the checks below, which the manual install leaves to you.

Pick the simulator interface. nl6_net_interface is required. It names the host NIC that faces the simulated network, and the role fails if it does not exist. Check the FORWARD policy. Traffic from a collector to the simulated devices needs the iptables FORWARD policy to be ACCEPT. Docker and ufw set it to DROP, and the role fails then. See Firewall rules. Check firewalld. If firewalld is active, configure it to forward between the collector and the simulated network. The role warns when firewalld is active but cannot check its policy. Allow internet access, or use a mirror. Each run fetches checksums.txt from github.com. See Internet access.

The collection lives in the nl6 repository under deploy/ansible. Install it by git tag: ansible-galaxy collection install 'git+https://github.com/labmonkeys-space/nl6.git#/deploy/ansible,vX.Y.Z' Or list it in requirements.yml: collections: - name: https://github.com/labmonkeys-space/nl6.git#/deploy/ansible type: git version: vX.Y.Z The collection version always equals the nl6 release. Collection X.Y.Z runs nl6 vX.Y.Z by default. Releases older than the collection have no deploy/ansible directory. If ansible-galaxy reports that the path does not exist at your tag, that release predates the collection. Install from main instead by replacing vX.Y.Z with main.
- hosts: simulator become: true roles: - role: labmonkeys.nl6.nl6 nl6_net_interface: enp2s0 The play ends by polling the nl6 API and prints the version that answered.

Variable Default Meaning nl6_version the collection version nl6 release without the v. nl6_package_url "" Download URL of the .deb or .rpm, for an air-gapped host or a local mirror. Replaces the GitHub release URL. nl6_package_checksum "" sha256:<hex digest> of the package. Required when nl6_package_url is set, ignored otherwise. nl6_web_port 8080 REST API port. nl6_gnmi_tls true The gNMI dial-in listener (port 9339) is TLS-only. Set false for a plaintext collector. nl6_net_interface "" Required. Host NIC facing the simulated network. The role fails if it does not exist. nl6_pyroscope_url "" Adds -profiling-pyroscope=<url> when set. nl6_extra_args [] Extra CLI flags appended to NL6_OPTS. One flag or value per element.

Wrong interface. With a bad nl6_net_interface the sysctls below land on nothing and device traffic is dropped silently. The role asserts the interface exists. Unverified download. The package is checked against the release checksums.txt. A custom nl6_package_url needs an explicit nl6_package_checksum. Reverse-path filtering. The role sets net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 and rp_filter=0 for all and for nl6_net_interface. Crash loop. Restart=on-failure turns a rejected argument into a restart loop while systemd reports "started". The role polls /api/v1/version for up to 60 s and fails if nl6 does not answer. Unusable extra args. See NL6_OPTS word-splitting. Version bump. See A version bump wipes the fleet.

nl6 keeps devices in memory only. The package postinstall runs systemctl try-restart nl6.service, so installing a different version restarts nl6 and every simulated device disappears. The role reads the installed version with dpkg-query or rpm -q and prints a warning when nl6 is installed and active and the version differs from nl6_version. To keep the fleet, save it with fleet.sh export before you change nl6_version. Replay it with fleet.sh import after the play finishes.
documents.s: A version bump wipes the fleet

documents.t: A change to /etc/nl6/nl6.conf restarts nl6 through a handler, which also wipes the fleet.

nl6 inserts a FORWARD ACCEPT rule for its own veth when it sets up its network namespace. That rule covers traffic leaving the namespace only. See Network namespace for the rule itself. Traffic from a collector to the devices relies on the FORWARD chain policy being ACCEPT, which is true on a stock Ubuntu cloud image. Docker and ufw set the policy to DROP. The role reads iptables -S FORWARD and fails when the policy is not ACCEPT. On such a host, allow forwarding to and from the simulated network yourself, or set the policy, before running the role. firewalld filters forwarded traffic in its own nftables table, which iptables -S FORWARD does not show. On a firewalld host the FORWARD check can pass while firewalld still drops collector traffic. The role prints a WARNING when firewalld.service is active and continues. The role installs no firewall rules and no routes, so routing into the simulated network is up to you.
Each run fetches checksums.txt from github.com, so the host needs internet access. Set nl6_package_url and nl6_package_checksum to use a mirror instead.
In check mode the role skips the package install, the FORWARD policy read and the FORWARD policy assert. The other asserts still run.

The unit runs nl6 $NL6_OPTS with EnvironmentFile=-/etc/nl6/nl6.conf. systemd splits the value on whitespace and has no quoting or escaping there. An element of nl6_extra_args therefore cannot contain whitespace, and the role also rejects ", $ and %, which break the quoted assignment or get expanded. Pass each flag and each value as its own list element, for example ["-auto-count", "5"]. nl6_pyroscope_url is checked the same way.
The role configures push mode only. Go allows one CPU profile at a time, so while the SDK pushes, a puller asking /debug/pprof/profile gets a 500. See Profiling.
Install packages to install the same package by hand. Fleet to export and replay a fleet across restarts. CLI flags for everything you can put in nl6_extra_args.

Out of the box you address simulated devices by their 10.42.x.x management IPs. With the CoreDNS sidecar you can resolve them by name instead, with forward <device-name>.nl6.local records and reverse PTRs. The records update automatically as devices come and go. nl6 runs an authoritative DNS server as a hidden primary; a stock CoreDNS runs as a secondary, transferring the zones via AXFR and refreshing on NOTIFY. No custom CoreDNS plugin. dig @localhost ──► CoreDNS :53 (secondary) ──AXFR/NOTIFY──► nl6 :5353 (primary) derived from the live device set Forward <device-name>.nl6.local → device management IP Reverse <ip> (PTR) → ip4.mgmt.<device-name>.nl6.local, which resolves forward to the same IP (round-trips)
Docker with Compose v2 (docker compose). The sidecar stack runs nl6 in a container, so you don't need host TUN/netns setup. See Docker. dig (or any DNS client) and curl on the host to verify.

The repo ships a ready-to-run stack at examples/coredns-sidecar/: git clone https://github.com/labmonkeys-space/nl6 cd nl6/examples/coredns-sidecar docker compose up -d It auto-starts a 10-device demo fleet (10.42.0.1 to 10.42.0.10) with the DNS subsystem enabled. On every device create/delete nl6 bumps the zone serial (debounced ~1s) and NOTIFYs CoreDNS, which re-transfers. The nl6 service runs with these DNS flags (see the CLI flags for the full set): command: - -dns-enable - -dns-domain=nl6.local - -dns-reverse-zone=42.10.in-addr.arpa - -dns-notify=coredns:53 …and the CoreDNS Corefile is a stock secondary block per zone: nl6.local:53 { secondary { transfer from nl6:5353 } log errors } 42.10.in-addr.arpa:53 { secondary { transfer from nl6:5353 } log errors }

# List the running fleet to pick a real name/IP (names are random per run): curl -s localhost:8080/api/v1/devices | jq -r '.data[].ip' dig @localhost -p 5353 nl6.local AXFR | grep ' A ' # the forward names + IPs # Reverse against CoreDNS (host :53): dig @localhost -x 10.42.0.5 +short # 10.42.0.5 -> ip4.mgmt.<name>.nl6.local. # Take the device name from that PTR, then resolve it forward: NAME=$(dig @localhost -x 10.42.0.5 +short | sed 's/^ip4\.mgmt\.//') dig @localhost "$NAME" +short # <name>.nl6.local. -> 10.42.0.5 # Publish + NOTIFY counters: curl -s localhost:8080/api/v1/dns/status | jq Names are synthesised. nl6 generates each device's sysName randomly, so the exact forward names change per run. Read them from the AXFR (dig @localhost -p 5353 nl6.local AXFR) or from /api/v1/devices. Duplicate names are disambiguated deterministically (lowest IP keeps the bare label).

Creating or deleting a device marks the zones dirty. A debounced worker waits for a quiescence window (-dns-debounce, default 1s), then bumps the SOA serial once and NOTIFYs each secondary. A large batch therefore coalesces into a single transfer rather than one per device. Try it: # Create a device, then watch the serial advance and CoreDNS pick it up. curl -s -XPOST localhost:8080/api/v1/devices \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"device_count":1,"start_ip":"10.42.0.50"}' curl -s localhost:8080/api/v1/dns/status | jq '.zones, .zone_bumps'

Different domain / subnets. Change -dns-domain and -dns-reverse-zone on the nl6 service, and add/rename the matching secondary blocks in the Corefile. A CoreDNS secondary needs one block per zone. Device IPs outside every configured reverse zone resolve forward-only (no PTR). No NOTIFY. Drop -dns-notify; CoreDNS still picks up changes on its SOA refresh interval, but less promptly.
DNS service discovery reference covers the full naming scheme, flags, zone boundaries, and operational caveats.

The simulator is published as a single container image at ghcr.io/labmonkeys-space/nl6, built from the root Dockerfile and pushed to the GitHub Container Registry. A release tag pushes :<version> and moves :latest; every push to main refreshes the floating :rc tag.

docker pull ghcr.io/labmonkeys-space/nl6:latest # The simulator needs TUN + netns privileges: NET_ADMIN to create interfaces # and SYS_ADMIN to enter the namespace (setns). --network=host isn't strictly # required but makes the HTTP control plane reachable on :8080 directly. docker run --rm -it \ --cap-add=NET_ADMIN \ --cap-add=SYS_ADMIN \ --device=/dev/net/tun \ --network=host \ ghcr.io/labmonkeys-space/nl6:latest \ -auto-start-ip 192.168.100.1 -auto-count 10 Host FORWARD policy. On hosts with Docker installed, the default FORWARD chain in iptables is DROP. The simulator inserts a FORWARD -i veth-sim-host -j ACCEPT rule at startup so per-device flow exporters can reach external collectors. On clean shutdown the rule is removed. See Flow export → Prerequisites.
# Host platform make docker-build # Multi-platform, pushed to the registry make docker-push The docker-push target pushes linux/amd64 + linux/arm64. Override the tag list with DOCKER_TAGS="...".

make docker-up # docker compose up --build make docker-down # docker compose down compose.yml runs two services: simulator: the image above with NET_ADMIN, SYS_ADMIN and /dev/net/tun, publishing 8080 (control plane) and 161/udp. Flags go in as CMD overrides: docker compose run simulator -auto-start-ip 192.168.100.1 -auto-count 5. bootstrapper: waits for the simulator's healthcheck, replays inventory/devices.json through the REST API with scripts/fleet.sh, then exits. No manifest is a clean no-op; copy inventory/devices.example.json to inventory/devices.json to opt in. The simulator has no on-disk persistence, so the manifest is what survives compose down && compose up.

A fleet is the set of devices a running nl6 simulator hosts. The scripts/fleet.sh helper captures a fleet to a JSON file (export) and replays it into another simulator (import). Use it to move an interesting test topology between hosts, snapshot a long-running scale lab before a redeploy, or ship a reproducible inventory alongside a bug report. For the underlying REST surface see Web API.
A running nl6 simulator with its REST API reachable (default :8080). curl and jq on the host running fleet.sh.

Capture the current device inventory from a running simulator: scripts/fleet.sh export http://sim-a:8080 nl6-inventory.json Expected output (from scripts/fleet.sh), with <version> and <N> filled in by your simulator: Probing nl6 version at http://sim-a:8080 ... {"version":"<version>"} Fetching device inventory ... <N> devices written to nl6-inventory.json The output is the raw GET /api/v1/devices response. It holds one entry per device with its ip, resource_file, snmp_port, any configured flow, traps, syslog and gnmi_dialout blocks, and any if_error_scenario, if_flap_scenario and optical_scenario set at creation. Import carries all of these to the target simulator. Server-assigned and read-only fields (id, interface, running, ssh_port, device_type, effective_intervals and the location fields) stay in the file for reference and are dropped on import. Import does not carry snmpv3 or write_community, because the device listing never returns them. Set them again on the target simulator if the fleet uses them. Import stops at the first device the target refuses. Two cases are refused on another simulator: A flow, traps, syslog or gnmi_dialout collector whose host does not resolve on the target. A gnmi_dialout block whose tls.ca_pem is over 64 KiB. A CA bundle loaded with -gnmi-dialout-tls-ca can be that large, while a create request is capped at 64 KiB. To import a fleet whose dial-out blocks are refused, drop them first: jq 'del(.data[].gnmi_dialout)' nl6-inventory.json > nl6-inventory-no-dialout.json If the file argument is omitted, nl6-inventory.json in the current directory is used.

Replay an inventory file against another simulator: scripts/fleet.sh import http://sim-b:8080 nl6-inventory.json --netmask 16 Expected output (from scripts/fleet.sh) for a file written by export, with <N> as the device count: Importing <N> entries (shape: get-response) to http://sim-b:8080/api/v1/devices Done. <N> entries imported. --netmask is a prefix length and defaults to 16, the flat 10.42.0.0/16 management plane the fleet now uses. POST /api/v1/devices accepts only 8, 16, or 24 (a dotted mask like 255.255.0.0 is rejected with 400), and the GET response does not echo a netmask, so import supplies one. Dotted netmask in an inventory file. A batch-manifest file ([{start_ip,...}]) is posted verbatim, so --netmask does not apply to it. An entry carrying its own dotted netmask field (e.g. from an older export) is rejected with 400. Regenerate the export, or rewrite the field to a prefix length (16). Import auto-detects the file shape: File shape Behavior {data:[{ip,...},...]} (export output) One POST per device, preserving per-device flow / traps / syslog [{start_ip, device_count,...},...] One POST per batch, for compact range manifests like inventory/devices.example.json

# Snapshot the source scripts/fleet.sh export http://sim-a:8080 my-fleet.json # Replay against a fresh target scripts/fleet.sh import http://sim-b:8080 my-fleet.json A 58-device sample lives at inventory/nl6-inventory.json. Drop it into any empty simulator to populate a heterogeneous fleet spanning many of the 31 device types nl6 ships with.
documents.s: Copy a fleet to another simulator

documents.t: Fail-fast, except on 409. The first failed POST aborts the run, so a partial import is obvious. The one exception is 409 Conflict, which means another creation batch holds the simulator's one-batch-at-a-time gate, not that anything is wrong with the request: import waits and retries that entry (RETRY_409_LIMIT, default 60 attempts; RETRY_409_DELAY, default 5s, for 5 minutes in total). Aborting there would be worse than waiting, because it is reachable on a normal boot: with -auto-start-ip the startup batch holds the gate while the container is already healthy, which is exactly when compose up runs this import. Raise RETRY_409_LIMIT if your startup batch takes longer than five minutes. A duplicate IP is not a 409. The simulator absorbs an already-present address as a success. Sequential POSTs. Each device or batch is POSTed in series, no parallelism. For very large fleets prefer the batch-manifest shape. One POST can create many devices via device_count. Server-assigned fields dropped. id, interface, and running are produced by the simulator at device-attach time and are not part of the POST surface.

Prebuilt native packages let you install nl6 with your system package manager and run it as a managed systemd service. You need no Go toolchain or source checkout. Platform Format Package manager Debian, Ubuntu .deb apt CentOS Stream, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux .rpm dnf NixOS flake nix Both amd64 and arm64 builds are published. The .deb/.rpm packages are attached to each GitHub Release; NixOS consumes the flake directly from the repository.

Path Contents /usr/bin/nl6 the simulator binary /usr/share/nl6/resources/ device resource data (SNMP/SSH/REST) /usr/share/nl6/web/ web console assets /usr/share/nl6/worldcities/ world-cities dataset for sysLocation (CC BY 4.0) /usr/lib/systemd/system/nl6.service the systemd unit /etc/nl6/nl6.conf flag file (NL6_OPTS), preserved across upgrades Runtime requirements. The simulator runs as root because it creates TUN interfaces, manages the nl6sim network namespace, and installs an iptables rule. The iproute2 (ip), iptables, and procps (sysctl) dependencies are pulled in automatically by apt/dnf.

Tested on Debian 13, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (amd64 and arm64). Download the .deb for your architecture from the latest release: nl6_<version>_amd64.deb or nl6_<version>_arm64.deb. Install it (the leading ./ tells apt it is a local file, so it still resolves dependencies): sudo apt install ./nl6_<version>_amd64.deb Continue with Configure and start the service.

Tested on Rocky Linux 10 and AlmaLinux 10 (amd64 and arm64). CentOS Stream 10 is not in the smoke matrix. Download the .rpm for your architecture from the latest release: nl6-<version>-1.x86_64.rpm or nl6-<version>-1.aarch64.rpm. Install it: sudo dnf install ./nl6-<version>-1.x86_64.rpm Continue with Configure and start the service.

The package installs the nl6 systemd unit but does not enable or start it automatically. The simulator needs root and operator-chosen flags first. These steps are the same on Debian/Ubuntu and the RHEL family. The unit ships with LimitNOFILE=1048576, so a packaged install needs no file-descriptor tuning. Set the flags. NL6_OPTS is passed verbatim to nl6; see the CLI flags reference for the full list. sudoedit /etc/nl6/nl6.conf # /etc/nl6/nl6.conf NL6_OPTS="-port 8080 -auto-start-ip 10.42.0.1 -auto-count 100" Enable on boot and start now: sudo systemctl enable --now nl6 Verify it is running: systemctl status nl6 journalctl -u nl6 -f # follow logs nl6 -version # prints the installed version curl -s localhost:8080/api/v1/version Expected output of the last command (from versionHandler in go/nl6/web.go), with your installed version: {"version":"<version>"} After editing /etc/nl6/nl6.conf, apply changes with sudo systemctl restart nl6. Running without the service. nl6 loads resources/ and web/ relative to its working directory. To run it by hand instead of via the service, start it from the data directory: cd /usr/share/nl6 && sudo nl6 -port 8080

# Upgrade (a running service is restarted automatically onto the new binary) sudo apt install ./nl6_<new-version>_amd64.deb # Debian/Ubuntu sudo dnf upgrade ./nl6-<new-version>-1.x86_64.rpm # RHEL family # Remove (your /etc/nl6/nl6.conf is left in place) sudo apt remove nl6 # Debian/Ubuntu sudo dnf remove nl6 # RHEL family

nl6 ships a flake exposing a package and a NixOS module. The recommended way to run it on NixOS is the module. It is fully declarative, needs no cachix CLI, and (with the cache below) installs the prebuilt binary instead of compiling. Add the flake input, the binary cache, and the service to your system flake. Because your system is already flake-based, no experimental-feature flags or extra tools are needed: { inputs.nl6.url = "github:labmonkeys-space/nl6?dir=deploy/packages/nix"; outputs = { self, nixpkgs, nl6 }: { nixosConfigurations.myhost = nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem { system = "x86_64-linux"; modules = [ nl6.nixosModules.nl6 { # Prebuilt binary cache: substitutes instead of compiling. # System-level settings are trusted, so no `cachix use` needed. nix.settings = { substituters = [ "https://nl6.cachix.org" ]; trusted-public-keys = [ "nl6.cachix.org-1:nfaq8JEbMcARjzc/oPyNIrcQrXKe13phUtMg0RucnLA=" ]; }; services.nl6 = { enable = true; extraFlags = [ "-port" "8080" "-auto-start-ip" "10.42.0.1" "-auto-count" "100" ]; }; } ]; }; }; } Rebuild: sudo nixos-rebuild switch. The service is now managed by systemd (systemctl status nl6).

To build or run the package directly with the nix CLI, that CLI needs the nix-command and flakes experimental features. If you see experimental Nix feature 'nix-command' is disabled, enable them in configuration.nix: nix.settings.experimental-features = [ "nix-command" "flakes" ]; then sudo nixos-rebuild switch (or, for a one-off, prepend nix --extra-experimental-features 'nix-command flakes' …). After that: nix build "github:labmonkeys-space/nl6?dir=deploy/packages/nix#nl6" --accept-flake-config --accept-flake-config lets Nix use the cache the flake advertises, but only for trusted users (root or trusted-users). If you are not trusted, use the declarative nix.settings cache from step 1 instead.

If a release does not yet carry packages for your platform, or you want to build from a specific commit, produce them locally with make packages (needs Go; nfpm is fetched automatically): make packages # → dist/*.deb and dist/*.rpm for amd64 + arm64 The full packaging reference lives in deploy/packages/README.md. It covers the layout, nfpm.yaml, the NixOS flake/module, the Cachix cache, and the container-based install smoke test.

Install with Ansible to install the .deb and start the service from a playbook. Docker to run the published container image instead. Quick start to build and run from source. CLI flags for everything you can put in NL6_OPTS.
Get a small fleet of simulated devices running on a Linux host in three commands. For full flag docs see CLI flags; for container workflows see Docker.

Linux host with root access (TUN interface and network-namespace creation require privileges). Go 1.27 or later. The canonical version is pinned in go/go.mod. Basic networking tools: ip, iptables. net-snmp client tools (snmpget, snmpwalk, snmpset) to poll and write to the devices. On Debian and Ubuntu these are the snmp package. Skip host setup. For a zero-prerequisite path, run the published container image. See Docker. The image bundles the dependencies and TUN/TAP support. On bare metal, install the prerequisites above; for large fleets see the host tuning in Scaling.

git clone https://github.com/labmonkeys-space/nl6.git cd nl6 make build GOARCH=$(go env GOARCH) cd go/nl6 The Makefile defaults to GOARCH=amd64, so passing the host architecture keeps the binary runnable on an arm64 host. make build stamps the version into the binary and writes it to go/nl6/nl6.

# Server only. Create devices later via the REST API. sudo ./nl6 # Auto-create 5 devices starting from 192.168.100.1 on a flat /16 (the default). sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 192.168.100.1 -auto-count 5 Once the simulator is up, open the web UI at http://localhost:8080/ or drive it via the REST API. See Web API.

# SNMP v2c query against the first auto-created device snmpget -v2c -c public 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0 # Walk interface table snmpwalk -v2c -c public 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1 # SSH (VT100 terminal emulation). Password: simadmin ssh simadmin@192.168.100.1 See SNMP reference for the protocol coverage and the dynamic HC counter layout.

Change device state: Enable SNMP SET to shut and unshut an interface over SNMP. Writes are off by default. Scale up: Scaling covers the 30k-device tuning. Flow export: Flow export how-to to plug nl6 into a NetFlow / IPFIX / sFlow collector. Device types: Device types lists the 31 simulated device types across 9 categories.

nl6 serves SetRequest at SNMPv1, v2c and v3, on one writable object: ifAdminStatus. That is enough to shut and unshut a simulated interface from a collector and watch the link telemetry that follows. Writes are off by default A stock fleet answers no SET at any version. snmpset against it reports Timeout: No Response, not an SNMP error, because a refused write is discarded rather than answered. That is what real hardware does with a community it does not accept. The device logs the reason once. If snmpset times out while snmpget works, that log line is the answer. Two separate gates, one per protocol family. A v3 message carries no community and a v1/v2c message carries no security level, so you configure whichever applies to the version you poll with. Version Gate Default v1, v2c a write community empty, so no write is admitted v3 a minimum security level authNoPriv

Start the simulator with a write community. It is separate from the read community, which nl6 never checks. Nothing validates the value, so keep it to characters your shell will not reinterpret when you pass it to snmpset. sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 192.168.100.1 -auto-count 5 \ -snmp-write-community s3cret Every device in that fleet now accepts a SET carrying s3cret: snmpset -v2c -c s3cret 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.2 i 2 Reads are unaffected and still need no community match, so snmpget -c public keeps working. The asymmetry is deliberate: a SET changes state, a poll does not.
documents.s: Enable writes for the whole fleet over SNMPv1 and v2c

documents.t: Add an engine ID to turn SNMPv3 on. The shipped defaults already reach the default minimum, so nothing else is needed: sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 192.168.100.1 -auto-count 5 \ -snmpv3-engine-id 800000090300AABBCCDD -snmpv3-auth defaults to md5, which reaches authNoPriv, and the minimum for a SET is authNoPriv. The user and password both default to simadmin: snmpset -v3 -l authNoPriv -u simadmin -a MD5 -A simadmin \ 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.2 i 2 To require encryption as well, raise the minimum and give the fleet a privacy protocol. Both are needed: a minimum the fleet cannot reach admits nothing. sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 192.168.100.1 -auto-count 5 \ -snmpv3-engine-id 800000090300AABBCCDD \ -snmpv3-auth sha1 -snmpv3-priv aes128 \ -snmp-set-min-security-level priv snmpset -v3 -l authPriv -u simadmin -a SHA -A simadmin -x AES -X simadmin \ 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.2 i 2 Running with -snmpv3-auth none leaves no reachable level at or above the default minimum, so no v3 SET is admitted at all. The startup log says so in the line that begins SNMP write admission.
documents.s: Enable writes for the whole fleet over SNMPv3

documents.t: Devices created over the REST API carry their own admission settings. Wait for the auto-start batch to finish. Only one device-creation batch runs at a time, and -auto-start-ip counts as one. A POST /api/v1/devices issued while the fleet is still coming up is refused with 409 Conflict and a Retry-After header. Poll GET /api/v1/status and wait for create_batch_in_progress to clear, or retry. curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "start_ip": "192.168.200.1", "device_count": 1, "netmask": "16", "write_community": "device-secret", "snmpv3": { "enabled": true, "engine_id": "800000090300AABBCCDD", "username": "simadmin", "password": "simadmin", "auth_protocol": 1, "set_min_security_level": "auth" } }' auth_protocol is 0 for none, 1 for MD5, 2 for SHA1. set_min_security_level takes none, auth or priv, and auth is already the default. It is spelled out above so the field is visible, not because omitting it would change anything. Raising it to priv needs a privacy protocol on the same block, or the device admits no v3 SET at all: "auth_protocol": 2, "priv_protocol": 2, "priv_password": "simadmin", "set_min_security_level": "priv" priv_protocol is 0 for none, 1 for DES, 2 for AES128. Either version then works against that device alone: snmpset -v2c -c device-secret 192.168.200.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.2 i 2 snmpset -v3 -l authNoPriv -u simadmin -a MD5 -A simadmin \ 192.168.200.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.2 i 2 A REST-created device does not inherit -snmp-write-community, and its write community is never echoed back. The rules are in SNMP → Write admission for a SET.
documents.s: Enable writes on a single device

documents.t: ifAdminStatus.<N> is 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.<N>, where <N> is the ifIndex. The values are up(1), down(2) and testing(3). Its read-only companion ifOperStatus.<N> is 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.<N>, and the examples read both back so you can see the derivation below at work. Walk the column first to see which interfaces a device has: snmpwalk -v2c -c public 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7 On the default profile that returns 48 interfaces, all administratively up: IF-MIB::ifAdminStatus.1 = INTEGER: up(1) IF-MIB::ifAdminStatus.2 = INTEGER: up(1) ... IF-MIB::ifAdminStatus.48 = INTEGER: up(1) The examples below use ifIndex 2, which on that profile is TenGigE0/0/0/0. Interface numbering is a property of the device profile, so check the walk before picking an index on a fleet created with the REST field round_robin: true or from your own resource files.

# Shut interface 2 snmpset -v2c -c s3cret 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.2 i 2 # Read both columns back snmpget -v2c -c public 192.168.100.1 \ 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.2 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.2 Expected output, since down(2) forces ifOperStatus (deriveOper in go/nl6/interface_state.go): IF-MIB::ifAdminStatus.2 = INTEGER: down(2) IF-MIB::ifOperStatus.2 = INTEGER: down(2) SNMPv1 works the same way with -v1, but reports fewer distinct errors. See when a write is refused.

# Shut interface 2 snmpset -v3 -l authNoPriv -u simadmin -a MD5 -A simadmin \ 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.2 i 2 # Read both columns back snmpget -v3 -l authNoPriv -u simadmin -a MD5 -A simadmin 192.168.100.1 \ 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.2 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.2

Shutting an interface moves ifOperStatus too, stamps ifLastChange, and pushes an update to any gNMI ON_CHANGE subscriber. The gNMI listener is on by default, so that part needs no extra flag. Link traps and syslog need a collector. The state change also fires the device's link-down trap and syslog message, but only on a device that has somewhere to send them. None of the startup commands above configure one, so nothing is emitted. To watch the telemetry, start the fleet with a collector address: sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 192.168.100.1 -auto-count 5 \ -snmp-write-community s3cret \ -trap-collector 127.0.0.1:1162 \ -syslog-collector 127.0.0.1:1514 Shutting an interface then sends linkDown, and unshutting it sends linkUp. Re-enabling does not always bring the interface back up. ifOperStatus is derived from ifAdminStatus and a modelled link state, and a SET of up(1) releases it to the link rather than forcing it up. On an interface whose link is down, the write succeeds and ifOperStatus still reads 2. A fleet started with -if-scenario 3 behaves this way on every interface. The derivation rule is in SNMP → The writable set.
documents.s: What the device does with it

documents.t: Symptom Cause Timeout: No Response under v1 or v2c Most often a wrong write community, or none configured. A timeout is also what an unreachable address, a fleet still starting, or a blocked port 161 looks like, so confirm snmpget works against the same device first. Unsupported security level under v3 The request is below the minimum. Raise the request's level, or lower -snmp-set-min-security-level. notWritable The OID is not ifAdminStatus. It is the only writable object. wrongValue The value is outside up(1), down(2), testing(3). wrongType The value is not an INTEGER. noCreation The ifIndex does not exist on that device, or the name has the wrong number of sub-identifiers. SNMPv1 has a smaller set of error values, so those four collapse under -v1: wrongValue and wrongType both report badValue, while notWritable and noCreation both report noSuchName.

Every boot prints the policy in one line, before any device exists. A boot with -snmp-write-community and -snmpv3-engine-id set prints: SNMP write admission (auto-start batch; REST-created devices use the create body, not these flags) — v1/v2c SET: admitted with the configured write community; v3 SET: minimum security level authNoPriv Grep the startup output for SNMP write admission. It reports what the auto-start batch got, so it is the fastest way to tell a configuration mistake from a network one.

Earlier releases admitted a write from any manager that could reach the port. To get that back: sudo ./nl6 -snmpv3-engine-id 800000090300AABBCCDD \ -snmp-write-community public -snmp-set-min-security-level none That makes every simulated device writable by anything that can route to it. The v3 half only matters when -snmpv3-engine-id is set; without it SNMPv3 is off and -snmp-set-min-security-level changes nothing. It is reasonable on an isolated lab network and when a harness predates the gates. It is not a setting to carry into a shared environment.

SNMP reference for the full SetRequest error ladder and the write-admission rules. CLI flags for every flag used above. Web API for the REST control plane, including POST /api/v1/devices/{ip}/interfaces/{ifIndex}/admin-status, which does the same job over HTTP.

nl6 can emit synthetic flow telemetry to any NetFlow v5 (Cisco), NetFlow v9 (RFC 3954), IPFIX (RFC 7011), or sFlow v5 collector. Each device generates flows appropriate to its role. An edge router emits different traffic shapes than a firewall or a data-center switch. This page is the operator-facing setup guide. For the CLI flags see CLI flags → Flow export; for protocol-level details and the sFlow caveat see Flow export reference.

By default, each device binds its own UDP socket inside the nl6sim namespace, so the collector sees flow packets arriving from the device's IP rather than the simulator host's. This is what makes per-device attribution work on collectors that key on the exporter source IP (OpenNMS, Elastiflow, nfcapd, etc.). Disable it by setting -flow-source-per-device=false. That falls back to a shared socket bound in the host namespace, one per (collector, protocol) pair.

# NetFlow v9 to a local collector on port 2055 sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 10.0.0.1 -auto-count 100 \ -flow-collector 192.168.1.10:2055 # IPFIX instead (port 4739 is the IPFIX default) sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 10.0.0.1 -auto-count 100 \ -flow-collector 192.168.1.10:4739 -flow-protocol ipfix # NetFlow v5 (Cisco; 30 records per PDU, no template) sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 10.0.0.1 -auto-count 100 \ -flow-collector 192.168.1.10:2055 -flow-protocol netflow5 # sFlow v5 (default UDP port 6343). See the sFlow caveat in the reference. sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 10.0.0.1 -auto-count 100 \ -flow-collector 192.168.1.10:6343 -flow-protocol sflow # Faster ticks for high-fidelity testing sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 10.0.0.1 -auto-count 10 \ -flow-collector 127.0.0.1:9999 -flow-tick-interval 1 # Fall back to the host IP as the source (shared socket) sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 10.0.0.1 -auto-count 100 \ -flow-collector 192.168.1.10:2055 -flow-source-per-device=false

The -flow-* CLI flags seed a single collector / protocol for the auto-start batch. To stand up a fleet that points at more than one collector, or mixes protocols, start the simulator with only the global flags and drive device creation via POST /api/v1/devices, one batch per collector / protocol.
documents.s: Run a heterogeneous fleet (multiple collectors / protocols)

documents.t: # 1. Boot with NO flow seed, only the global knobs (tick cadence, # template cadence, source-per-device policy). sudo ./nl6 \ -flow-tick-interval 1 \ -flow-template-interval 300 \ -flow-source-per-device=true # 2. Batch A → NetFlow v9 to collector A. curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "start_ip": "10.0.0.1", "device_count": 50, "flow": {"collector": "192.168.1.10:2055", "protocol": "netflow9"} }' # 3. Batch B → IPFIX to collector A (different protocol, same host). curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "start_ip": "10.0.1.1", "device_count": 30, "flow": {"collector": "192.168.1.10:4739", "protocol": "ipfix"} }' # 4. Batch C → sFlow to collector B. curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "start_ip": "10.0.2.1", "device_count": 20, "flow": {"collector": "192.168.1.20:6343", "protocol": "sflow"} }' GET /api/v1/flows/status then reports three collector records, one per (collector, protocol) tuple. The response fields are in Flow export reference → Status API.

The same device IP can belong to only one flow config (one flow block per device). If you need the same device to appear on multiple collectors, run multiple simulator processes. The nl6sim netns + per-device-source-IP scheme isn't designed to multicast. -flow-tick-interval is simulator-wide. One ticker drives every exporter regardless of batch. A per-device tick_interval in the REST body is rejected with 400. No warnings entry is emitted; the request does not create any device. -flow-tick-interval sets the simulator-wide cadence and is honored. It controls batching, not volume: a slower tick puts more records in each datagram rather than proportionally reducing the record rate. Volume is set by the profile's concurrent-flow count and the expiry timeouts. A value of zero or less is refused at startup. A value above 1h is logged and replaced by the 5s default. effective_intervals.flow_tick_interval in the device read-back reports the period actually latched. Collector-side rp_filter tuning applies per collector host, not per protocol. See the next section. To silence the fleet's flow export without changing its configuration, start with -fidelity or toggle it with POST /api/v1/fidelity. Do not stretch the tick interval for this. See Fidelity mode.

Trap and syslog export use the same namespace plumbing, so this section applies to them too. Each export has its own flag: -flow-source-per-device for flow, -trap-source-per-device for traps and -syslog-source-per-device for syslog. All three default to on. When an export's flag is on, its packets originate from inside the nl6sim namespace and must traverse the veth-sim-host ↔ veth-sim-ns pair to reach the collector. Three things have to be in place: iptables installed on the simulator host. At startup the simulator inserts iptables -I FORWARD 1 -i veth-sim-host -j ACCEPT so that hosts with a default-DROP FORWARD policy (common when Docker is installed) allow per-device egress. The rule is removed on clean shutdown. Without iptables a warning is logged and flows are silently dropped on such hosts. See Network namespace. Route to the collector from the namespace. The namespace has a default route via veth-sim-host (10.254.0.1), so any collector reachable from the host via its normal routing table is reachable from the namespace. If you've customised host routing verify with: sudo ip netns exec nl6sim ip route get <collector-ip> Collector-side rp_filter. Reverse-path filtering on the collector machine may drop packets whose source IP (e.g. 10.0.0.x or 10.42.0.x) isn't reachable back through the receiving interface. This applies to flow, trap and syslog datagrams and to syslog TCP and TLS connections. Loose mode fixes it: sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=2 sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.<iface>.rp_filter=2 2 is loose mode; 0 disables filtering entirely. The simulator auto-configures its own rp_filter sysctls. No user action is needed there.

If the collector isn't seeing flows, walk through these in order: Confirm export is enabled and running. curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/flows/status Expect data.devices_exporting > 0 and sent_packets on each data.collectors[] record steadily increasing. A climbing send_failures means the kernel refused the datagrams. Sniff on the simulator host. Packets should appear with device IPs as sources: sudo tcpdump -ni any udp port <collector-port> Check the FORWARD rule. Its packet counter should be non-zero: sudo iptables -L FORWARD -v -n Sniff on the collector host. If packets arrive but the collector doesn't count them, the problem is rp_filter or a firewall rule on that host, not the simulator. As a diagnostic, restart with -flow-source-per-device=false.
