One buffer element is one tick, so a catalogue tick with one notification per list entry is dropped or delivered whole. ON_CHANGE streams own a 16-deep listener channel (state events are rare; depth 16 absorbs multi-second collector stalls). Both drop counters are simulator-wide and exposed via GET /api/v1/gnmi/status as updates_dropped and state_events_dropped respectively. Per-leaf ON_CHANGE acceptance. ON_CHANGE is accepted only when every subscription's resolved path touches the state-engine-backed leaves; counter leaves are rejected because counters change continuously under the analytical engine (every observation produces a different value, which would degenerate to unbounded fan-out). The rejection error names the offending leaf and recommends SAMPLE. Leaf ON_CHANGE SAMPLE state/name ✓ ✓ state/ifindex ✓ ✓ state/oper-status ✓ ✓ state/admin-status ✓ ✓ state/last-change ✓ ✓ state/counters/* (12 leaves) ✗ (rejected with InvalidArgument) ✓ ON_CHANGE event sources. Mutations come from the per-device flap scheduler (-if-flap-scenario), the REST control plane (POST /api/v1/devices/{ip}/interfaces/{ifIndex}/{oper,admin}-status) and its auto-revert, and an SNMP SET of ifAdminStatus.<N>. Every transition fans out as a SubscribeResponse{update} to every matching subscriber within ~milliseconds. See interface state engine for the full picture. Heartbeat. Per gNMI §3.5.1.5.2, heartbeat_interval lets a client request periodic re-emission of the current value even when nothing has changed. Set the field on an ON_CHANGE subscription to enable; sub-second values are clamped to 1 second. heartbeat_interval=0 (unset) means no heartbeat. The target emits only on actual state transitions. Mixed-mode rejection. A single SubscribeRequest that mixes ON_CHANGE and SAMPLE subscriptions is rejected with InvalidArgument. The two paths have different emission models (event-driven vs ticker-driven); weaving them in one stream would inflate complexity for negligible value. Standard collectors (e.g. gnmic) naturally issue two separate requests.

Boot the simulator with one device for these examples: sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 192.168.100.1 -auto-count 1 Then from the host: # Capabilities: sanity check the target is reachable gnmic -a 192.168.100.1:9339 --skip-verify capabilities # Get all counters for one interface gnmic -a 192.168.100.1:9339 --skip-verify get \ --path '/interfaces/interface[name=MgmtEth0/RP0/CPU0/0]/state/counters' # Get in-octets across every interface (wildcard) gnmic -a 192.168.100.1:9339 --skip-verify get \ --path '/interfaces/interface[name=*]/state/counters/in-octets' # Subscribe: stream every counter, every 5 seconds gnmic -a 192.168.100.1:9339 --skip-verify subscribe \ --path '/interfaces/interface[name=*]/state/counters' \ --sample-interval 5s # Subscribe ONCE: one snapshot, then exit gnmic -a 192.168.100.1:9339 --skip-verify subscribe \ --path '/interfaces/interface[name=*]/state/counters/in-octets' \ --mode once For a step-by-step check of a collector against a small fleet, see Validate a gNMI collector.

curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/v1/gnmi/status | jq { "subsystem_active": true, "tls_enabled": true, "listeners": 1, "active_subscriptions": 0, "updates_sent": 0, "updates_dropped": 0, "tls_handshake_failures": 0, "listener_accept_failures": 0, "state_events_emitted": 0, "state_events_dropped": 0 } subsystem_active is false when -gnmi-disable is set. listeners equals the device count when active. Every counter is cumulative since process start; updates_dropped increments per backpressure-discard event. updates_sent counts gNMI Updates, not leaves: under the IOS-XR JSON_IETF layout one Update carries a whole list entry, so the same traffic counts fewer Updates than in PROTO. The state-engine counters are explained in the interface state engine reference. tls_enabled reports the dial-in transport the subsystem is configured for, so you can tell a TLS fleet from a plaintext one without reading the simulator's flags. It describes the configuration rather than any live listener, so read it alongside subsystem_active: when that is false there are no listeners for it to apply to. tls_handshake_failures counts connections that were accepted and whose TLS handshake then failed. The usual causes are a client connecting without --skip-verify (or with a wrong --tls-ca), and a client dialing plaintext against the TLS listener. It stays 0 under -gnmi-tls=false, where no handshake happens. The first failure is logged once per process; the counter keeps moving after that. listener_accept_failures counts Accept errors on the per-device listener. These are faults on the simulator's side, not client misconfigurations. At fleet scale the realistic one is file-descriptor exhaustion. What tls_handshake_failures counts. In older releases the field carried Accept errors. gRPC runs the TLS handshake after Accept returns, so the field could never report a handshake failure and read 0 in every situation the tls_handshake_failures paragraph above describes. If you are comparing against an older deployment, a value going from 0 to non-zero is the corrected counter working, not a new fault. The Accept signal now lives in listener_accept_failures.

Read-only. Set returns Unimplemented. The simulator's deterministic-state guarantee is incompatible with mutation. No POLL. Returns Unimplemented. STREAM/SAMPLE and ONCE cover the common cases. No suppress_redundant. A SAMPLE stream sends every interval, including the held value of an interface whose oper-status is not up(1) (see Interface state). Single shared certificate. All devices present the same CA-signed cert. Real fleets have per-device PKI; the simulator does not. No client-cert auth. The simulator runs in lab contexts; mutual-TLS is out of scope. No subinterfaces, no /system, no LLDP without a catalogue. A type without a catalogue serves only the interface state leaves listed above, plus optical-channel under /components on optical transport types. juniper_mx10004 and cisco_asr9902 also serve the subtrees their catalogues list, including subinterfaces and /system. No type serves LLDP.

Port surface. Each device adds one TCP listener on port 9339 (or whatever -gnmi-port says). Per-listener cost is ~10 KiB RSS + 1 fd + 1 goroutine. At 30,000 devices the total is ~320 MiB RSS. Per-device source IP. Listeners bind inside the nl6sim netns so the source IP for accepted connections matches the device IP. Same model as SNMP / SSH / HTTPS REST. Collector-side rp_filter. If your collector rejects packets from the 10.42.0.0/16 (or whatever device subnet) range, set net.ipv4.conf.*.rp_filter=0 or 2. Same caveat already documented for flow / trap / syslog. Slowloris hardening. Per-device gRPC servers cap concurrent streams at 16, reap idle connections after 5 minutes, and ping clients every 30s with a 10s ack timeout. The Subscribe handler enforces a 30-second deadline on the initial SubscribeRequest. Clients that open a stream and never send the subscription_list are rejected with DeadlineExceeded. The 17th concurrent stream on a single TCP connection is queued at the HTTP/2 SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS layer until a slot frees. gRPC does not surface a status code in this case, and the client's Subscribe.Recv blocks until a slot frees. A collector holding more than 16 streams on one connection will see the 17th hang silently. To service >16 parallel streams, open a second grpc.ClientConn (multiple TCP connections each get their own quota). Observable to clients: the 16-stream cap per connection is observable to clients that previously opened more than 16 parallel streams per device-connection. The realistic ceiling is 2 to 3 (one primary collector and maybe a debug session); 16 is conservative. ON_CHANGE on subtree paths is rejected. The /interfaces/interface[name=*]/state subtree includes 12 counter leaves; ON_CHANGE on a subtree that touches a counter leaf is rejected with InvalidArgument (the error names the offending leaf and recommends SAMPLE). Subscribers wanting ON_CHANGE coverage of the state leaves should enumerate them explicitly: e.g., one sub per state/oper-status, state/admin-status, state/last-change. The whole-/state subtree is incompatible with ON_CHANGE under the analytical counter engine because counter values change continuously.

SNMP reference covers the IF-MIB counter source, including the analytical sine-wave model. Architecture shows where the gNMI dial-in server sits in the simulator's component map. CLI flags is the canonical flag catalog.

A gNMI catalogue, resources/<type>/gnmi.json, lists the subtrees a device type serves beyond the shared interface paths every device serves and the optical paths only optical transport types (ciena_waveserver5) serve. This page describes the file for profile authors. For what a running device serves and how to subscribe, see gNMI dial-in.

Key Meaning notification.origin / native_origin the origins served; a request with an empty origin maps to origin notification.origin_aliases request origins accepted as another spelling of origin or native_origin, such as a YANG module name (openconfig-interfaces) or Junos's Native; the prefix origin of the response follows aliased_origin_prefix. The generator adds every subtree's module as an alias of origin, mapped to the origin of the subtrees naming it (native_origin for a native sensor model such as junos-fabric, origin when both use it), so the bindings list only spellings no module names, such as Native notification.aliased_origin_prefix prefix origin of a response to a request whose origin is an origin_aliases key: canonical (default) or empty; a request with no origin or a canonical one always gets the canonical origin. The MX10004 uses empty: a module-name or Native: request is answered with no prefix origin, as hardware does, while an origin-less request gets openconfig or juniper, as vJunos 25.4 does notification.response_origin module answers every request with the rendering subtree's YANG module as the prefix origin (openconfig-interfaces:interfaces/...), as IOS-XR does; every subtree then carries its module, and it cannot be combined with aliased_origin_prefix: empty notification.json_ietf_layout leaf (default) answers JSON_IETF with one update per leaf; container answers with one update per requested node, its value the node's leaves nested as RFC 7951 JSON, as IOS-XR does. container needs prefix: list-entry and JSON_IETF in encodings notification.prefix list-entry emits one Notification per list entry with the entry path as prefix and leaf-relative updates (Junos); flat emits absolute paths notification.encodings the encodings Capabilities advertises; others are refused with Unimplemented notification.extension juniper-header attaches Juniper's telemetry header extension (registered id 1) to every response models ModelData entries Capabilities advertises components, neighbors chassis inventory and BGP peers, the key sources for component and neighbour subtrees components[].tags leaf groups a component reports beyond its type's, selected by a tag:<name> leaf filter; an IOS-XR FPD module carries firmware-version, a slot container no type subtrees[].path the list-entry path with * keys; / is a root entry with no keys subtrees[].aliases optional subscription paths without wildcards that request the whole subtree, with an empty origin or the subtree's origin; several subtrees of one origin may carry the same alias and all of them answer it subtrees[].alias_leaves optional leaf paths relative to the entry; a request through an alias then renders only the leaves at or below one of them instead of the whole subtree; load refuses it on a subtree without aliases, an entry with keys or covering no leaf, and an always leaf outside it subtrees[].keys one key source per wildcard, listed in the order the wildcards are filled (an element with several keys fills them in sorted key-name order): interfaces (the ifDescr table; optional filter of whitespace-separated terms, each at most once: iftype:<n>[,<n>...] keeps the interfaces whose IF-MIB ifType is listed, name:<ifDescr>[,...] keeps only the named interfaces, !name:<ifDescr>[,...] drops them; an interface is listed when every term admits it), subinterfaces (directly after an interfaces key: per interface, the index of every ifDescr row named <interface>.<index> whose index is a uint32, unit 0 included; the entry reads that row's counters, and an interface without such rows has no entry), components (optional filter, optional parent naming the component whose children are the keys), neighbors, or static with names subtrees[].leaves relative path, YANG type, optional enum, a generator binding, and an optional filter subtrees[].echo_origin under aliased_origin_prefix: empty, the prefix carries the request's own origin spelling; the MX10004 property subtrees use it, so openconfig-platform:/components/component/properties/... is answered with origin openconfig-platform notification.decimal_encoding PROTO wire form of decimal64 leaves: double (default, double_val) or decimal_val (gNMI Decimal64 with the leaf's fraction digits as precision, what Junos sends); JSON forms are the RFC 7951 string either way; every form is rounded to the leaf's digits subtrees[].leaves[].digits decimal64 fraction-digits (1..18), written by the generator from the YANG model, or declared on an extra binding leaf; absent means two; refused on a non-decimal leaf subtrees[].alias_only the subtree answers only a request equal to one of its aliases, never path coverage; load refuses it without aliases. How a sensor sends a shape the YANG path does not cover without the shape leaking into other subscriptions subtrees[].leaves[].decimal_encoding per-leaf override of notification.decimal_encoding on a decimal64 leaf (bindings decimal_encodings map); the MX10004 sends temperature as Decimal64 and the transceiver optic readings as doubles subtrees[].leaves[].always rendered whenever its entry renders at all, even when the request path does not cover it (bindings always list); how a Junos sensor sends identity leaves such as name and init-time with every counters notification subtrees[].leaves[].members a union leaf's member types in YANG declaration order, written by the generator with nested unions flattened and leafref members resolved to their targets; enum then names the enumeration members' values, and digits the first decimal64 member's fraction digits. A union with a member the runtime cannot serve (binary, bits, empty, ...) gets no members. A value takes the first member that accepts it: an enumeration only its names, a string-like member anything, an integer member an integral value in range (3.7, as a number or a string, falls through rather than truncating; a plain integer leaf refuses the string 3.7 and the resolver skips it), a decimal64 member any number. The ASR 9902 CPU state/index (ALL or uint32) sends ALL as a string and a numbered CPU as uint_val, a JSON number in JSON_IETF. A union without members is served as a string; load refuses members on another type subtrees[].leaves[].filter narrows the leaf to the components matching the value (temperature, tag:<name> or a component type, the components key-source vocabulary); the leaf is omitted from every other entry of the subtree An interfaces key with a filter outside that grammar fails to load, as does one with a repeated term, an empty name, or a name both kept and dropped. Names match ifDescr exactly, no globs: nothing on a device beyond ifDescr and ifType tells a Routing Engine port from a line-card port of the same ifType, so a generated profile names the ports it treats differently. An interface whose profile ships no ifDescr row is listed under the synthesised name the catalogue serves as its key, and a name term matches that name. A subinterfaces key with a filter, names or parent fails to load too. Under prefix: list-entry one entry renders as exactly one Notification, so every leaf an entry serves belongs in one subtree. A per-component leaf such as state/temperature/instant is therefore a filtered leaf of the inventory subtree, not a second subtree serving the same entries. Two subtrees of one origin on one path are legal when their entry sets are disjoint; the shipped MX10004 keeps the static CPU0:CORE0 subtree beside the inventory subtree that way. Loading refuses the pair when their entries overlap, by subtree index, path and the first colliding entry, and names the leaf filter as the remedy where the subtree has a components key. The check enumerates the key sources it can resolve without a device (components, neighbors, static). A pair with an interfaces key on both sides at the same position is decided from the two filters alone, because the interface name set exists only per device: it loads when the filters are disjoint by construction (both carry iftype sets with no common value, both carry name lists with no common name, or one carries a name list wholly inside the other's !name list) or when another key position is disjoint, and is refused otherwise, naming both subtrees and both filters. The shipped cisco_asr9902 splits its subinterface counters by iftype:6 and iftype:161, and the shipped juniper_mx10004 splits its interface entry by iftype:6 !name:fxp0 and name:fxp0. A pair with interfaces keys at different positions is refused, since filters on different path keys prove nothing; a pair with an interfaces key on one side only is not checked.

Binding Value ifcounter:<IF-MIB column> the same counter SNMP serves, e.g. ifHCInOctets; columns joined by + serve their sum, e.g. ifHCInUcastPkts+ifHCInMulticastPkts+ifHCInBroadcastPkts ifstate:name|ifindex|oper|admin|last-change interface state engine sine:base,amplitude,period_s deterministic wave seeded by device IP and entry key counter:rate_per_s monotonic counter with seeded jitter inventory:<field> / neighbor:<field> from components / neighbors const:<literal> / key:<n> / timestamp:now|boot literal, the n-th key value, nanosecond timestamps device:sysname|id the device sysName (falling back to the device ID), or the device ID inventory:serial_no_per_device the component's serial_no with its trailing digits replaced by a per-device suffix from the IPv4 (four hex digits of the low 16 bits plus the ordinal's last two digits), so devices and components never share a serial; a device without an IPv4 serves the constant. SSH output is static text, so show chassis hardware, show chassis routing-engine and show chassis power print the catalogue constants Time-based bindings share the interface counter cycler's start as their epoch, so a catalogue counter equals the SNMP counter read at the same instant.

-gnmi-catalog <file> replaces the catalogue of every type that carries one with that file. A type without a catalogue keeps none, so ciena_waveserver5 keeps its optical resolver and a legacy type keeps its encodings. A gnmi.json in a resource directory replaces that type's embedded catalogue, including for types that ship none. Catalogues are generated, not hand-edited: make gen-gnmi-catalog runs go/cmd/gnmi-catalog over a pinned Juniper/yang checkout for juniper_mx10004 and a pinned YangModels/yang vendor/cisco/xr/2422 checkout for cisco_asr9902, each with its gnmi-bindings.json. For cisco_asr9902, -modules reads only the modules in go/cmd/xr-chassis/yang-modules.txt, which capabilities-asr9k-x64.xml advertises. The generator's -path flag adds directories that are searched only to resolve imports, and the Makefile passes native/jti/models because Juniper's augments and deviations import junos-* modules. A module under -path is also loaded when a binding subtree names it in module, which is how the Junos native sensor models (junos-fabric, junos-fpc-env) are read without walking every JTI model. A binding subtree may set yang_path when Junos renders a sensor under a prefix that differs from its YANG tree: the leaves are looked up at yang_path and the catalogue keeps path as the rendered prefix. A drift test regenerates the file and fails when the committed copy differs. CI runs it through make test-gnmi-drift, which clones the pinned checkouts and fails if they are missing. A plain go test run skips it when the YANG cache is absent; make yang-cache populates the cache.

The MX10004 reproduces what vJunos-router 25.4R1.12 sends. It serves PROTO and JSON only, and JSON_IETF is refused with the Junos message. It sends one notification per list entry, with prefixes such as openconfig:/interfaces/interface[name=xe-0/0/0]. Native sensors sit under the juniper origin. The component tree carries the MX10004 hardware's cardinality: 393 components across the chassis, both control boards and both routing engines with their sensors, the LC480 in FPC0 with two 24-port PICs and the LC9600 in FPC1 with six 4-port QSFP-DD PICs, every port and transceiver, the FPC sensors, two PEMs with sensors, two fan tray controllers, 24 fans and six switch fabric boards with seventeen sensors each; sensor-bearing components serve the full temperature record with instant, avg, min and max as Decimal64 precision 1. FPC1's sensor set is modelled on the LC480's, because no public source names the LC9600's. The Routing Engine serves eight CPUs under /system/cpus/cpu, the count MX10004 hardware reports, although Juniper documents the RE X10 as a 10-core CPU. Every port carries a transceiver component serving the static transceiver state (transceiver/state/{connector-type, date-code, ethernet-pmd, form-factor, present, serial-no, vendor, vendor-part, ...}) in the component's notification and the analog leaves (state/enabled, state/input-power/instant, state/output-power/instant, state/laser-bias-current/instant, doubles) under the component[name=*]/transceiver prefix, plus properties/property[name=wavelength]/state/{configurable,value} on the port component. A subscription to /components/component/transceiver/state/ also carries oper-status alone under a component[name=*]/state prefix for every port and every transceiver, as hardware does. That path is an alias carried by four subtrees; the two oper-status subtrees are alias_only, so /components/component/state does not repeat them. A /components/component/transceiver path on a device type without a catalogue is refused with NotFound naming the path. Each interface's out-queues carry exactly queue-number, queued-bytes, queued-pkts, hp-red-drop-pkts and lp-red-drop-pkts. The out-queue and fabric leaves follow MX10004 hardware, not vJunos. vJunos sends eleven more buffer and drop leaves. Do not add them to make the catalogue match vJunos. A counters subscription also carries name, init-time, state/high-speed and state/parent-ae-name, because those leaves are marked always, and nothing else from the interface entry. The router's ONCE chunking of one interface into several notifications is not modelled. The subinterfaces are the device's five logical units: unit 0 (xe-0/0/0.0) and the VRF units xe-0/0/0.100, xe-0/0/0.200 and xe-0/0/0.999 on xe-0/0/0, which show route instance detail names, and fxp0.0 on the management port fxp0. Each is also an ifTable row of its own, at ifIndex 73 to 76 and 78, and a line of show interfaces terse, and its state/name and state/ifindex read that row. fxp0 is the 73rd interface of the list, beside the 72 ports, because it is an Ethernet port (ifType 6), but it is a Routing Engine port, not a line-card one, so a subtree of its own keyed name:fxp0 serves it: the OpenConfig interface state, state/high-speed and the IF-MIB counters, and no out-queue, hardware-port, init-time, parent-ae-name or FCS and pause statistics. The line-card and out-queue subtrees exclude it with !name:fxp0, so the 576 out-queues belong to the 72 ports. No line-card sensor stands behind fxp0, so its subtree marks no leaf always: a counters subscription renders its counters and nothing else, while a line-card port's notification also carries the sensor's identity leaves. The loopback lo0 and its unit lo0.0 are IF-MIB rows (ifIndex 79 and 80) and terse lines but not gNMI interfaces: the catalogue's interface leaves describe an Ethernet port, so a loopback is filtered out by ifType. No other port has a subinterface, and no unit is listed as an interface on dial-in or dial-out. Every subinterface carries the eight state/counters leaves, ipv4/state/counters and ipv6/state/counters with octets, packets and multicast octets and packets each, and init-time. A subscription to /interfaces/interface/subinterfaces/subinterface/state/counters is a subtree alias scoped by alias_leaves. It renders the 8 state/counters/* leaves, the 16 ipv4/state/counters/* and ipv6/state/counters/* leaves and init-time, as the Junos sensor does. The subinterface state/* leaves come only from a subscription to .../subinterface/state. The subinterface totals ride the unit's own ifTable row's HC counters and agree with SNMP. The family counters are independent synthetic counters at their own rates; nothing ties them to the totals, so do not derive a remainder from them. BGP serves the two neighbours' state (with state/peer-group), their afi-safis/afi-safi entries for IPV4_UNICAST (28 leaves, with the ipv4-unicast containers) and IPV6_UNICAST (27 leaves, with the ipv6-unicast containers), and two peer-groups, EBGP-TRANSIT (external, both neighbours) and IBGP-CORE (internal, no members), each with afi-safi entries (21 and 20 leaves, including total-paths and total-prefixes); the transit group's totals stay above its members' received counts, and the peer-group prefix counters are outside the pinned model and declared as extra leaves because hardware sends them. The module names openconfig-interfaces, openconfig-platform, openconfig-system and openconfig-network-instance are accepted as the openconfig origin and Native as juniper, which is what an operator types against a real MX. The notifications are the same as for the canonical origin except the prefix origin: a module-name or Native request gets none, and a property subscription gets the module name, as the router sends. A subscription to /junos/system/linecard/packet/usage/, with origin juniper or none, returns the packet-usage counters under the component paths Junos renders them at. A subscription to /junos/system/linecard/fabric/, with origin juniper, Native, junos-fabric or none, returns the fabric sensor under the prefixes hardware renders it at, one notification per edge with the 14 uint64 leaves of junos-fabric.yang. Edges between line card PFEs render under junos/fabric-statistics/fabric-message/edges[...]/class-stats[priority=*]/transmit-counts, once per class high and low. Edges to and from the switch fabric render under the keyless junos/fabric-statistics/fabric-message/edges[...]/class-stats/transmit-counts and name only SWITCH-FABRIC slot 0, PFE 0. The edge count follows nl6's two line cards with 4 + 12 PFEs: every PFE to every other, themselves included, in both classes, plus one edge each way between every PFE and the switch fabric, 544 notifications. The partial notifications with fewer leaves that the router also sends are not modelled. A subscription to /junos/system/linecard/environment/, with origin juniper, Native, junos-fpc-env or none, returns, per FPC, one power record, one temperature record per sensor and five voltage rails near their nominal voltage, with the leaves of junos-fpc-env.yang. That subtree is YANG-derived: no capture exists, so the prefix depth, the sensor names and the values are nl6's reading of the model, not what an MX sends. The header extension carries the hostname and sensor name. ON_CHANGE is served on catalogue paths. The stream starts with the snapshot of every covered leaf in the catalogue shape, then sync_response. On an interface state change it sends one notification for the entry whose interface moved, carrying the ifstate leaves whose field changed (oper-status on an oper change, admin-status on an admin change, last-change on any change) and the entry's always leaves. Every other leaf, whatever its binding (inventory, constants, keys, neighbours, IF-MIB columns, timestamps, device fields, ifstate name and ifindex), is sent in the snapshot and on heartbeat only. A subscription covering a counter leaf (ifcounter or counter) is refused with InvalidArgument and the counter message described under Subscribe semantics; one covering a sensor leaf (a sine binding such as a temperature) is refused the same way, because a sensor reading changes continuously.

The ASR 9902 interface set comes from its chassis model: 48 front ports and two management ports, Bundle-Ether1, BVI1, Loopback0, Null0, and the VLAN subinterfaces HundredGigE0/0/0/8.100, HundredGigE0/0/0/8.200 and Bundle-Ether1.300. SNMP ifTable, show interfaces brief and gNMI agree on this set. ifTable and show interfaces brief list the VLAN subinterfaces as interfaces of their own. gNMI serves them only in their parent's subinterfaces/subinterface list, as IOS-XR does. A subscription to /interfaces/interface/state/counters sends two notifications per physical port, Bundle-Ether, BVI and Null0, with the 19 counter leaves. A Loopback sends one notification with counters/carrier-transitions only. A subscription to /interfaces/interface/subinterfaces/subinterface/state/counters sends only the VLAN subinterfaces the profile ships (.100, .200 and .300), so there is no index 0. A HundredGigE subinterface carries the 19 leaves. A Bundle-Ether subinterface omits in-/out- unicast-pkts, multicast-pkts, broadcast-pkts and last-clear. The router shows last-clear on some subinterfaces only; nl6 ties it to the parent kind, which the reference does not confirm. Interface and subinterface counters read the IF-MIB row's HC counters, so they agree with SNMP. in-pkts and out-pkts are the sum of the unicast, multicast and broadcast counters. Loopback0 and Null0 declare speed 0 and carry no traffic. Their ifPhysAddress is empty and their ifMtu is 1500. The interface kinds and leaf sets follow an ASR 9902 on IOS-XR 24.2.2; which interfaces exist, their ifTypes and speeds are chosen.

cisco_asr9902 sets json_ietf_layout: container. A JSON_IETF Get then returns one Notification with no prefix per requested path. It holds one update per concrete instance of the path, with the response origin, and the value nests every leaf below that node. A request that names every list key it crosses has one instance. The counters alias /interfaces/interface/state/counters crosses the interface list without a key, so it gets one update per interface. Lists become arrays, and each entry repeats its keys as members, so /components answers {"component": [{"name": "...", "state": {...}}, ...]}. Scalars keep the per-leaf JSON_IETF form: 64-bit integers and decimals are quoted strings, 32-bit integers and booleans are bare. A leaf marked always that sits outside the requested node is left out, because the nested value cannot hold it. A list key repeated inside a value is the path key cast through the subtree's state/<key> leaf when the catalogue has one, whichever leaves the request covered, because an OpenConfig list key is a leafref to that leaf. So a numbered CPU entry under /system/cpus is {"index": 0, "state": {"index": 0, ...}} and the aggregate is {"index": "ALL", ...}. A key with no such leaf in the catalogue stays a JSON string. The path key is a string in every encoding, as gNMI requires. A JSON_IETF Subscribe in ONCE or SAMPLE mode sends one update per list entry, at the entry path with its keys, with no prefix. PROTO, ON_CHANGE and the paths the shared resolver answers keep one update per leaf, so /interfaces/interface/state stays per-leaf on an ASR 9902. The layout follows Cisco's xrdocs article Getting started with gNMI, which shows it for IOS-XR 7. It is not verified on IOS-XR 24.2.2, because the reference capture is PROTO only.

By default every nl6 device is a gNMI dial-in target: a collector opens the connection and calls Subscribe. With dial-out the roles reverse. The device opens a gRPC connection to a collector and streams telemetry to it. Dial-out is firewall/NAT-friendly (outbound only, no inbound service) and is the mechanism behind Arista EOS gNMIReverse. Dial-out is opt-in and per-device, so the fleet can run mixed: some devices serve dial-in on :9339 while others push dial-out to a collector. dial-in (default) dial-out (opt-in) collector ── Subscribe ─▶ device device ── Publish(stream) ─▶ collector (source IP = device IP; one ClientConn + stream per device)

nl6 ships the Arista gNMIReverse flavor: Publish(stream gnmi.SubscribeResponse) → google.protobuf.Empty. It is fire-and-forget, with no per-message ack. The payload is the standard gnmi.SubscribeResponse, the exact message nl6's dial-in Subscribe produces, so dial-out and dial-in values agree byte-for-byte at the same instant. The DialoutTransport seam leaves room to add the SONiC gNMIDialOut flavor later; only gnmireverse is implemented today. Every pushed notification carries the device identity in-band: Notification.Prefix.Target is set to the device's management IP (the same job the Arista client's -target_value flag does). Collectors can attribute messages by target instead of source IP. This is useful behind NAT/proxies and a prerequisite for any future shared-transport mode. Dial-in responses are unaffected (servers echo a client-set target; they don't invent one).

Mode Behaviour sample (default) Re-resolve every configured path on a fixed interval (sample_interval, clamped to a 1s floor) and push a SubscribeResponse. on-change Push on interface-state transitions via the same InterfaceState fan-out dial-in ON_CHANGE uses. Only oper-status, admin-status, and last-change fire on a change; name and ifindex are static and appear in the initial snapshot only. Any counter leaves a path covers are ignored, so a subtree path like the default /interfaces/interface[name=*]/state works (counters are filtered at emit). A path that covers only counters (e.g. .../state/counters/in-octets) is rejected at attach, since it could never fire on-change. Paths are gNMI paths under /interfaces/interface[name=*]/state/.... On optical transport types, a sample subscription also accepts the optical-channel paths under /components/component[name=*]/optical-channel/ (see Optical telemetry). An on-change subscription refuses an optical path at attach, because optical values change continuously. The default path is the full state subtree (/interfaces/interface[name=*]/state). A subinterface, such as the juniper_mx10004 unit xe-0/0/0.0, is not an interface of that list, so dial-out lists the same interfaces dial-in does. The one difference is a loopback: this resolver has no ifType filter, so the juniper_mx10004 dial-out list carries lo0, which the dial-in catalogue leaves out.

Each dial-out device owns one grpc.ClientConn and one Publish stream, never a shared pool. A single Go ClientConn caps at ~100 concurrent HTTP/2 streams with no automatic multi-connection, so a shared pool would silently bottleneck at fleet scale; per-device is also the faithful simulation (each real device is its own dial-out client). When network namespaces are enabled the client dials from inside the device's netns with the source IP pinned to the device IP, reusing the existing veth + FORWARD egress rule (no new netns / iptables surface). Hostname collectors are resolved per-dial in the host namespace (the sim netns has no resolver), so DNS failover is picked up on every reconnect and the gRPC authority stays the hostname. TLS ServerName verification works against the collector's certificate. Only IPv4 records are used (the sim netns is IPv4-only); a hostname resolving exclusively to AAAA records fails the dial with a clear error. In-namespace dial concurrency is bounded (64 concurrent dials, 10s per-dial timeout) so an unreachable collector cannot exhaust OS threads at fleet scale.

Own reconnect loop. A broken Publish stream ends the RPC, so the exporter wraps dial→publish in a capped exponential backoff loop (1s → 30s), resetting after a stream stays up. Drop-on-outage, no buffering. During a collector outage telemetry is dropped, matching vendor behaviour. A slow collector cannot stall the device. Sends go through a bounded channel with drop-oldest (counted as updates_dropped). Shutdown-only stop. StopGnmiDialout runs only at process exit (same constraint as trap/syslog/gNMI Stop); there is no runtime restart path.
Two levels, mirroring flow / trap / syslog:

Flag Default Meaning -gnmi-mode dial-in dial-in (serve gNMI) or dial-out (also push) for the auto-start batch -gnmi-dialout-collector none Collector host:port (required when -gnmi-mode=dial-out) -gnmi-dialout-flavor gnmireverse Dial-out wire flavor -gnmi-dialout-encoding json_ietf json_ietf or proto -gnmi-dialout-sub-mode sample sample or on-change -gnmi-dialout-interval 10s SAMPLE cadence (1s floor) -gnmi-dialout-tls true Use TLS (false = plaintext, Arista -collector_tls=false parity) -gnmi-dialout-tls-insecure false Skip collector cert verification (dev only) -gnmi-dialout-tls-ca none PEM CA bundle to verify the collector (empty = system roots) -gnmi-dialout-mtls false Present the shared cert as a client cert (mutual TLS) REST-created devices do not inherit these. They opt in per device.
documents.s: Global seed flags ([seed], auto-start batch only)

documents.t: { "start_ip": "10.42.0.1", "device_count": 1, "gnmi_dialout": { "collector": "10.0.0.5:6030", "flavor": "gnmireverse", "encoding": "json_ietf", "mode": "on-change", "paths": ["/interfaces/interface[name=*]/state/oper-status"], "sample_interval": "10s", "tls": { "enabled": true, "insecure_skip_verify": false, "ca_pem": "", "mtls": false } } } Omitting gnmi_dialout leaves the device dial-in only. Unknown fields are rejected (400).

tls.enabled=false selects a plaintext gRPC connection. When enabled, the collector is verified against ca_pem (or the system roots), or verification is skipped with insecure_skip_verify (dev only). The simulator's shared TLS certificate is a server leaf cert. It can be presented as a client cert (mtls: true) but cannot verify the collector, which is why ca_pem exists. ca_pem is the bundle inline, not a path. This block is settable over REST, and a path here would let any API caller name a file for the simulator to open. That is an arbitrary-file-read primitive, where even the error distinguishes "could not read" from "no certificates here". A path is accepted only from -gnmi-dialout-tls-ca, read once at startup by the operator who launched the process. tls.ca_file is no longer accepted It named a file the simulator opened at dial time. Requests carrying it are now rejected with a message naming both replacements, rather than silently ignored. Move the bundle inline as ca_pem, or pass the path on the command line.

GET /api/v1/gnmi/dialout/status: { "subsystem_active": true, "collectors": [ { "collector": "10.0.0.5:6030", "flavor": "gnmireverse", "devices": 100, "streams_active": 100, "updates_sent": 1234567, "updates_dropped": 0, "reconnects": 2, "send_failures": 0 } ], "devices_exporting": 100 } collectors is sorted by collector, then by flavor, so repeated requests list the rows in the same order. The sort compares the strings, so 10.0.0.10:6030 comes before 10.0.0.9:6030. Counters are monotonic across device deletion (a deleted device's totals persist in the per-(collector, flavor) aggregate).

The collector-side rp_filter caveat is the same as flow / trap / syslog: relax net.ipv4.conf.*.rp_filter to 0 or 2 to accept connections whose source IP is a 10.42.0.0/16 device address. No data is buffered during a collector outage. Test collectors: goarista/gnmireverse/server (reference), or Nokia gNMIc listen.

nl6 simulates NVIDIA DGX and HGX GPU servers with per-GPU SNMP metrics, nvidia-smi and dcgmi SSH output, and DCGM-shaped REST endpoints. The SNMP OID layout under NVIDIA's PEN (1.3.6.1.4.1.5703) is defined by nl6. NVIDIA publishes no SNMP GPU MIB; real DCGM exposes a Prometheus /metrics endpoint, not SNMP. The metric vocabulary and the command output are modelled on DCGM.
DCGM simulation: per-GPU SNMP objects with types, units and value behaviour, the SSH commands and the REST paths.

Device Profile GPUs VRAM/GPU System RAM sysObjectID NVIDIA DGX-A100 nvidia_dgx_a100 8 80 GB 1 TB 1.3.6.1.4.1.5703.1.2.1 NVIDIA DGX-H100 nvidia_dgx_h100 8 80 GB 2 TB 1.3.6.1.4.1.5703.1.2.2 NVIDIA HGX-H200 nvidia_hgx_h200 8 141 GB 2 TB 1.3.6.1.4.1.5703.1.2.3 See Device types → GPU servers for where these sit in the broader device catalogue.

The OIDs a collector polls from a simulated GPU server. Every object below the PEN is nl6's own definition and resolves against no vendor MIB. Anchor vendor detection on the full dotted prefix .1.3.6.1.4.1.5703., never on the bare digits: 5703 occurs inside 15703, 45703 and inside instance identifiers, so a substring rule claims unrelated devices as NVIDIA GPU servers. The arc used to sit under 1.3.6.1.4.1.53246, a PEN IANA allocates to an unrelated company. Every sub-identifier below the PEN is unchanged, so a rule written for the old arc needs only its prefix replaced. A GET under the old arc answers noSuchObject (SNMPv2c/v3) or error-status = noSuchName (SNMPv1); nothing under it carries a value.

Pattern 1.3.6.1.4.1.5703.1.1.1.1.<X>.<gpu>, with <gpu> from 0 to 7. Values come from the resource file and do not change. X Object Example 1 GPU name NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 2 GPU UUID GPU-a1b2c3d4-... 3 GPU serial 1234567890ABC 4 PCI bus ID 00000000:07:00.0 13 Driver version 535.129.03 14 CUDA version 12.2 15 ECC errors, corrected 0 16 ECC errors, uncorrected 0 17 NVLink active links 18

Same pattern, <X> from 5 to 12. Values come from the metrics cycler, which moves to the next point once per minute. Adjacent points can hold the same value. Reading an OID does not move its value. See DCGM → Value behaviour. Eight metrics times eight GPUs is 64 dynamic OIDs per device. X Metric Unit 5 GPU utilization percent 6 VRAM used MiB 7 VRAM total MiB, constant 8 Temperature degrees Celsius 9 Power draw watts 10 Fan speed percent 11 SM clock MHz 12 Memory clock MHz

The profiles also serve system (1.3.6.1.2.1.1), the IF-MIB interface tables (1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1, 1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1) and Host Resources (1.3.6.1.2.1.25). The interface counters are served by the same cycler as every other device type; see SNMP → Dynamic IF-MIB counters.

nl6 simulates three NVIDIA GPU servers with eight GPUs each: nvidia_dgx_a100, nvidia_dgx_h100 and nvidia_hgx_h200. The metric vocabulary and the nvidia-smi and dcgmi output are modelled on NVIDIA Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM). The server models, sysObjectID values and the collector OID contract are in GPU simulation.

1.3.6.1.4.1.5703 is NVIDIA's IANA-registered PEN, so sysObjectID identifies a simulated DGX as an NVIDIA system. Nothing below the PEN is published by NVIDIA. NVIDIA ships no SNMP GPU MIB, and real DCGM exposes a Prometheus /metrics endpoint, not SNMP. Treat the layout below as nl6's contract with its collectors, never as a vendor specification. The arc used to sit under 1.3.6.1.4.1.53246, which is no longer served; see GPU simulation. No OID below 5703 has an explicit SNMP type. A numeric value is encoded as INTEGER and any other value as OCTET STRING.
documents.s: The OID layout is nl6's own

documents.t: Every per-GPU OID is 1.3.6.1.4.1.5703.1.1.1.1.<column>.<gpu>, with <gpu> from 0 to 7. Static columns come from the *_snmp_gpu.json resource file and never change. Column Name Type H100 example 1 GPU name OCTET STRING NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 2 GPU UUID OCTET STRING GPU-d4e8f2a1-7b3c-4d9e-a1f0-8c2d3e4f5a6b 3 GPU serial OCTET STRING 1560833002DEF 4 PCI bus ID OCTET STRING 00000000:07:00.0 13 Driver version OCTET STRING 535.129.03 14 CUDA version OCTET STRING 12.2 15 ECC errors, corrected INTEGER 0 16 ECC errors, uncorrected INTEGER 0 17 NVLink active links INTEGER 18 (A100: 6) Dynamic columns come from the metrics cycler. Eight columns times eight GPUs gives 64 dynamic GPU OIDs per device. With the three Host Resources OIDs under Standard MIBs, each device serves 67 dynamic OIDs. Column Name Type and unit Behaviour 5 GPU utilization INTEGER, percent 0 to 100 6 VRAM used INTEGER, MiB Follows utilization, 5 to 98 percent of VRAM total 7 VRAM total INTEGER, MiB Constant: 81920 (A100, H100), 144384 (H200) 8 Temperature INTEGER, degrees Celsius Rises with utilization, clamped to 25 to 95 9 Power draw INTEGER, watts Follows utilization, clamped to the profile's power range 10 Fan speed INTEGER, percent 0 (liquid cooled) unless the GPU is above 70 °C, then 5 to 19 11 SM clock INTEGER, MHz 60 to 100 percent of the base clock, higher under load 12 Memory clock INTEGER, MHz 70 to 100 percent of the base clock, higher under load

Each GPU holds a pre-generated cycle of 100 points per metric, seeded from a hash of the device IP and the GPU number. The point served depends on the time since the device was created: one point per minute, so a cycle lasts 100 minutes. Reading a column does not move it, so two collectors polling the same OID read the same value, and a walk that reads a dynamic OID without returning it changes nothing. Every metric of every GPU of a device reads the same point at the same instant, so power, temperature, fan speed and both clocks follow the utilization they were derived from. VRAM total is constant. One SNMP request reads the point once, so every OID in a GET, GETNEXT or GETBULK comes from the same point, even across a minute boundary. Up to v0.38.1 every read returned the next point and each metric had its own cursor, so the value moved per read and the derived metrics drifted apart from utilization. The per-profile ranges the cycles are drawn from: Parameter A100 H100 H200 Utilization base, percent 15 to 85 20 to 90 20 to 90 Temperature base, °C 35 to 75 35 to 80 35 to 78 Power draw, W 100 to 400 150 to 700 150 to 700 SM base clock, MHz 1410 1980 1980 Memory base clock, MHz 1512 2619 2619

The profiles also serve system, the IF-MIB interface tables and Host Resources (1.3.6.1.2.1.25). Interface counters come from the same engine as every other device type; see SNMP. Three Host Resources OIDs are dynamic and come from the device's metrics cycler, not the static resource file. They behave like the per-GPU metrics, including the minute-boundary case, described in Value behaviour. OID Name Behaviour 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.3.3.1.2.1 hrProcessorLoad.1 Cycling CPU percent, moves to the next point once per minute 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.2.3.1.5.1 hrStorageSize.1 Constant physical memory total from the device profile, never advances 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.2.3.1.6.1 hrStorageUsed.1 Cycling physical memory used, moves to the next point once per minute The other Host Resources OIDs, including storage row 2, are static.

Each profile answers exactly these fourteen commands, and nothing else. The output is static text from the *_ssh.json resource file. It does not track the SNMP metric values. Command Output nvidia-smi GPU summary table for all eight GPUs, with processes nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY Per-GPU memory detail nvidia-smi -q -d UTILIZATION Per-GPU utilization detail nvidia-smi -q -d TEMPERATURE Per-GPU temperature and thresholds nvidia-smi -q -d POWER Per-GPU power draw and limits nvidia-smi topo -m GPU topology matrix dcgmi discovery -l GPUs discovered by DCGM dcgmi health -c DCGM health check show version OS version with NVIDIA driver details uname -a Kernel details hostname Host name free -h System memory summary lscpu CPU details lspci | grep -i nvidia NVIDIA PCI devices

Each profile serves seven GET paths on the device's HTTPS API port (8443 by default). The bodies are static JSON from the *_api.json resource file and do not track the SNMP metric values. There is no per-GPU path such as /api/v1/gpu/devices/{id}. The top-level fields differ between profiles on every path except /api/v1/gpu/devices. Path Profile Top-level fields /api/v1/gpu/status A100 gpu_count, driver_version, cuda_version, dcgm_version, overall_health, gpus /api/v1/gpu/status H100, H200 gpu_count, driver_version, cuda_version, dcgm_version, gpus /api/v1/gpu/devices All count, devices /api/v1/gpu/topology A100 nvlink_version, nvswitch_count, gpu_count, connectivity, numa_affinity /api/v1/gpu/topology H100, H200 gpu_count, nvlink_version, nvswitch_count, topology, links_per_gpu, bandwidth_per_link_gbps, total_bandwidth_per_gpu_gbps, connections /api/v1/dcgm/health A100 overall_health, checks, last_check /api/v1/dcgm/health H100, H200 overall_health, checks, gpu_health /api/v1/dcgm/config A100 dcgm_version, monitoring_interval_ms, features, watched_fields /api/v1/dcgm/config H100, H200 dcgm_version, monitoring_enabled, collection_interval_ms, health_check_interval_s, profiling_enabled, watched_fields /api/v1/system/info A100 hostname, os, kernel, architecture, nvidia_driver, cuda_version, dcgm_version, dgx_software_version, cpu_model, cpu_sockets, cpu_cores_total, gpu_count, gpu_model, infiniband_ports, infiniband_speed_gbps /api/v1/system/info H100 hostname, os, kernel, architecture, driver_version, cuda_version, dcgm_version, dgx_software_version, cpu, gpu, network /api/v1/system/info H200 hostname, os, kernel, architecture, driver_version, cuda_version, dcgm_version, hgx_software_version, cpu, gpu, network /api/v1/system/memory A100 system_memory, gpu_memory, swap /api/v1/system/memory H100, H200 total_gb, used_gb, free_gb, shared_gb, buff_cache_gb, available_gb, swap_total_gb, swap_used_gb, swap_free_gb

nl6 maintains a per-device, in-memory interface state engine that owns oper-status, admin-status, and last-change for every known ifIndex. SNMP, gNMI Get, and gNMI Subscribe ON_CHANGE all read from the same slot table. Values agree byte-for-byte at every instant. State can be mutated by a scheduled link-flap scenario, by a REST control plane or by an SNMP SET of ifAdminStatus.<N>. A derived ifOperStatus transition also fires the device's role-tagged link trap and syslog entries for that interface. Every counter the cycler derives from the octet dial holds while the derived ifOperStatus is not up(1), and resumes from the held value when it returns. This is the capability reference. For the gNMI subscribe semantics see gNMI reference.

The engine is the single source of truth for ifOperStatus.<N>, ifAdminStatus.<N> and ifLastChange.<N>. SNMP and gNMI reads go through it, and an ON_CHANGE subscription receives an event on every mutation. The engine stores the link state and ifAdminStatus. ifOperStatus is derived from the pair per RFC 2863 and is never stored. Three mutation sources: the flap scheduler, the REST control plane and an SNMP SET of ifAdminStatus.<N>. The flap scheduler and the REST oper-status POST move the link. The REST admin-status POST and the SET move admin. No gNMI Set. Every derived ifOperStatus transition fires the role-tagged linkDown / linkUp trap and interface-down / interface-up syslog entries of the device's catalog for that ifIndex. Per-interface bandwidth does not scale with admin-status changes, and gNMI SAMPLE subscriptions do not support suppress_redundant. For an ifIndex the device does not own, the engine reports ifAdminStatus up(1) but ifOperStatus unknown(4). IF-MIB has no unknown admin value. SNMP does not serve such an ifIndex from the engine, but a template that reads it does: {{.IfAdminStatus}} on an on-demand fire with a pinned IfIndex reads up(1). Check the device's interface list before trusting the admin value.

Every octet, packet, error and discard column the counter engine derives holds while the derived ifOperStatus is not up(1). That covers admin-down, a subinterface reading lowerLayerDown(7) because its parent is down, and an interface seeded down at boot (an empty optic bay). An interface that boots in a non-up state reads its pre-seeded base from the first poll. When the interface returns to up(1) the columns resume from the held value with no jump. The traffic the dial would have produced during the hold is dropped, never replayed. Counters never decrease, even under tight flapping. SNMP, both gNMI resolvers, gNMI dial-out and the sFlow counter_sample read the same held value at the same instant. A gNMI SAMPLE stream keeps sending the held value every interval. The sFlow counter_sample status word reads admin and oper from the same engine. ifLastChange, ifSpeed and ifHighSpeed do not hold: a down port keeps its line rate, as IOS-XR and Junos do. Two surfaces do not follow the hold. The SSH CLI counter text is static profile JSON. Flow records (NetFlow, IPFIX, sFlow flow samples) name a fixed ingress ifIndex and keep flowing regardless of interface state. Roll-up. An interface with one lower layer (a <port>.<unit> subinterface, or an interface stacked on one port in ifStackTable) serves a fixed share of its parent's served octet delta instead of its own dial. The shares of one parent's children sum below 1, so on every Counter64 column and on the error and discard columns a parent is at least the sum of its children at every instant, held or not. An interface stacked on two or more lower layers is an aggregate (a bundle) and serves the sum of its members' served deltas. Its octet columns equal the member sum exactly, and its packet columns read within one packet per member of it. The composition is applied after each parent's or member's own hold, so a member cable pull lowers the bundle and a held parent holds its children. A bundle's own oper-status does not follow its members, so a bundle whose members are all down stays up.

The flag tables for -if-scenario, -if-failure-pct, -if-flap-scenario and -if-flap-global-cap are in CLI flags → Interface-state scenarios. The flap scheduler is always started, so REST-created devices with a non-clean if_flap_scenario register and flap regardless of the CLI default.

-if-scenario seeds the initial ifAdminStatus and link state of every simulated interface, so you can reproduce common network conditions without editing resource files. ifOperStatus is never seeded; it is derived from admin and link. The seed is applied once per device, when the engine is built, to every device the process creates: the auto-start batch and REST-created devices alike. There is no read-time override, so a SET, a REST POST or a flap is read back by the next GET, walk, gNMI read or REST view under every scenario. Scenario Name ifAdminStatus Link ifOperStatus Use case 1 all-shutdown down (2) as shipped down (2), derived Planned maintenance, device decommission 2 all-normal (default) as shipped shipped ifOperStatus derived; down (2) where shipped admin is down Normal steady-state operations 3 all-failure up (1) down down (2) Link failures, SFP issues, cable pull 4 pct-failure up (1) down where ifIndex % 100 < n, else up down for n% Partial outage, staged rollout testing n is -if-failure-pct, default 10. Scenario 4's rule is deterministic, so results are reproducible across restarts. Scenario 2 does not force anything up. It seeds admin from the shipped ifAdminStatus and the link from the shipped ifOperStatus, and most shipped profiles declare both up. ifOperStatus is still derived, so a row shipped admin-down with ifOperStatus 1 reads down (2). Five profiles ship interfaces down: Profile ifAdminStatus down (2) ifOperStatus down (2) asr9k none ifIndex 44 and 45 cisco_asr9902 none ifIndex 15 to 24, 35 and 36, 41 to 48 cisco_nexus_9500 ifIndex 33 to 64 ifIndex 3 to 10, 21 to 30, 41 to 50, 61 to 64 juniper_mx960 none 27 interfaces, ifIndex 2, 5, 7 and every third ifIndex from 10 to 79 palo_alto_pa3220 none ifIndex 2 Those interfaces boot down under the default scenario. Use scenario 3 if you want every interface down regardless of profile. The seed is initial state, not a transition. It fires no link trap, no syslog and no gNMI ON_CHANGE update, and ifLastChange reads 0 until something changes. lldpRemTable only emits a row when both ends of a link are oper-up. Scenarios 1 and 3 therefore empty every device's neighbour table, and scenario 4 drops the rows whose local or remote port it put down. ifAlias reflects configured intent and stays. Scenario 1 shuts the port and preserves the link underneath it. Admin-down forces ifOperStatus to down(2) while the link keeps whatever the profile declared. A SET of ifAdminStatus to up(1) or a REST admin-status POST brings an interface back to the value its link had reached, which for most profiles is up. Scenario 3 seeds the link down, so it survives an admin bounce. Shutting and unshutting a port under scenario 3 leaves ifOperStatus = 2: the scenario models a cable pull, and an administrative bounce does not repair a cable. RFC 2863 describes this: admin-up releases ifOperStatus to the physical layer rather than forcing it up. Paired with a link-flap scenario: Under scenario 1 every flap is masked (see Link-flap scenarios). Unshutting a port shows whatever its link had reached. Under scenarios 3 and 4 the first up-flap brings a failed interface back, because the port is administratively up and a flap is a real link event. For a fleet that stays down, leave -if-flap-scenario at clean or use scenario 1. The scenario reaches the interfaces the counter engine knows: those with an ifXTable .6 (ifHCInOctets) row in the device's resource files. An ifAdminStatus or ifOperStatus row for any other ifIndex is served from the resource file unchanged. To spot-check a scenario, walk the two columns: snmpwalk -v2c -c public 10.42.0.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7 # ifAdminStatus snmpwalk -v2c -c public 10.42.0.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8 # ifOperStatus

Scenario Mean inter-flap (per interface) Down duration Use case clean (default) ∞ (no flaps) n/a Steady-state regression testing rare ~6 hours uniform 1 to 10 s Background variance for long-running fleets typical ~15 minutes uniform 1 to 30 s Stress-testing collector alarm pipelines aggressive ~1 minute uniform 1 to 5 s Chaos / churn measurement Inter-arrival times are exponentially distributed (Poisson process). A flap sets the link down, and the matching up-event follows after the down duration. ifLastChange moves, and an ON_CHANGE update fires, only when the derived ifOperStatus moves. A flap on an interface whose ifAdminStatus is DOWN or TESTING is masked: the link moves, nothing observable changes, ifLastChange does not advance, and no trap, syslog or ON_CHANGE update fires. The link is still there when the port is unshut. This is what the hardware does, so -if-scenario 1 -if-flap-scenario aggressive never reports ifAdminStatus = down(2) with ifOperStatus = up(1). The REST oper-status endpoint sets the link too, so the same masking applies and its 202 body reports "masked": true. The down-up pair is atomic per (device, ifIndex). A new flap is not scheduled while the interface is already down. -if-flap-global-cap 10 caps simulator-wide event rate at 10/s, backpressuring the scheduler when needed. Default 0 is unlimited. At 30k devices × typical, the expected steady-state rate is ~30k / 900s ≈ 33 events/s. A cap below that floor systematically delays the scheduler, and a cap of 50 leaves 50% headroom for bursts.

A subinterface is an interface whose ifDescr is another interface's ifDescr followed by . and an unsigned integer, such as xe-0/0/0.0 under xe-0/0/0. The gNMI catalogue uses the same rule for its subinterfaces key source. An interface whose name does not say which port it rides on gets a parent from the profile's ifStackTable: an ifStackStatus.<higher>.<lower> row of active(1). The name rule decides first. Shipped profiles with subinterfaces: juniper_mx10004, juniper_mx240 and juniper_mx960: the logical units their CLI shows, by name. The MX10004 also states each unit's port in ifStackTable. cisco_asr9902: three VLAN subinterfaces, by name, each also stated over its port or bundle in ifStackTable. nokia_7750_sr12: router interface toWAN, stacked on port 1/1/1. Where a profile states a parent both ways the rows agree, so the hierarchy is the same with or without the table. The RFC 2863 marker rows (ifStackStatus.0.<I>, ifStackStatus.<I>.0) give no interface a parent and are not logged. A stacked interface follows its parent the same way, but gNMI still lists it under /interfaces/interface, because it is not a <port>.<unit> subinterface. A subinterface goes down with its parent. Its ifOperStatus reads lowerLayerDown(7) while its parent is not up, unless its own state already forces a value. Its own ifAdminStatus = down(2) still reads down(2). The subinterface's stored link and admin values are not written, so it comes back with its parent. A parent transition is also a transition of each subinterface it moves. ifLastChange is stamped with the parent's time, and the subinterface gets its own ON_CHANGE update. This holds for every mutation source: the flap scheduler, the REST endpoints, auto-revert and SNMP SET. No link trap or syslog message fires for that move. RFC 2863 sends linkDown on entering down(2) and linkUp on leaving it, and a move between up(1) and lowerLayerDown(7) does neither. A subinterface's own move to or from down(2) still fires them. The flap scheduler does not schedule an interface without a physical link of its own: a subinterface, or a softwareLoopback(24) such as lo on linux_server, Loopback0 on cisco_asr9902 and system on nokia_7750_sr12.

Sets the interface's link state, the physical-layer reading. ifOperStatus is derived from (ifAdminStatus, link), so this endpoint moves what a collector observes only when the interface is administratively up. The path is named for the leaf a caller is trying to move, not the leaf it writes. Body: { "status": "UP" | "DOWN" | "TESTING", "duration": "<go-duration>" // optional } Returns: 202 Accepted with the outcome on success: { "link": "UP", "oper_status": "DOWN", "admin_status": "DOWN", "masked": true } masked is true whenever ifAdminStatus is DOWN or TESTING. It is also true on a subinterface whose link is UP while its parent is not up, because it reads LOWER_LAYER_DOWN whatever the link does. In that state the link state you now hold is not what collectors see. While it is set, no link trap, syslog message or gNMI ON_CHANGE update will fire from this interface and ifLastChange will not move, whatever the link does. It is a property of the interface, not of the request, so a POST that changes nothing still reports it. 400 Bad Request for malformed body, unknown status, or unknown ifIndex (400 body includes validIfIndexes array) 404 Not Found for unknown device IP 503 Service Unavailable when the device has no metrics cycler / state engine Examples: # Force ifIndex 3 down indefinitely curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices/10.42.0.1/interfaces/3/oper-status \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"status":"DOWN"}' # Flap ifIndex 3 down for 30 seconds; auto-revert to the prior value curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices/10.42.0.1/interfaces/3/oper-status \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"status":"DOWN","duration":"30s"}' # Stage a fault on a shut port: accepted, link moves, reads stay down curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices/10.42.0.1/interfaces/3/oper-status \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"status":"UP"}' # {"link":"UP","oper_status":"DOWN","admin_status":"DOWN","masked":true} # Raising admin-status afterwards surfaces the link with no further request. # Bad ifIndex: 400 with valid list curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices/10.42.0.1/interfaces/999/oper-status \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"status":"DOWN"}' # {"error":"ifIndex 999 not present on device","validIfIndexes":[1,2,3,...]}

Same shape and semantics, mutates ifAdminStatus.<ifIndex>. Accepted statuses are UP / DOWN / TESTING (per IF-MIB ifAdminStatus enum). oper-status follows admin-status, asymmetrically, per RFC 2863: DOWN and TESTING force ifOperStatus to down(2) / testing(3). UP forces nothing. It releases ifOperStatus to the link state, so an interface whose link is down stays down(2). An admin bounce therefore does not repair a simulated link fault. Under -if-scenario 3 ("link failures, SFP issues, cable pull"), shutting and unshutting a port leaves ifOperStatus = 2, because the cable is still out. The link trap, the syslog message and the ON_CHANGE update fire exactly when the derived ifOperStatus moves, and ifLastChange is stamped exactly then. An admin change that does not move it, such as UP → DOWN over an already-down link, reports the admin leaf alone and leaves ifLastChange where the link-down transition put it, which is what RFC 2863 defines that object to mean. An SNMP SET of ifAdminStatus.<N> is a third source through the same funnel (see the SNMP reference), so a SET and this POST are indistinguishable to every reader. There is no way to hold an interface operationally up while it is administratively down. RFC 2863 forbids that state, and no mutation source can produce it.

When duration is set, the handler: Snapshots the pre-mutation value at POST time. For oper-status that is the link, not the derived ifOperStatus, so a masked POST's revert restores the link it found instead of writing the mask into it Performs the requested mutation immediately Registers a timer keyed by (ip, ifIndex, leaf) After duration elapses, reverts the slot back to the snapshotted value An admin-status revert goes through the same admin funnel as the POST. Oper therefore follows the restored admin value. It is released to whatever the link has reached, not forced up, and fires the matching link trap only if that moves it. Properties: A subsequent duration POST on the same leaf cancels the prior timer (the new timer's snapshot wins) Deleting the device or shutting the simulator down cancels all pending timers duration is capped at 24 hours; values above this are rejected with 400 Auto-revert bypasses -if-flap-global-cap, which limits only scheduler-driven flaps If the slot was already at the requested status when the POST arrived (idempotent no-op), the auto-revert still fires but returns the slot to that same snapshotted value. The auto-revert is therefore harmless on already-target slots.

A REST POST that flips a state field is observable simultaneously via: Surface Read path Value SNMP GET ifOperStatus.3 .1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.3 INTEGER: 2 gNMI Get /interfaces/interface[name=Gi0/3]/state/oper-status state engine openconfig-interfaces:DOWN gNMI Subscribe ON_CHANGE on same path state-change event update {oper-status: openconfig-interfaces:DOWN} All three read the same engine slot, so the values match byte-for-byte at every instant. Trap and syslog firings follow state transitions. Every derived ifOperStatus transition also fires the device's role-tagged link trap and syslog entries for that ifIndex, so a POST DOWN puts a linkDown trap and an interface-down syslog message on the wire. A vendor overlay may fire more than one entry per role; cisco_ios fires both %LINK-3-UPDOWN and %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN. Role-tagged entries are excluded from the random Poisson pick, so a link trap on the wire always corresponds to a state transition. The on-demand endpoints (POST .../trap, POST .../syslog) still fire an entry without moving state.

GET /api/v1/gnmi/status reports two counters for the state engine: { "subsystem_active": true, "tls_enabled": true, "listeners": 30000, "active_subscriptions": 12, "updates_sent": 567, "updates_dropped": 0, "tls_handshake_failures": 0, "listener_accept_failures": 0, "state_events_emitted": 42, "state_events_dropped": 0 } state_events_emitted: cumulative count of state-change events successfully fanned out to ON_CHANGE listeners. Counts per-listener, not per-event: a flap on a device with 3 listeners increments by 3. state_events_dropped: per-listener drop count when a depth-16 channel overflows. Drop policy is oldest-drop.

Per-device cost. The state engine adds ~24 bytes per ifIndex. At 30k devices × ~10 interfaces that is ≈ 7 MiB total. Each ON_CHANGE subscriber adds one depth-16 listener channel and one goroutine, ≈ 4 KiB.

nl6 can model inter-device links and expose them as a standards-compliant LLDP-MIB (IEEE 802.1AB, OID root 1.0.8802.1.1.2) neighbor table on every participating device, plus a transparent ifAlias link label. The intended consumer is an NMS's LLDP link-discovery daemon: point it at the simulator and it builds a topology map of the fleet.

The simplest fleet: four auto-start devices wired into two point-to-point pairs on ifIndex 1. (Auto-start devices use the default asr9k profile; ifIndex 1 is its management port, which is fine for a link.) Create pairs.json: { "links": [ { "a": {"ip": "10.0.0.1", "ifindex": 1}, "b": {"ip": "10.0.0.2", "ifindex": 1} }, { "a": {"ip": "10.0.0.3", "ifindex": 1}, "b": {"ip": "10.0.0.4", "ifindex": 1} } ] } sudo ./nl6 -auto-start-ip 10.0.0.1 -auto-count 4 -topology-config pairs.json The graph loads at startup; the four devices come up in the background and the links resolve lazily. Verify: snmpwalk -v2c -c public 10.0.0.1 1.0.8802.1.1.2 # local + neighbor (10.0.0.2) snmpget -v2c -c public 10.0.0.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0 # this device's (random) sysName snmpget -v2c -c public 10.0.0.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.18.1 # ifAlias = to_<peer-sysName>_<peer-port> curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/v1/topology/status | jq # {subsystem_active:true, configured_links:2, active_links:2}

A realistic example is the minimal 5-stage Clos from containerlab's min-5clos. It has two superspines, two pods of two spines + two leaves each, and a client on a leaf in each pod. Twelve devices, eighteen links, with a sensible device type per tier: Tier Device type Nodes IPs Ports used Superspine cisco_crs_x (144-port core) 2 10.0.0.1 to 10.0.0.2 1 to 4 (to the 4 spines) Spine arista_7280r3 4 10.0.1.1 to 10.0.1.4 1 to 2 up (superspines), 3 to 4 down (leaves) Leaf cisco_catalyst_9500 4 10.0.2.1 to 10.0.2.4 1 to 2 up (spines); 3 to a client on leaf1 / leaf3 Client linux_server 2 10.0.3.1 to 10.0.3.2 1 (to its leaf) superspine1 (10.0.0.1) superspine2 (10.0.0.2) / | | \ / | | \ spine1 spine2 spine3 spine4 ...full mesh superspine↔spine... (10.0.1.1) (.2) (.3) (.4) / \ / \ | \ | \ leaf1 leaf2 ... leaf3 leaf4 (10.0.2.1)(.2) (10.0.2.3)(.4) | | client1 (10.0.3.1) client2 (10.0.3.2) Boot the server and create the four tiers: sudo ./nl6 # subsystems are always-on; no topology flag needed curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"start_ip":"10.0.0.1","device_count":2,"netmask":"16","resource_file":"cisco_crs_x.json"}' # superspines curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"start_ip":"10.0.1.1","device_count":4,"netmask":"16","resource_file":"arista_7280r3.json"}' # spines curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"start_ip":"10.0.2.1","device_count":4,"netmask":"16","resource_file":"cisco_catalyst_9500.json"}' # leaves curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"start_ip":"10.0.3.1","device_count":2,"netmask":"16","resource_file":"linux_server.json"}' # clients Wire the fabric. Save it as clos.json and POST it: { "links": [ { "a": {"ip":"10.0.0.1","ifindex":1}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.1.1","ifindex":1} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.0.1","ifindex":2}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.1.2","ifindex":1} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.0.1","ifindex":3}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.1.3","ifindex":1} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.0.1","ifindex":4}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.1.4","ifindex":1} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.0.2","ifindex":1}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.1.1","ifindex":2} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.0.2","ifindex":2}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.1.2","ifindex":2} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.0.2","ifindex":3}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.1.3","ifindex":2} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.0.2","ifindex":4}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.1.4","ifindex":2} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.1.1","ifindex":3}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.2.1","ifindex":1} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.1.1","ifindex":4}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.2.2","ifindex":1} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.1.2","ifindex":3}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.2.1","ifindex":2} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.1.2","ifindex":4}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.2.2","ifindex":2} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.1.3","ifindex":3}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.2.3","ifindex":1} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.1.3","ifindex":4}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.2.4","ifindex":1} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.1.4","ifindex":3}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.2.3","ifindex":2} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.1.4","ifindex":4}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.2.4","ifindex":2} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.2.1","ifindex":3}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.3.1","ifindex":1} }, { "a": {"ip":"10.0.2.3","ifindex":3}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.3.2","ifindex":1} } ] } curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/topology \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data @clos.json Now each tier shows its fabric neighbors. A spine (10.0.1.1) has 4 neighbors, two superspines (ports 1 to 2) and two leaves (ports 3 to 4). A leaf (10.0.2.1) has 3, two spines and its client: snmpwalk -v2c -c public 10.0.1.1 1.0.8802.1.1.2.1.4 # spine: 4 lldpRem rows snmpwalk -v2c -c public 10.0.2.1 1.0.8802.1.1.2.1.4 # leaf: 3 lldpRem rows curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/v1/topology/status | jq # configured_links:18, active_links:18 Each device's sysName is randomly generated at creation (e.g. SPINE-AB12), so the ifAlias labels (to_<peer-sysName>_<peer-port>) and lldpRemSysName values uniquely identify the far end of every fabric link. Read a device's own name with snmpget … 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0.

Take one end of the spine1↔leaf1 link down and its neighbor rows disappear on both sides, while the ifAlias (configured intent) stays: # leaf1 (10.0.2.1) port 1 faces spine1 (10.0.1.1) port 3 curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices/10.0.2.1/interfaces/1/oper-status \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"status":"DOWN"}' curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/v1/topology/status | jq '.active_links' # now 17 snmpwalk -v2c -c public 10.0.1.1 1.0.8802.1.1.2.1.4 | wc -l # spine1: one fewer neighbor snmpget -v2c -c public 10.0.2.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.18.1 # leaf1 ifAlias unchanged Walk anchor. LLDP lives at 1.0.8802.*, which sorts before the mib-2 tree. A walk rooted at 1.3.6.1 never reaches it. Anchor at 1.0.8802 (and point your NMS's LLDP discovery at the LLDP root).

A link is a single undirected edge between two endpoints, each an (deviceIP, ifIndex) pair. The graph is simulator-wide and owned by the manager. It is the single source of truth, and each device derives its own LLDP local-system data, local-port table, and remote (neighbor) table from the edges touching it. One link per local port (point-to-point). A second link on a port that is already used is rejected. Lazy resolution. A link is validated syntactically at add time (no self-loop, no duplicate, one link per port). Device existence and ifIndex ownership are resolved later, when SNMP is served. So a link may reference a device that hasn't been created yet (e.g. an auto-start batch still spinning up). The edge stays inert until both ends resolve. Edges are pruned automatically when a referenced device is deleted.

sudo ./nl6 -topology-config links.json { "links": [ { "a": {"ip": "10.0.0.1", "ifindex": 1}, "b": {"ip": "10.0.0.2", "ifindex": 2} }, { "a": {"ip": "10.0.0.2", "ifindex": 3}, "b": {"ip": "10.0.0.3", "ifindex": 1} } ] } Syntactic validation failures are fatal at startup. Unknown JSON fields are rejected.

Method & path Body Result POST /api/v1/topology {"links":[{"a":{...},"b":{...}}]} 201; all-or-nothing (a rejected link rolls back the batch) GET /api/v1/topology none 200 {"links":[…]} DELETE /api/v1/topology {"a":{...},"b":{...}} 204, or 404 if the link is absent GET /api/v1/topology/status none 200 {"subsystem_active", "configured_links", "active_links"} GET /api/v1/topology/graph none 200 {"nodes":[…], "edges":[…]}, viz-ready, with live per-link state active_links counts links whose both endpoints are resolvable and operationally up. Those are the links currently producing a neighbor row. The difference between configured_links and active_links is your down-link count.

GET /api/v1/topology/graph returns the topology as a single viz-ready object. It joins the link graph with device identity and live per-link state, so a client renders from one fetch: { "nodes": [ { "ip": "10.0.0.1", "sysName": "core1", "type": "Cisco CRS-X", "degree": 4 }, { "ip": "10.0.0.9", "degree": 1, "missing": true } // dangling endpoint, no live device ], "edges": [ { "a": {"ip":"10.0.0.1","ifindex":1,"ifName":"Hu0/1"}, "b": {"ip":"10.0.0.2","ifindex":2,"ifName":"Eth1"}, "active": true }, { "a": {…}, "b": {…}, "active": false, "downEnd": "b" } // downEnd: "a" | "b" | "both" ] } The graph is edge-driven. Nodes are the distinct endpoints of configured links (a link-less device does not appear); a link endpoint with no live device is flagged missing: true. active uses the same liveness rule as /topology/status; downEnd is omitted when the edge is active. This is the data source for the web-console visualization, and is handy on its own for reconciling a deployed topology against intent (missing nodes + inactive edges surface dangling links automatically).

Per device with at least one configured link: OID Value lldpLocChassisIdSubtype.0 (…1.3.1.0) 4 (macAddress) lldpLocChassisId.0 (…1.3.2.0) 6-byte MAC 02:42:<ipv4> lldpLocSysName.0 (…1.3.3.0) device sysName lldpLocSysDesc.0 (…1.3.4.0) device sysDescr lldpLocPortTable (…1.3.7.1.{2,3,4}.<ifIndex>) port id subtype 5, lldpLocPortId/Desc = ifDescr lldpRemTable (…1.4.1.1.{4..10}.0.<localPort>.1) the peer's chassis id, port id, sysName, sysDesc ifAlias (1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.18.<ifIndex>) to_<peerSysName>_<peerIfDescr> The neighbor row index is {lldpRemTimeMark=0, lldpRemLocalPortNum=ifIndex, lldpRemIndex=1}. Stitching. lldpRemChassisId/lldpRemPortId on one device are derived from the peer's own canonical sources (the 02:42:<ipv4> chassis MAC and the peer's ifDescr). These are identical to what the peer advertises in its local data, so Enlinkd matches the two half-links.

lldpRemTable rows are oper-status-aware. A neighbor row is served only while both endpoints are operationally up. Take either port down (flap scenario, or POST .../oper-status DOWN) and the row disappears on both sides; bring it back up and the row returns. A device type with no interface-state engine is treated as up. Because the two ends live on different devices, the both-sides property is eventually-consistent. ifAlias reflects configured intent and is present regardless of oper-status. So ifXTable shows what should be connected and the LLDP table shows what is actually up. Diff the two to find down links. An ifAlias is emitted only for a link whose peer is resolvable; an unresolvable peer yields no label (never a malformed to__), leaving any static ifAlias in place.

LLDP lives at 1.0.8802.1.1.2, which sorts before the standard mib-2 tree. A walk anchored at 1.3.6.1 will never reach it. Anchor at the LLDP root: snmpwalk -v2c -c public 10.0.0.1 1.0.8802.1.1.2 snmpget -v2c -c public 10.0.0.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.18.1 # ifAlias link label

When a topology is deployed, the web console (http://<host>:8080/) shows an Inter-device topology panel. It is gated on configured_links > 0, so no topology means no panel. It renders GET /api/v1/topology/graph with a locally-vendored sigma.js + graphology stack (no CDN; works in the nl6sim namespace / airgapped). Live liveness. Edges are green when up, red when down; nodes are labeled by sysName (type + degree on hover), and dangling endpoints render grey. The view refreshes on the console's poll cadence. It recolors in place on a state change and only re-runs the layout when the graph structure changes, so nodes don't jump every tick. Two layouts. Tiered (the default) places devices in horizontal fabric bands ranked by device model, so a Clos fabric reads top-down; Force is a deterministic, seeded Fruchterman-Reingold layout.
