A Force/Tiered toggle in the topology panel switches between them. Click-to-flap. Click an edge to toggle the link (down one end; click again to restore). The edge thickens on hover so it's an easy target. Click a node to fail the device (downs all its links) after a confirm dialog. Both reuse POST .../oper-status; the canvas refreshes immediately after. Scale guard. Above 500 nodes / 2000 links the panel shows a summary (device/link/active counts) with a render anyway control instead of drawing the graph.

Capability bitmaps (lldpRemSysCapSupported/Enabled), lldpStatistics / lldpConfiguration, gNMI/openconfig-lldp, multi-neighbor (shared-segment) ports, and operator-supplied custom alias text. The visualization is poll-driven (no SSE push) and does not persist layout positions.

The load-test scenario subsystem is driven entirely over REST under /api/v1/scenarios. A scenario moves through the fixed lifecycle submitted → armed → running → stopped, with armed → canceled and running → aborted branches. It finalizes an immutable report that an operator diffs against a monitor's received counts. See the scenarios guide for how to use these endpoints to run a fidelity check and troubleshoot failures.

JSON everywhere, snake_case field names, direct objects (no envelope). Success returns the resource directly. Errors return {"error": "<message>"}, plus "field": "<json.key>" for 400 validation failures (fail-fast, so only the first offending field). 409 bodies name the current phase, the scenario ID, and the verb that could not resolve. Timestamps are RFC 3339 with millisecond precision (2006-01-02T15:04:05.000Z07:00). Request bodies are decoded with DisallowUnknownFields (a typo'd or unknown key is a 400). POST /api/v1/scenarios caps its body at 1,865,536 bytes (≈1.78 MiB); POST /api/v1/scenarios/{id}/start reads at most 1 KiB. The submit cap holds a ceiling-sized participant list (100,000 entries × 18 bytes for "255.255.255.255",) plus a shared 64 KiB allowance for all other fields. Send participant lists as compact JSON, because pretty-printing adds bytes per entry and can exceed the cap on its own. A large rate_profile or abort_predicate on a ceiling-sized list can exceed it too. An over-cap body returns a 400 naming the cap, with no "field" key, because the limit trips during transport decoding.

Verb Path Success Errors POST /api/v1/scenarios 202 {id, config_sha256} 400, 409 POST /api/v1/scenarios/{id}/arm 200 readiness 404, 409 POST /api/v1/scenarios/{id}/start 200 status 404, 409 POST /api/v1/scenarios/{id}/stop 200 report 404, 409 GET /api/v1/scenarios/{id}/report 200 report 404, 409 GET /api/v1/scenarios/{id}/metrics 200 Prometheus text 404 GET /api/v1/scenarios 200 {scenarios:[{id,phase}]} none GET /api/v1/scenarios/{id} 200 status 404 DELETE /api/v1/scenarios/{id} 200 {} 404, 409 {id} is the zero-padded monotonic scenario ID (s-000001).

Registers a scenario and validates it structurally. Returns the allocated ID and the config fingerprint. Refused (409) only when 8 scenarios are already non-terminal. Exclusivity is per device, not per submit, so scenarios with disjoint participants run concurrently and overlapping ones are refused at arm, where membership is finally known. Submit cannot make that call: participants_cidr resolves against the live fleet, so at submit the participant set is not merely unknown but unknowable. Request body: { "participants": ["10.42.0.1", "10.42.0.2"], "protocol": "syslog", "rate": 10, "window": "2s", "seed": 42 } Field Type Required Meaning participants []string yes¹ Device management IPs, as a set. At most 100,000 entries, no repeats (a duplicate is a 400). Each must be an IPv4 dotted quad; IPv6 and IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:10.42.0.1) are a 400. Existence is checked at arm, not here. participants_cidr []string yes¹ Compact prefix selector: IPv4 CIDR prefixes in canonical (masked) form, at most 1,024 entries. The participant set is the union of participants and every live device whose IP falls inside any prefix, resolved at arm time. 400 at submit for: a non-canonical prefix (10.42.1.5/16, and the error names the canonical form), an IPv6 or IPv4-mapped prefix, a duplicate prefix, or a prefix nested inside another (it adds nothing to the union). An explicit participants entry covered by a prefix is allowed and makes that address's absence loud. ["0.0.0.0/0"] spells whole-fleet. protocol string yes Participating push protocol: "syslog", "netflow9", "ipfix", "gnmi-dialout", "snmp-trap", "sflow", or "netflow5". rate number yes Per-device events/second. Finite, > 0, ≤ 1000 (the scheduler's 1 ms floor). Drives the emission cadence for syslog and snmp-trap (one event per scheduler pop). For flow protocols it sets the record rate by sizing each participant's flow cache, and it has a per-device ceiling; see Choose participant cardinality and rate. For gnmi-dialout, rate does not control emission, because the stream runs at its dial-out SAMPLE interval. No nl6_scenario_target_rate gauge is published for such a run. Always required and fingerprinted. window string yes Measurement window length as a Go duration ("2s", "5m"). > 0, ≤ 24h. T1 = T0 + window; the window is half-open [T0, T1). seed number no Pins every random draw the scenario makes (determinism / reproducibility). rate_profile object no Time-varying intensity λ(t) (see below). Omitted or {"kind":"constant"} keeps the flat rate. expect_participants number no Declared participant cardinality: how many devices you expect the selectors to resolve to. Exact. Start is refused when the participating count differs in either direction, because a silently different denominator is what makes a run incomparable to its baseline. Must be between 1 and 100,000; an explicit 0 is a 400 (use omission to mean "no expectation", so a caller that computes this number and hits a zero-length bug cannot silently lose the guard). Without participants_cidr it must also be <= the number of declared participants, since the armed set cannot exceed the list. A larger value is unsatisfiable by construction and is refused at submit rather than deferred to a 409 at start. Also checked when scheduling an absolute T0, so a doomed schedule is refused immediately instead of at fire time. Fingerprinted in config_sha256, because it is declared intent. Don't know the number yet? Submit without it, arm, read participants_armed, then re-submit with it. abort_predicate object no Self-abort a runaway run when a mid-run ledger metric crosses a threshold (see below). ¹ At least one of participants / participants_cidr must be non-empty; both empty is a 400. Removed request fields​ A removed request field is a breaking change for a harness: a submit carrying it returns a 400. The submit config carries no version of its own, so it moves with nl6_version and removals are listed here. Field Why drain It configured nothing: the post-window phase is a barrier, not a duration. The refusal keys on the key's presence, so "", null, 0s and a non-string value are all 400; delete the key. A body that never carried it keeps its config_sha256, so baselines stay comparable. The drain ledger bucket and the drain_end timestamp are unaffected. Abort predicate (abort_predicate)​ An optional guard that aborts the scenario through the standard running → aborted pipeline when a fleet-wide ledger metric stays over a threshold for a grace period, so a bad experiment stops itself before drowning the collector. {"metric": "send_failures", "threshold": 100, "grace": "5s"} Field Meaning metric Ledger counter to watch: send_failures | dropped | deferred | sent (= in_window + drain). threshold Abort when the fleet-wide sum of metric exceeds this. > 0. grace The threshold must hold this long before aborting (Go duration; omitted = 0). The predicate is evaluated on a 1 s cadence using approximate mid-run reads of the live atomics (no drain barrier). The resulting report is a normal aborted artifact (see the scenarios guide). Rate profiles (rate_profile)​ By default a scenario emits at the flat rate with an exact fixed-interval cadence. A rate_profile instead shapes emission over the window as a non-homogeneous Poisson process drawn by inversion of the integrated intensity Λ(t). This gives production-shaped load, not a flat trickle. Every profile's peak rate is capped at 1000 events/s and must stay strictly positive. kind Fields λ(t) constant (default) none flat rate, exact cadence (deterministic count) linear start_rate, end_rate ramps linearly from start_rate at T0 to end_rate at T1 sine mean_rate (default rate), amplitude (< mean_rate), period (duration) mean_rate + amplitude·sin(2π·t/period) staged stages: [{duration, rate}, …] piecewise-constant; the last stage extends to T1 { "participants": ["10.42.0.1"], "protocol": "syslog", "rate": 10, "window": "5m", "seed": 42, "rate_profile": { "kind": "linear", "start_rate": 5, "end_rate": 200 } } rate is still required (it is the fixed-cadence rate and the sine mean default). A given (seed, profile) is fully reproducible: the per-device arrival stream is seeded from (seed, device IP), so the fleet is deterministic yet devices are not phase-locked. An over-cap profile is still governed by the shared global rate limiter. Response 202: {"id": "s-000001", "config_sha256": "9b8d8c9c…969314"} config_sha256 is the SHA-256 over the canonicalized (key-sorted) request JSON, so two byte-different-but-equal submissions fingerprint identically. 400 examples: {"error": "scenario: unknown protocol \"snmp\" (supported: syslog, netflow9, ipfix, gnmi-dialout, snmp-trap, sflow, netflow5)"} {"error": "invalid window \"nope\": …", "field": "window"} {"error": "json: unknown field \"bogus\""}

Resolves participants against the live fleet, installs the per-device participation handles, and publishes the armed gate, which suppresses background telemetry for participants. Unknown or ineligible devices are reported in excluded rather than failing the arm. Re-arming re-resolves membership from scratch. The excluded set is rebuilt and the armed count can go down. Counters already accrued for a participant that stays armed carry forward. Re-arming also cancels a pending absolute-T0 start, reported as "scheduled_start_cancelled": true. A scheduled start that fails on its own (every participant deleted, or a device-creation batch in progress at T0) leaves the scenario armed, logs the failure and releases the schedule without retrying. Response 200 (readiness): { "id": "s-000001", "phase": "armed", "participants_armed": 1, "excluded": [ {"device": "10.42.0.9", "reason": "device not found", "remediation_hint": "create the device before arming, or remove it from the scenario"} ], "excluded_total": 1 } The excluded rows are capped at 1,000; the counts are not. Arm-time exclusions get 900 rows and 100 are reserved for devices deleted between arm and start, whose identity you cannot recover otherwise. So readiness carries at most 900 rows and the report up to 1,000. excluded_total is always present (including 0) and is the authoritative count; the report's participants_excluded derives from it. excluded_by_reason gives reason → count over every exclusion whenever there is one. excluded_truncated: true appears only when rows were dropped. Fix what the rows show, re-arm, and the next batch surfaces. Prefix selectors silence only "not found". An address inside a participants_cidr prefix that matches no device produces no excluded row, while a matched device that cannot participate still gets one. List an address in participants as well to make its absence loud. Prefix matches resolve in address order, so re-arming an unchanged fleet returns a byte-identical response. Declared expectation. With expect_participants set, readiness echoes it as participants_expected and adds an expectation_mismatch diagnosis when the counts disagree. Arm discloses the mismatch; start enforces it. Situation What it means short, and exclusions account for it Devices were found and rejected; see excluded_by_reason. short, with no exclusions The selectors matched fewer live devices than expected, typically a prefix one bit too narrow. more than declared The fleet holds matching devices your expectation omits. Resolved-set ceiling (409). The resolved union is bounded by the same 100,000 cap, checked before any state changes. A refused re-arm leaves the previous arm intact, and a refused first arm leaves the scenario submitted.

Freezes fleet membership (device create/delete is rejected while running, so counter deltas cannot be corrupted mid-window), publishes the running gate at T0, and starts the scenario-owned scheduler. Refused (409) when 0/N participants armed. The window self-closes at T1 (auto-stop). Returns the status object. An optional body schedules the start at an absolute T0 so a run aligns to a wall-clock schedule without a warm operator: {"at": "2026-07-18T22:00:00Z"} The scenario stays armed and a controller timer fires the start at at (surfaced as scheduled_start in the status). A past at (or an unparseable one) is a 400 {"error","field":"at"}. A DELETE before T0 cancels cleanly. The timer is stopped, transports are released, and no report is produced. Omit the body to start immediately.

Ends emission, drains in-flight fires, finalizes the immutable report, and unfreezes the fleet. Idempotent: a scenario that already auto-closed at T1 returns 200 with the same report (only a stop with no finalized result, such as one before start, is a 409). Returns the report.

Returns the finalized report. 409 while the scenario has not reached a terminal phase (submitted / armed / running). What each protocol counts as one record, including sFlow and gNMI dial-out, is in the report schema. The format query parameter selects the representation (default JSON): ?format=csv returns a flat text/csv projection of counters[] (header row + one row per participant, join-ready on (protocol, source_ip, collector)); see the CSV projection. ?format=html returns a self-contained text/html page (embedded CSS, no external fonts / JS / frameworks): stat cards, the per-time-bucket loss-localization bar chart, run-tag panel, identity totals, and the participant table with per-row status. It is the human-readable view of the same data. Open it in a browser or attach it to a run. JSON stays the machine source of truth.

Returns the scenario's live state in Prometheus text-exposition format (text/plain; version=0.0.4). It needs no third-party client dependency. Scrape it directly. Deterministic ordering (participants sorted by source IP). 404 for an unknown id. It is valid in every phase. A submitted scenario has no participant rows yet. It shows only nl6_scenario_phase and nl6_scenario_target_rate, or only nl6_scenario_phase for gnmi-dialout. Metric Type Labels Meaning nl6_scenario_phase gauge id, phase 1 on the active phase label (info-style) nl6_scenario_target_rate gauge id configured base rate (events/s); for a rate_profile scenario this is the constant base rate, not the instantaneous λ(t); absent for gnmi-dialout, which paces to its SAMPLE interval, not to a rate nl6_scenario_sent_total counter id, protocol, source_ip, collector records sent (in_window + drain) per participant nl6_scenario_emitted_total counter (same tuple) records emitted (identity total) per participant nl6_scenario_in_window_total counter (same tuple) records sent inside the measurement window per participant nl6_scenario_drain_total counter (same tuple) records sent during the drain tail per participant nl6_scenario_suppressed_pre_window_total counter (same tuple) fires suppressed before T0 per participant nl6_scenario_send_failures_total counter (same tuple) transport send failures per participant nl6_scenario_dropped_total counter (same tuple) records dropped after the drain end per participant Every counter is labeled on the report join tuple (protocol, source_ip, collector), so summing a family reproduces the matching report summary total. For example, sum(nl6_scenario_sent_total) equals summary.sent. Because each counter only advances in-window, a Prometheus range query (increase(nl6_scenario_sent_total[…]) over [T0,T1]) reproduces the report totals. Every lifecycle transition is also written to the process log as a structured scenario=<id> phase=<phase> line for correlation.

{ "id": "s-000001", "phase": "running", "config_sha256": "9b8d8c9c…969314", "seed": 42, "transitions": [ {"phase": "submitted", "at": "2026-07-18T09:00:00.000Z"}, {"phase": "armed", "at": "2026-07-18T09:00:03.000Z"}, {"phase": "running", "at": "2026-07-18T09:00:05.000Z"} ] } transitions is the ordered lifecycle log; it is how a SIGTERM-driven aborted is observable after the fact. While a scenario is running (or after it finalizes), status also carries the live window and a counts block for unattended observability: { "id": "s-000001", "phase": "running", "protocol": "syslog", "window": "30s", "t0": "2026-07-18T09:00:05.000Z", "t1": "2026-07-18T09:00:35.000Z", "elapsed": "12.3s", "remaining": "17.7s", "counts": {"participants_armed": 2, "emitted": 1220, "sent": 1220, "in_window": 1220, "drain": 0, "suppressed_pre_window": 0, "send_failures": 0, "dropped": 0} } counts uses approximate mid-run atomic reads (no drain barrier). It is a live progress snapshot that may lag an in-flight fire. The finalized report is the exact record. t0/t1 are the actual window bounds (the running gate's, or the finalized result's).

{"scenarios": [{"id": "s-000001", "phase": "running"}]} Lists every registered scenario with its phase, in ID order. That is up to 8 non-terminal scenarios plus the 8 most recent terminal ones; older terminal scenarios are reaped. Empty scenarios: [] when none.

Releases the scenario. An armed scenario is canceled. Transports release and no report is produced. A submitted or terminal scenario is dropped, releasing any devices it held. A running scenario is refused (409). Stop or abort it first. After a successful DELETE, the ID returns 404.

Phase arm start stop report DELETE submitted → armed 409 409 409 drop armed → armed (re-resolves membership) → running (409 if 0/N) 409 409 cancel running 409 409 → stopped (report) 409 409 stopped / aborted 409 409 200 (idempotent) 200 drop canceled 409 409 409 409 drop

The load-test scenario subsystem is a telemetry-fidelity instrument. You arm a bounded experiment over a set of simulated devices, run it for a fixed window, and get back an exact, machine-readable report of what nl6 sent. Diff that sent-ledger against what your monitor received and any delta localizes missed or duplicated telemetry. That is fidelity in both directions. nl6 owns the ground truth: its send count is exact and, with a fixed seed, reproducible. So the report is the authority. A shortfall is real wire/collector loss, not measurement noise.

arm run [T0,T1) stop connect, stay silent → gated push only → finalize report │ │ │ nothing on the wire exactly what nl6 immutable sent-ledger (measurement pre-roll) emits, counted at send you diff vs received Bounded window. A scenario suppresses background telemetry for its participants, emits only during [T0,T1), then finalizes an immutable report. A sent-ledger, not a guess. Every record is counted at the send site into exactly one bucket (in_window / drain / send_failures / dropped / suppressed_pre_window); sent = in_window + drain is the reconciliation denominator. Seven protocols, one shape. Any one of syslog · SNMP trap/inform · NetFlow v5/v9 · IPFIX · sFlow · gNMI dial-out. Each device opts in via its own export config; the scenario gates whichever protocol it targets. Localize, don't just total. The report splits in-window sends into equal time sub-windows (loss localization) and tags each run per protocol so you can isolate it on a shared collector.

Page What it covers REST API Every endpoint, request/response shape, and error code. Scenarios The operating guide: lifecycle, fidelity mode, run tagging, reconciliation, troubleshooting. Runbooks Copy-pasteable worked recipes, one per use case. Report schema Every field, the ledger identity, loss localization, and the semver policy. Collector ceiling Method for measuring what a collector actually accepts, and not mistaking a drain rate for a capacity. New to it? Walk the lifecycle, then pick a matching runbook. There is a runnable end-to-end example under examples/scenario-syslog-fidelity/. It holds a compose stack (nl6 + a counting collector) and a run.sh that reproduces a documented known result.
Concurrency. Up to 8 scenarios run at once, each device in at most one; see the submit reference. In-memory only. Fetch the report before restarting.

The report is the machine-readable output of a finalized scenario. It is the authoritative record of what nl6 sent, which an operator diffs against a monitor's received counts to localize missed or duplicated telemetry. It is built once at stop/abort, immutable thereafter, and served by GET /api/v1/scenarios/{id}/report (also returned by stop). See the API reference and the scenarios guide.

{ "summary": { "id": "s-000001", "phase": "stopped", "protocol": "syslog", "metadata": { "config_sha256": "9b8d8c9c…969314", "resolved_participants_sha256": "3f1c…a204", "seed": 42, "nl6_version": "v0.16.0", "t0": "2026-07-18T09:00:05.000Z", "t1": "2026-07-18T09:00:07.000Z", "drain_end": "2026-07-18T09:00:07.500Z", "sub_window_count": 10, "sub_window_duration": "200ms", "run_tags": { "protocol": "syslog", "mechanism": "window_source_ip", "value": "", "pen": 0, "pen_required": true, "degraded": true, "note": "no PEN configured (-scenario-pen); SD-PARAM lever unavailable, isolate by source IP + [t0,t1)" }, "fidelity": {"silent_at_start": true, "changed_during_window": false} }, "duration": "2s", "participants_armed": 2, "participants_excluded": 1, "emitted": 40, "sent": 40, "in_window": 40, "drain": 0, "suppressed_pre_window": 0, "send_failures": 0, "dropped": 0, "informational": {"background_suppressed": 0, "requested": 40, "deferred": 0, "informs_acked": 0, "informs_pending": 0}, "sub_windows": [4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4], "excluded": [ {"device": "10.42.0.9", "reason": "device not found", "remediation_hint": "create the device before arming, or remove it from the scenario"} ] }, "counters": [ {"protocol": "syslog", "source_ip": "10.42.0.1", "collector": "10.0.0.9:514", "emitted": 20, "sent": 20, "in_window": 20, "drain": 0, "suppressed_pre_window": 0, "send_failures": 0, "dropped": 0, "informational": {"background_suppressed": 0, "requested": 20, "deferred": 0, "informs_acked": 0, "informs_pending": 0}, "sub_windows": [2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2]} ], "applications": [], "l7_values": [] } (The example is a syslog run, so applications and l7_values are empty. See applications[] and l7_values[] for populated flow-scenario examples.) The top-level blocks always serialize in the order summary, counters, applications, l7_values, so a streaming consumer sees the aggregate first and can rely on the trailer position of the two flow blocks.

Field Type Meaning id string Scenario ID (s-000001). phase string Terminal phase: stopped (window elapsed / explicit stop) or aborted (graceful shutdown). protocol string Participating protocol. metadata object The reproducibility fingerprint + actual window timestamps (see below). duration string t1 − t0 as a Go duration, from the monotonic clock. It is the window that actually ran. participants_armed number Devices that armed and ran. participants_excluded number Declared participants that did not arm. This is the true total, derived from the exclusion counter rather than from len(excluded), which is capped (see excluded_truncated). emitted … dropped number Fleet-wide sums of the per-device identity buckets below. informational object Fleet-wide sum of the disclosure counters (see counters[].informational). Outside the identity. sub_windows array Fleet-wide loss localization: in-window sends per time bucket, as the element-wise sum of the counters[].sub_windows rows. Length metadata.sub_window_count; sums to in_window. See Loss localization. excluded array Exclusions, each {device, reason, remediation_hint}, capped at 1,000 rows. The cap and the two fields below are described under arm. excluded_truncated bool Present (true) only when the row cap dropped rows. excluded_by_reason object reason → count over every exclusion. Absent when there are none.

The reproducibility fingerprint plus the timestamps the run actually observed. Copy the (config_sha256, seed) back into a resubmit on the same nl6_version to re-run a scenario exactly. To resubmit an archived body that carries a drain key, strip it first; see Removed request fields. config_sha256 pins what you declared, and resolved_participants_sha256 pins what actually ran. A participants_cidr scenario resolves against the live fleet, so one config fingerprint can produce different participant sets. When two runs share a config fingerprint but disagree on counts, the resolved digest tells you whether the fleet or the pipeline changed. Field Type Meaning config_sha256 string SHA-256 over the canonicalized submit config, which is the declared intent. resolved_participants_sha256 string SHA-256 identifying the devices that actually participated. Computed over the set counters[] serializes, after devices lost between arm and start are pruned. An explicit list and a prefix selector resolving to the same devices agree. seed number The seed that pinned every random draw. nl6_version string Simulator version that produced the report. Reproduction is guaranteed only on the same version. t0 RFC3339-ms Actual window open (emission start). t1 RFC3339-ms Actual window close. This is the planned T1, or the abort instant for an early abort (never later than planned T1). drain_end RFC3339-ms When the drain barrier finished and the report was finalized. Observed, not configured: typically milliseconds after t1, or the give-up instant if the barrier hit its ceiling. incomplete_joins array Absent on a healthy run. Names the finalize waits that did not complete within the budget: syslog-scheduler, trap-ticker, flow-ticker. See The drain barrier is bounded. drain_stragglers number Absent on a healthy run. An upper bound on the admissions still in flight when the barrier gave up. Fleet-wide, never folded into dropped. See The drain barrier is bounded. sub_window_count number Loss-localization granularity: the number of equal time buckets [T0,T1) is sliced into (currently 10). sub_window_duration string Width of one bucket as a Go duration, computed as the planned window / sub_window_count (the basis fires were bucketed against). See Loss localization. rate object Rate disclosure: {requested_per_device, paced, achieved_per_device}. paced=false means this protocol's emission cadence is not driven by the scenario rate at all (gnmi-dial-out streams at its own SAMPLE interval), so achieved_per_device still reports what happened but the request explains none of it. achieved_per_device counts in-window records only, so a capture it is compared against must be bounded to [t0, t1). See achieved_per_device is an in-window rate. fidelity object Fleet-silence disclosure, always present: {silent_at_start, changed_during_window}. silent_at_start is the fidelity value in force at t0. changed_during_window is true when fidelity was toggled, or a timed revert fired, between t0 and finalize. A true there means non-participant push started or stopped mid-window, so the collector-side rate covers a mixture. rate_cap object Shared-cap disclosure {per_second, shared_with}, emitted for syslog only and only when -syslog-global-cap is in force at the run's start. shared_with names the syslog scenarios whose windows overlapped this one, recorded as they begin, so a peer deleted before finalize is still named. An empty list does not mean the bucket was uncontended: background firing spends a token per pop even when the gate suppresses the fire, so a solo run on a busy fleet without -fidelity is still throttled. run_tags object How this run's traffic can be isolated, as {protocol, mechanism, value, pen, pen_required, degraded, note}. mechanism values are listed under Run-tag levers. achieved_per_device is an in-window rate​ achieved_per_device = sum(counters[].in_window) / (t1 - t0) / len(counters) in_window counts the records whose socket write returned inside [t0, t1), and the denominator is that same window. Records written after T1 count under drain instead. That bucket is tiny, because post-T1 fires are suppressed at generation and only work admitted at T1 can land in it. To compare against a capture, bound the capture to [t0, t1). That is the whole correction. Do not adjust the figure by a drain, and do not divide sent by the window plus a drain. The tail is bounded by admitted work, not by a duration. The rate is comparable across runs of different window lengths. A short window costs precision, not bias. For an absolute rate, measure on the wire with the capture bounded to [t0, t1) and template records excluded.

At T1 no new fire initiates. Finalize joins the scenario's scheduler and its trap and flow tickers, then the drain barrier waits for every send admitted before T1 to return from its write. On a healthy run this takes milliseconds. A syslog TCP or TLS device bounds one write at 2 s and serialises the fires queued behind it, so a stalled collector can hold finalize for 2 s per queued fire. All four waits share one 60 s budget. A wait that does not finish in it is named in incomplete_joins. If the barrier itself gives up, drain_stragglers is an upper bound on the admissions still outstanding. One admission is one write on the syslog and trap paths, or a whole paginated batch on the flow paths, so one flow straggler can stand for hundreds of records. The barrier logs one warning at 30 s and a give-up line at 60 s. Those two fields are the reliable signature of a give-up; a drain_end about 60 s past t1 is not. Nothing is cancelled, because a write parked in the kernel cannot be interrupted. Abandoned work keeps moving counters after the report is taken. So a report carrying either field is a lower bound over a set that was still moving, and an unidentified subset of participants may not satisfy the ledger identity. The 60 s ceiling exceeds docker stop's default 10 s grace, so raise stop_grace_period if a containerised abort must finish its report. Reproducing resolved_participants_sha256​ The encoding is deliberately the dumbest one that a checker can reproduce without a parser: each participating address followed by \n, in byte order, SHA-256, hex. So a collector that recorded which sources it received from can answer "did I receive from the same fleet nl6 sent from?" with one string comparison: # "$IPS" = the source addresses your collector saw during [t0,t1) printf '%s\n' "$IPS" | LC_ALL=C sort | sha256sum LC_ALL=C is required, not decoration. Under a UTF-8 locale, glibc's collation ignores punctuation at the primary level, so sort orders 10.42.10.1 before 10.42.1.2 while byte order puts 10.42.1.2 first. That yields a different digest and an operator reads a false "different fleet" from the very comparison this section exists to enable. macOS/BSD sort happens to agree with byte order, so the mistake reproduces only on the Linux collector hosts that are the actual audience. Byte order is a deliberate departure from the address order used for the excluded[] rows. Those rows are read by humans, where 10.42.0.10 sorting before 10.42.0.2 looks broken; this is input to a hash function, where any total order does, and byte order is the one every language sorts strings in by default. The trailing newline after the final address is part of the encoding.

metadata.run_tags.mechanism names the in-band lever a run's traffic can be filtered by on a shared collector. Every protocol is also bounded by the window [T0,T1) and the participant source IPs; the lever is the second discriminator where the wire format has one. Protocol mechanism Lever PEN? NetFlow v9 netflow9_source_id filter received flows by the device's Source ID no IPFIX ipfix_odid filter by the Observation Domain ID (enterprise IE is a secondary, PEN-only lever) no sFlow v5 sflow_sub_agent_id filter by sub_agent_id no gNMI dial-out gnmi_synthetic_path dial-out stamps the device IP in Notification.Prefix.Target; filter by target no Syslog 5424 syslog_sd_param RFC 5424 SD-PARAM [nl6@<PEN> runId="<id>"] yes SNMP trap/inform snmp_enterprise_varbind enterprise varbind under the nl6 PEN yes NetFlow v5 window_source_ip no taggable field, so isolate by participant source IPs + [T0,T1) n/a A PEN-dependent lever needs -scenario-pen. Without it, mechanism is window_source_ip and degraded is true. How to use the levers when reconciling is in Scenarios → Run tagging.

One row per participant, keyed by the join tuple (protocol, source_ip, collector). This is the same tuple a collector groups its received counts by, so the two sides line up row-for-row. Every ledger field is always present (explicit zeros, never omitted), so a zero-valued row still diffs cleanly. What one record means differs for two protocols: sFlow counts raw flow_sample records, never samples × sampling_rate, so the synthetic sampling rate cannot manufacture phantom loss. The periodic counters_sample is a keepalive. It flows continuously, including before T0, and is never counted. So the datagram sequence number is not 0 at T0; key on the sample sequence instead. gNMI dial-out gates both SAMPLE and ON_CHANGE. Arming needs a live Publish stream, otherwise the device is excluded. In the window a notification counts sent when written to a live stream and send_failures when the stream is down. Field Meaning protocol Participating protocol. source_ip Device management IP (the emitter). collector Configured collector host:port for this device (empty if the device was deleted post-window). emitted Records generated: gate-passed fires + emission-suppressed pre-window fires. sent in_window + drain, the loss denominator for reconciliation (convenience; derived). in_window Records sent (write returned success) with the write-return timestamp in [T0, T1). drain Records whose write returned at or after T1, the drain barrier's tail. Bounded by the writes already in flight at T1, so on a healthy run it is 0; it is not a configurable grace period. suppressed_pre_window State-driven / on-demand fires that occurred before T0. They are counted but not emitted on the wire. send_failures Resolve / encode / write errors (nl6 could not send). dropped Records generated but never confirmed on the wire. The barrier waits for every fire it admitted, so this is not a "slow write" bucket: the real causes are a fire that reached the barrier after it closed (the detach/teardown race) and a shutdown-race socket drop. informational.background_suppressed Informational, quarantined in its own sub-object. Counts background-cadence fires the gate suppressed for this participant during the scenario. Deliberately not a flat sibling of the identity buckets and not part of the ledger identity. informational.informs_acked / informs_pending SNMP INFORM ack settlement (best-effort, collector-side). An origination counts sent at first-transmit; informs_pending = originations − acked at report time (still-awaiting-ack). Zero for fire-and-forget traps and non-trap protocols. Outside the identity. informational.requested Scheduler demand, meaning every fire the scenario scheduler popped (pre-limiter). requested = sent + deferred + send_failures + dropped. informational.deferred Fires the shared global cap had no token for. They are throttled, not fired, NOT lost. Outside the identity and the loss denominator, so a cap throttle never masquerades as pipeline loss. sub_windows Loss localization: this participant's in-window sends per time bucket. Length metadata.sub_window_count; sums to in_window. See Loss localization. The six identity fields (emitted + the five loss buckets) are flat siblings. The nested informational object carries five disclosure counters, always present: background_suppressed, requested, deferred, informs_acked, informs_pending. A consumer computing the identity iterates the flat fields and never has to know which keys to exclude.

For scenarios on a flow protocol (netflow5 / netflow9 / ipfix), one row per distinct (l4_proto, dst_port, application_id) across all sent flow records, the trusted-sender reference for validating a collector's per-application aggregation. Rows are sorted ascending by the numeric (protocol, dst_port, application_id) key, so on one port a plain row sorts before the NBAR2 rows. The block is always present ([] for non-flow and sflow scenarios). Additive block per the evolution policy below. "applications": [ {"l4_proto": "tcp", "dst_port": 443, "app_hint": "https", "records": 3, "bytes": 3000, "packets": 30, "avg_bytes_per_second": 500.0, "sub_window_bytes": [300, 300, 300, 300, 300, 300, 300, 300, 300, 300]}, {"l4_proto": "tcp", "dst_port": 443, "application_id": 50332091, "application_name": "ssl", "app_hint": "https", "records": 2, "bytes": 2000, "packets": 20, "avg_bytes_per_second": 333.3, "sub_window_bytes": [200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200]} ] (A 6-second window carrying 3000 in-window bytes → 3000 / 6 = 500.0 B/s.) The join key has three parts, and the third is what separates NBAR2 traffic from plain traffic on the same port. The first row above is plain IPFIX (or NetFlow) traffic to 443/tcp; the second is Cisco AVC traffic to the same port whose records carried an applicationId. A consumer that groups only on (l4_proto, dst_port) sees both rows for one port and must sum them to get the old single row. application_id is the 32-bit value the record's IE 95 carries: the RFC 6759 classification engine id in the top 8 bits and the selector in the low 24, so engine 3 (IANA-L4, port-based) with selector 443 is 3 × 2^24 + 443 = 50332091. It is resolved from the sending device's NBAR2 catalog at the moment the record is counted, never from a per-record index, so two device types whose catalogs list applications in different orders still fold into one row per wire id. A collector that decodes applicationId as a big-endian integer (IPFIXcol2 with octetArrayAsUint, for instance) compares the number directly. Field Type Meaning l4_proto string Transport protocol name (tcp / udp / icmp; numeric fallback). Join key, part 1. dst_port number Flow destination port. Join key, part 2. ICMP records carry zero source and destination ports (ICMP has no transport ports), so ICMP traffic aggregates under a single (icmp, 0) row. application_id number Wire applicationId (IE 95) as an integer. Join key, part 3. Omitted on a row of plain records (no NBAR2), so a fleet with no NBAR2 device serializes exactly as before this field existed. application_name string The catalog's applicationName for application_id, the same string the device advertises in its RFC 6759 application table. Omitted with application_id. Informational, like app_hint. app_hint string Convenience label from a built-in well-known-port map (443 → https, 53 → domain, …); "" for unmapped ports. Informational: collector classification is user-configurable, so join on the key, never on the hint. records number Sent flow records for this row (sent basis: in-window + drain). For a pure flow scenario, Σ applications[].records == summary.sent. bytes number Sum of the records' flow byte counters, exactly what a conforming collector sums for the same window. packets number Sum of the records' flow packet counters. avg_bytes_per_second number In-window bytes ÷ (t1 − t0) (actual window). The headline rate reference. Drain bytes stay in bytes (the reconciliation total) but are excluded here: the denominator is the window, and a drain byte was written outside it, so counting it would credit the window with bytes it did not carry. (There is no "drain time" to add to the denominator; the tail is a barrier, not a span.) In-window bytes = Σ sub_window_bytes. sub_window_bytes array In-window bytes per localization bucket (drain bytes excluded, the same convention as sub_windows vs sent). Informational: collectors interpolate a flow's bytes across its [start, end] interval, so per-bucket comparison is approximate; reconcile on totals (see validation methodology). sflow scenarios are excluded by design: an sFlow collector derives byte volumes by sampling extrapolation (frame_length × sampling_rate), not by summing record byte counters, so these totals are not the numbers a correct sFlow collector would report.

One row per distinct (application_id, field, value) across all sent records that carried that value, positioned after applications. field is http_host (the HTTP host, Cisco IE 12235 under PEN 9) or http_uri (the URI half of the HTTP URI statistics field, IE 9357). Rows are sorted ascending by (application_id, field, value). The block is always present and is [] unless an NBAR2 participant sent a record carrying a host or a URI. "l7_values": [ {"application_id": 50331728, "application_name": "http", "field": "http_host", "value": "www.example.com", "records": 6, "bytes": 6000, "packets": 60, "avg_bytes_per_second": 1000.0}, {"application_id": 50331728, "application_name": "http", "field": "http_uri", "value": "/index.html", "records": 10, "bytes": 10000, "packets": 100, "avg_bytes_per_second": 1666.7} ] Field Type Meaning application_id number Wire applicationId of the records, as in applications[]. Join key, part 1. application_name string The catalog's name for it. Informational. field string http_host or http_uri. Join key, part 2. value string The hostname or URI as a string. For http_host this is the hostname WITHOUT the six-byte prefix 03 00 00 50 34 02 the wire carries in front of it (Cisco's layout); for http_uri it is the URI without the NUL and hit count that follow it. Join key, part 3. records / bytes / packets number Sent-basis totals of the records carrying this value, the applications[] convention. avg_bytes_per_second number In-window bytes ÷ actual window, the applications[] convention. The invariant is an inequality. For each field, Σ l7_values[field].records ≤ Σ applications[].records, and equality is not required: a DNS or SSL record carries no host and no URI, so it contributes to applications[] and to no row here. Equality holds only when every sent record carried exactly one value of that field. To reconcile http_host against a collector, strip the six-byte prefix from the decoded IE 12235 value first; a record whose value is exactly the six bytes carried no host and belongs to no http_host row. libfds types both IE 12235 and IE 9357 as strings, and IPFIXcol2 drops non-printable bytes from a string unless its nonPrintableChar output option is on: off, it shows the URI alone (the NUL and count vanish) and a host as P4www.example.com (the prefix's two printable bytes and then the name); on, every byte is a \u00XX escape. The 2-byte hit count that follows the URI on the wire is not part of the key.

Every counter row (and the summary) satisfies, exactly: emitted = in_window + drain + send_failures + dropped + suppressed_pre_window sent = in_window + drain The informational counters sit outside it by design. Use sent (in_window + drain) as the number to reconcile against a collector's received count.

The report is a versioned contract. Consumers should tolerate unknown fields. Backward-compatible: new fields may be added to summary or counters; a new top-level block may be added after counters. Existing field names, types, units, and the summary-before-counters order never change in a backward-compatible release. Breaking: renaming/removing a field, changing a type or unit, or reordering the top-level blocks. While nl6_version is 0.x, a breaking change ships in a minor bump, as SemVer allows for major version zero. It is called out under Upgrade notes in the release notes. The ledger identity above is a stability guarantee. It holds in every version that ships these fields. config_sha256 covers only the submit config, not the report shape; the report contract is tracked by nl6_version. The submit config has no separate version of its own; it moves with nl6_version too, and a removed request field is a breaking change for harnesses. Removals are listed in Removed request fields. Future projections (additional protocols in counters, richer loss-localization blocks) are additive under this policy. Read the exclusion count from participants_excluded, never from len(excluded), which is capped.

A fleet total answers how much was lost; sub_windows answers where, by device-set (the per-participant counters[] rows, keyed on the join tuple) and by time (the array within each row). The planned window [T0,T1) is sliced into metadata.sub_window_count equal buckets, each metadata.sub_window_duration wide; sub_windows[i] counts the in-window sends whose write-return time fell in bucket i ([T0 + i·d, T0 + (i+1)·d)). An early abort shortens the run but not the bucket basis. Buckets past the abort instant are empty. Bucketing choice. A fixed count (10), not a fixed duration, so the report stays bounded and window-length-independent (a 10 s window → 1 s buckets; a 10 min window → 60 s buckets). Scope. Localizes in-window sends only: sum(sub_windows) == in_window for every row and the summary. Drain-tail sends are post-T1 by definition and carry no sub-window (reconcile them via the drain total). How to use it. Bucket your collector's received records by receive-time relative to the report's t0, with the same width, and diff per bucket. The hosts need synced clocks. JSON only. The CSV projection does not carry it.

GET /api/v1/scenarios/{id}/report?format=csv serves a flat text/csv projection of counters[], with one header row plus one row per participant, join-ready on the first three columns: protocol,source_ip,collector,emitted,in_window,drain,suppressed_pre_window,send_failures,dropped,background_suppressed syslog,10.42.0.1,10.0.0.9:514,20,20,0,0,0,0,0 syslog,10.42.0.2,10.0.0.9:514,20,20,0,0,0,0,0 The informational.background_suppressed counter flattens to a trailing background_suppressed column. summary-level fields are not in the CSV. It is purely the per-device counter projection, so it joins directly against a collector's received-counts export on (protocol, source_ip, collector).

nl6 serves NETCONF on three device profiles. The third, huawei_ne8000, serves only what a YANG-Push collector reads, see YANG-Push over UDP-notif. cisco_catalyst_9500 serves the IOS XE dialect over SSH. A client opens an IOS XE style establish-subscription and receives a notification each time the interface state engine changes an interface. juniper_mx10004 serves a Junos dialect over SSH and over mutual TLS (RFC 7589). A client opens a create-subscription on the NETCONF stream and receives the mib2d link events of the interface state engine. juniper_mx10004 can also dial a NETCONF client itself with call home. The subsystem is off by default. A default fleet behaves exactly as without it.

Name Type Default Description -netconf-enable bool false Enable the NETCONF subsystem. cisco_catalyst_9500 and huawei_ne8000 devices listen on -netconf-port. juniper_mx10004 devices listen on -netconf-port and on -netconf-tls-port. -netconf-port int 830 TCP port of the per-device NETCONF over SSH listener. -netconf-authorized-keys path empty OpenSSH authorized_keys file. Its keys log in as simadmin on every NETCONF SSH listener, next to the password. Key options are ignored. A YANG-Push collector such as NetGauze needs it. -netconf-tls-port int 6513 TCP port of the per-device NETCONF over TLS listener. -netconf-tls-client-ca path empty PEM file with the CA that must have signed the client certificates. The path is flag-only. Requires -netconf-enable. -netconf-tls-client-identity fingerprint=username none One entry of the client identity table. Repeat the flag for more entries. The fingerprint is the SHA-256 of the client certificate, with or without the 04: prefix. Requires -netconf-enable. -netconf-tls-default-username string empty NETCONF user for a client certificate that is not in the identity table. Empty means such a client is refused. Requires -netconf-enable. -netconf-callhome-client host:port empty NETCONF client the auto-started juniper_mx10004 devices dial with call home. Empty means no call home. Requires -netconf-enable. -netconf-callhome-device-id string empty DEVICE-ID in the call-home preamble. Empty means each device's sysName. Requires -netconf-callhome-client. huawei_ne8000 devices also open the SSH listener on -netconf-port, with a dialect for YANG-Push collectors. See YANG-Push over UDP-notif. Other device types never open NETCONF ports. The three identity flags are global and apply to the whole fleet.

The sections Connect, Subscribe and Notifications describe the IOS XE dialect of cisco_catalyst_9500. The Junos dialect has its own section below. The login is the device SSH login (simadmin / simadmin). The host key is the shared simulator host key. The server accepts only the netconf SSH subsystem. It refuses shell, exec and every other request. One NETCONF session runs per SSH connection. The connection closes when the session ends. A session lives as long as the client keeps it, and nl6 does not close idle sessions. ssh -s -p 830 simadmin@10.42.0.1 netconf The hello advertises base 1.0 and 1.1, notification, interleave, the draft ietf-event-notifications, ietf-yang-push, the two Cisco deviation modules cisco-xe-ietf-event-notifications-deviation and cisco-xe-ietf-yang-push-deviation, and ietf-interfaces. Framing switches to chunked after both sides advertise base 1.1.

nl6 follows the IOS XE draft dialect. <establish-subscription xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-event-notifications" xmlns:yp="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-yang-push"> <stream>yp:yang-push</stream> <yp:xpath-filter>/interfaces-ios-xe-oper:interfaces/interface[name='GigabitEthernet1/0/24']/oper-status</yp:xpath-filter> <yp:dampening-period>0</yp:dampening-period> </establish-subscription>

The module is interfaces-ios-xe-oper, backed by Cisco-IOS-XE-interfaces-oper. Leave out the [name=...] predicate to watch every interface. The predicate accepts single or double quotes. Path Pushes /interfaces-ios-xe-oper:interfaces/interface[name=K]/oper-status The oper-status leaf. /interfaces-ios-xe-oper:interfaces/interface[name=K]/admin-status The admin-status leaf. /interfaces-ios-xe-oper:interfaces/interface[name=K] The interface row. The subscription must carry <stream>, an xpath-filter and dampening-period 0. A subscription to an interface that does not exist is accepted and gets one empty push-update. Statistics changes alone never push.

Request Reply Accepted subscription subscription-result notif-bis:ok and a subscription-id. IDs start at 2147483648. Missing <stream>, unknown module, a path below interface that is not a leaf above notif-bis:error-no-such-option Container /interfaces-ios-xe-oper:interfaces notif-bis:error-no-such-option Path under /if:interfaces-state (ietf-interfaces) notif-bis:error-other Malformed XPath, or neither dampening-period nor period notif-bis:error-other Missing xpath-filter notif-bis:error-other Periodic subscription (period) notif-bis:error-no-such-option dampening-period other than 0 rpc-error, type protocol, tag invalid-value, bad-element dampening-period establish-subscription in the RFC 8639 namespace rpc-error, tag unknown-namespace More than 256 subscriptions in one session notif-bis:error-other delete-subscription of a live ID notif-bis:ok delete-subscription of an unknown or deleted ID notif-bis:error-no-such-subscription kill-session of another session <ok/> kill-session of the own session or an unknown ID rpc-error, tag invalid-value, bad-element session-id close-session <ok/>, then the connection closes Any other operation, including get and create-subscription rpc-error, tag operation-not-supported
Right after the reply, each subscription receives the current value of its selection. The first interface (lowest ifIndex) arrives as push-update. Every other interface arrives as push-change-update.

<notification xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:notification:1.0"><eventTime>2026-10-29T11:10:17.42Z</eventTime><push-update xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-yang-push"><subscription-id>2147483648</subscription-id><datastore-contents-xml><interfaces xmlns="http://cisco.com/ns/yang/Cisco-IOS-XE-interfaces-oper"><interface><name>AppGigabitEthernet1/0/1</name><oper-status>if-oper-state-ready</oper-status></interface></interfaces></datastore-contents-xml></push-update></notification> A subscription to a missing interface gets <datastore-contents-xml/>.

<notification xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:notification:1.0"><eventTime>2026-10-29T11:12:49.20Z</eventTime><push-change-update xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-yang-push"><subscription-id>2147483651</subscription-id><datastore-changes-xml><yang-patch xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-yang-patch"><patch-id>null</patch-id><edit><edit-id>edit1</edit-id><operation>merge</operation><target>/interfaces/interface=GigabitEthernet1%2F0%2F24</target><value><interface xmlns="http://cisco.com/ns/yang/Cisco-IOS-XE-interfaces-oper"><oper-status>if-oper-state-lower-layer-down</oper-status></interface></value></edit></yang-patch></datastore-changes-xml></push-change-update></notification> eventTime has two fractional digits and a Z suffix. The interface name in <target> is percent-encoded, so / becomes %2F. last-change and discontinuity-time in a row use six fractional digits and +00:00.

nl6 state admin-status oper-status Admin up, link up if-state-up if-oper-state-ready Admin up, link down if-state-up if-oper-state-lower-layer-down Admin down if-state-down if-oper-state-no-pass Admin testing if-state-test if-oper-state-test Link testing, admin up if-state-up if-oper-state-test Link unknown, dormant or not present if-state-up if-oper-state-unknown, -dormant, -not-present A change pushes one notification per affected subscription, newest subscription first. no shutdown sends if-oper-state-invalid, then if-oper-state-lower-layer-down, then if-oper-state-ready. nl6 sends the first two steps to each subscription in turn, newest subscription first. Then it sends if-oper-state-ready to all of them, again newest first. The captures cannot tell this order apart from an order by leaf type (row, admin leaf, oper leaf). An admin-status subscription re-sends its unchanged value when anything else in the row changes.

juniper_mx10004 devices serve this dialect over SSH and over TLS. nl6 follows the behaviour of a vJunos-router 25.4R1.12 and puts the profile's own Junos version (24.2R1.17) in the junos namespace of every reply. The two transports differ only in how the session starts.
The login is the device SSH login (simadmin / simadmin) and the subsystem is netconf, as on the IOS XE profile. ssh -s -p 830 simadmin@10.42.0.1 netconf

The server writes its hello first, as soon as the transport is ready. Over SSH that is when the netconf subsystem is requested. Over TLS there is no subsystem step, so it is right after the handshake. Two comment lines come before the hello. The second names the NETCONF user. The hello lists 19 capabilities, among them notification, interleave, ietf-netconf-monitoring and the Junos http://xml.juniper.net/netconf/junos/1.0. <!-- No zombies were killed during the creation of this user interface --> <!-- user ncuser, class j-super-user --> <hello xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:base:1.0"> <capabilities> <capability>urn:ietf:params:netconf:base:1.0</capability> ... </capabilities> <session-id>22853</session-id> </hello> Framing is base 1.0 end-of-message (]]>]]>) only. nl6 never switches to chunked framing, even when the client advertises base 1.1.

Request Reply create-subscription with <stream>NETCONF</stream> (or no stream) <ok/>. Link events follow. A second one adds nothing. create-subscription with any other stream rpc-error syntax error, bad-element create-subscription get with the RFC 5277 streams filter (urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netmod:notification) An empty <data>. get with a netconf-state filter (ietf-netconf-monitoring) <data> with the hello capabilities under netconf-state/capabilities. get with no filter <data> with a reduced <configuration>, then an empty <database-status-information>. get with any other subtree filter, such as interfaces-state (ietf-interfaces) rpc-error syntax error with the filtered element as bad-element. An xpath filter carries no child element and gets the unfiltered reply; the device's xpath behaviour was not captured. get-configuration The same reduced <configuration> without the <data> wrapper. close-session <ok/>, then a newline, the comment <!-- session end at ... --> and a newline, then the connection closes. kill-session of another session <ok/> and the other session closes. establish-subscription (draft or RFC 8639 namespace) rpc-error syntax error, repeated twice in one reply. Anything else, including get-interface-information and kill-session of the own or an unknown ID rpc-error syntax error with the request name as bad-element. The refusal has this shape: <rpc-error> <error-type>protocol</error-type> <error-tag>operation-failed</error-tag> <error-severity>error</error-severity> <error-message>syntax error</error-message> <error-info> <bad-element>bogus-rpc</bad-element> </error-info> </rpc-error> The reduced <configuration> holds only <version> and <system><host-name>.

A derived oper change on an interface sends two notifications, back to back, with the same eventTime. The event is a mib2d SNMP_TRAP_LINK_DOWN or SNMP_TRAP_LINK_UP. The first notification is the state-system-syslog form. <notification xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:notification:1.0"> <eventTime>2026-10-30T16:51:31+00:00</eventTime> <state-system-syslog> <state> <system> <syslog> <messages> <message> <timestamp>1793379091841089</timestamp> <id>SNMP_TRAP_LINK_DOWN</id> <severity>WARNING</severity> <facility>DAEMON</facility> <priority>28</priority> <pid>18896</pid> <log-message>SNMP_TRAP_LINK_DOWN: ifIndex 529, ifAdminStatus down(2), ifOperStatus down(2), ifName ge-0/0/1</log-message> <application>mib2d</application> <structured-data> <parameters> <parameter><name>snmp-interface-index</name><value>529</value></parameter> <parameter><name>admin-status</name><value>down(2)</value></parameter> <parameter><name>operational-status</name><value>down(2)</value></parameter> <parameter><name>interface-name</name><value>ge-0/0/1</value></parameter> </parameters> </structured-data> </message> </messages> </syslog> </system> </state> </state-system-syslog> </notification> The second is the syslog/junos/events/event form. <notification xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:notification:1.0"> <eventTime>2026-10-30T16:51:31+00:00</eventTime> <syslog> <junos> <events> <event> <id>SNMP_TRAP_LINK_DOWN</id> <type>2</type> <priority>28</priority> <facility>3</facility> <timestamp> <seconds>1793379091</seconds> <microseconds>841089</microseconds> </timestamp> <pid>18896</pid> <message>SNMP_TRAP_LINK_DOWN: ifIndex 529, ifAdminStatus down(2), ifOperStatus down(2), ifName ge-0/0/1</message> <daemon>mib2d</daemon> <hostname>r1</hostname> <attributes><key>snmp-interface-index</key><value>529</value></attributes> <attributes><key>admin-status</key><value>down(2)</value></attributes> <attributes><key>operational-status</key><value>down(2)</value></attributes> <attributes><key>interface-name</key><value>ge-0/0/1</value></attributes> </event> </events> </junos> </syslog> </notification> The listing joins each <parameter> and <attributes> element onto one line. The wire form spreads them over more lines. eventTime is whole seconds with a +00:00 offset. hostname is the device sysName. Change Event Physical interface oper up to down SNMP_TRAP_LINK_DOWN, severity WARNING, priority 28. Physical interface oper down to up SNMP_TRAP_LINK_UP, severity NOTICE, priority 29. Logical unit oper down to up SNMP_TRAP_LINK_UP, severity INFORMATIONAL, priority 30. Logical unit oper up to down Nothing. Admin change that leaves oper as it was Nothing. nl6 sends each event at once.

Each juniper_mx10004 device listens on -netconf-tls-port when -netconf-enable is set. The listener binds whether or not a client CA is configured. The transport follows RFC 7589 and the behaviour of Junos. TLS 1.2 only. A TLS 1.3-only client is refused. Mutual TLS. A client without a certificate, or with one from another CA, is refused at the handshake. The server certificate is the shared simulator certificate, the same one the HTTPS REST surface and gNMI use. With no client CA configured, every handshake is refused. The startup log says so. A later PUT /api/v1/netconf/tls with a CA applies to the next connection.

A client certificate that passes the handshake maps to a NETCONF user by its SHA-256 fingerprint. nl6 looks in the identity table first and then uses the default username. With neither, the handshake completes and the connection closes with no hello, as Junos does. The user only names the session in the hello comment. nl6 has no per-user authorisation. A fingerprint is 04: followed by the 32 SHA-256 bytes as upper-case hex pairs. Input may also be bare hex or colon-separated pairs without the prefix, in any case. The table is fleet-wide. A change applies to new connections and running sessions keep their user. sudo ./nl6 -netconf-enable \ -netconf-tls-client-ca client-ca.pem \ -netconf-tls-client-identity 04:AA:BB:...=ncuser \ -netconf-tls-default-username guest

Endpoint Purpose GET /api/v1/netconf/tls The client CA PEM, the identity table and the default username. Fingerprints use the 04: spelling. Answers 404 when the subsystem is off. PUT /api/v1/netconf/tls Replace the whole table. An omitted field clears it. Answers 404 when the subsystem is off, 400 for a bad body. GET /api/v1/tls/ca The PEM of the CA that signed the shared server certificate. Content type application/x-pem-file. { "ca_pem": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
", "identities": {"04:AA:BB:...": "ncuser"}, "default_username": "guest" } ca_pem is inline, never a path. It may hold certificate blocks only. Any other PEM block, such as a private key, is a 400.

The shared server certificate carries only a 0.0.0.0 IP SAN. A client that verifies the host name against the device IP fails. Skip host-name verification and pin the CA from GET /api/v1/tls/ca instead. curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/v1/tls/ca > nl6-ca.pem

A juniper_mx10004 device can open the NETCONF connection itself and dial a NETCONF client, as Junos outbound-ssh with services netconf does. On that connection the device is the SSH server and the NETCONF server, with the same host key, login and Junos dialect as its port -netconf-port listener. The listeners keep running, and all sessions of a device share one session space, so kill-session works across them. Other profiles have no call home. A request whose profiles all lack call home gets a 400. A round-robin batch that mixes profiles creates the others without call home and counts them in devices_unsupported. Enable it for the auto-start batch with -netconf-callhome-client, or per request with a netconf_callhome block: curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "start_ip": "10.0.0.1", "device_count": 100, "resource_file": "juniper_mx10004.json", "netconf_callhome": {"client": "192.0.2.10:4334"} }' client must be an IPv4 address or a host name, because devices dial over IPv4 only. An IPv6 address gets a 400. device_id in the block sets the DEVICE-ID of the preamble. It defaults to each device's sysName. -netconf-callhome-client seeds only the auto-start batch. Without -auto-start-ip it configures nothing, and nl6 logs a warning.

Junos call home is not strict RFC 8071. Before its SSH identification string the device writes a preamble, each line ending in CRLF: MSG-ID: DEVICE-CONN-INFO MSG-VER: V1 DEVICE-ID: <device id> <empty line> A client that expects the SSH banner as the first bytes, as RFC 8071 describes, rejects the device. A client for Junos reads the preamble, takes the device id from it, and then starts the SSH client handshake. nl6 sends the preamble because vJunos-router 25.4R1.12 sent it.

nl6 reproduces what vJunos did with keep-alive retry 3 timeout 15: One session per client. While it is up the device does not dial again. Connect attempts happen on a fixed 15 s cycle, with no backoff and no retry limit. After a session ends, for any reason, the device dials on the next tick, 0 to 15 s later. Each device has its own random offset into the cycle, so a large batch does not dial at one instant. While a session is up the device sends an SSH keepalive every 15 s and closes the connection when 3 intervals pass without a reply. A client that accepts the connection but does not complete the SSH handshake within the same 45 s is dropped. Dials leave from the device IP inside the device namespace. Call home allows 64 concurrent dials. gNMI dial-out has its own 64, so an unreachable client of one does not slow the other.

This vJunos configuration produced the reference capture: set system services netconf ssh set system services netconf notification set system services outbound-ssh client nms device-id vj-r1 set system services outbound-ssh client nms services netconf set system services outbound-ssh client nms keep-alive retry 3 timeout 15 set system services outbound-ssh client nms reconnect-strategy sticky set system services outbound-ssh client nms 192.0.2.10 port 4334 In containerlab the vrnetlab image puts fxp0 in the mgmt_junos instance. Add set system services outbound-ssh routing-instance mgmt_junos, or the device never dials.

GET /api/v1/netconf/callhome/status reports one row per client, sorted by client. { "subsystem_active": true, "clients": [ { "client": "192.0.2.10:4334", "devices": 100, "sessions_up": 98, "connect_attempts": 412, "connect_failures": 14, "handshake_failures": 0, "sessions_ended": 300, "devices_unsupported": 0 } ] } Field Meaning devices Devices with call home to this client. sessions_up Devices whose call-home connection is open. connect_attempts Dials, including those of deleted devices. connect_failures Dials that failed, or whose preamble could not be written. handshake_failures Connections that closed before the SSH handshake completed. A client that rejects the preamble shows up here. sessions_ended Call-home sessions that ended after the SSH handshake. devices_unsupported Devices created with a call-home block whose profile has no call home. Call-home sessions also count in sessions of GET /api/v1/netconf/status.

GET /api/v1/netconf/status reports the subsystem. { "subsystem_active": true, "listeners": 4, "sessions": 1, "subscriptions": 3, "notifications_sent": 12, "notifications_dropped": 0, "listeners_tls": 2, "sessions_tls": 1, "tls_handshake_failures": 0 } Field Meaning subsystem_active true when -netconf-enable is set. All other fields are zero when false. listeners Devices with an open NETCONF listener. sessions Open NETCONF sessions. subscriptions Live subscriptions across all sessions. notifications_sent Notifications written to a client. notifications_dropped Notifications dropped because a slow client let its queue of 100 fill. The oldest is dropped first. listeners_tls Devices with an open NETCONF over TLS listener. sessions_tls Open NETCONF sessions over TLS. tls_handshake_failures TLS handshakes that failed. This also counts benign TCP probes and aborts at the idle deadline, as the gNMI counter does. A push can also be lost one stage earlier, before it is rendered. Each session listens to the interface state engine on a 16-deep channel. An event dropped there is not counted in notifications_dropped. It appears in state_events_dropped of GET /api/v1/gnmi/status, the counter that state-change fan-out to gNMI and NETCONF shares.

nl6 emulates one real device per profile and serves less where it has no capture. The IOS XE list is in Cisco Catalyst 9500 NETCONF limitations. The first entry there matters most. An admin change on a link-down interface sends a trap and a syslog message but no NETCONF notification, as on the real switch. The VRP list is in Huawei NE8000 YANG-Push limitations. The Junos list is in Juniper MX10004 NETCONF limitations. The main points are these. nl6 sends link events only. The background syslog stream of a real device is absent. get and get-configuration return a reduced configuration and every other RPC is a syntax error. Only a fingerprint table plus a default username maps a client. There is no mapping by certificate name. The framing is base 1.0 only. The TLS alert bytes differ from Junos. The refusal is the same. make test-interop-netconf-junos diffs the Junos dialect against a real vJunos-router over TLS and SSH: the hello, the RPCs and the link events of one interface disable and enable. Call home has these limits: SSH only. TLS call home (port 4335) is not served. One client per device. Junos allows several. The Junos secret option, which adds the host key and an HMAC to the preamble, is not emulated. The SSH identification string and the host key are those of the listener, SSH-2.0-Go and the shared RSA key. vJunos sends SSH-2.0-JSSH_4.1 with an ed25519 key. The keepalive request is keepalive@openssh.com. The name Junos uses was not visible in the encrypted capture. While a keepalive is unanswered nl6 sends no further one, because its SSH library allows one outstanding request per connection. Junos sends one every interval. The connection closes after the same 3 intervals.

Read this before building anything against ciena_waveserver5 that you intend to run against real hardware. This device type exists so a monitoring team can implement and validate optical use cases without a lab. The failure mode that matters is not synthetic-looking values, it is the false pass: you build against nl6, it works, you deploy against a real Waveserver, and it breaks. A team that cannot see where the simulation ends will trust it past its edges. This file is where it ends.

The shipped value is: 1.3.6.1.4.1.1271.3 That is the waveserver subtree node, confirmed from the public MIB mirror. It is not the per-model product OID a real Waveserver 5 returns, because CIENA-PRODUCTS-MIB is not in the public mirror and the real value is behind the Ciena support portal. Consequence: sysObjectID-based device detection will not match what your system learns from real hardware. If your provisioning keys on sysObjectID, treat this value as unknown rather than as ground truth. Replace it here if you can confirm the product OID.
documents.s: sysObjectID is a placeholder, and device detection will mis-identify

documents.t: nl6 computes {instant, avg, min, max} over a trailing window and answers every request live. A real Waveserver accumulates 15-minute PM bins with 96 bins of history, plus 24-hour bins, and exposes bin boundaries, bin state and suspect-interval flags. Consequence: anything that consumes bin semantics does not exist here. There is no bin rollover to observe, no historical bin retrieval, and no suspect-interval marking. A rule that waits for a bin to close will never fire.
documents.s: Statistics are instantaneous, not 15-minute PM bins

documents.t: Every value is a deterministic function of elapsed time: sinusoidal dials, a closed-form cascade, per-channel jitter from a fixed seed. They are shaped to be physically coherent (OSNR drives Q drives BER drives uncorrectable blocks; attenuation moves power but not OSNR), not to reproduce any measured trace. Real coherent optics exhibit noise, transients and correlations this model does not attempt. Use nl6 to validate that your logic reacts correctly to a given shape. Do not use it to characterise what shapes real hardware produces.
documents.s: Values are analytic, not captured from hardware

documents.t: Absent Why post-fec-ber Defined by OpenConfig, but Ciena removed it from their model. Serving it would let a rule pass here that could never fire against real hardware. Deliberate; a test asserts its absence. Per-counter supported / invalid-data-flag Present on every counter in ciena-waveserver-pm. The supported equivalent on the OpenConfig surface is leaf absence (the post-fec-ber precedent above: absent, tested, distinguishable from zero). invalid-data-flag will not be implemented: no faithful expression exists on this surface, and every candidate is a guess about portal-gated hardware behaviour. This is the post-fec-ber reasoning applied symmetrically. NETCONF, and the native ciena-waveserver-* models nl6 serves the OpenConfig surface over gNMI only. A team that talks to real Waveservers over NETCONF with Ciena's own models is exercising a different interface entirely. Flow export (NetFlow / IPFIX / sFlow) Correct, not missing. A layer-1 transport platform performs no layer-3/4 inspection and exports no flow records, so nl6 must not either. A batch flow seed skips this type; an explicit flow block naming it is rejected with 400. gNMI dial-out Not gated by type. The shipped dial-out flavor is gnmireverse, which is Arista-specific, and this device dials out with it like every other type. A sample subscription accepts the optical paths. An on-change subscription refuses them at attach. OTLP No Ciena source claims OTLP support. If you want optical telemetry in an OTel pipeline, bridge it: nl6 -> gNMI -> gnmic -> OTLP -> collector. Emitting OTLP device-side would be a false pass. cwsAlarmActiveTable / cwsAlarmHistoryTable A real Waveserver exposes active alarms as SNMP tables for polling. Not simulated. Alarm conditions other than pre-FEC SD/SF wsLinkStateAlarmNotification carries ~30 condition flags (LOS, LOL, LOF, LOM, BDI, TTI mismatch, ODU and Ethernet-layer defects). nl6 drives only OtuPreFecSd and OtuPreFecSf; every other flag is emitted as a literal inactive(0) and never becomes active.

This one is a property of Ciena's model that nl6 reproduces faithfully, and it will shape how you write correlation rules. Ciena publishes an optical alarm as one notification type, wsLinkStateAlarmNotification, whose varbinds carry the current state of every condition flag. It is not a raise/clear pair of distinct traps the way linkDown and linkUp are. So a raise is identifiable from its varbinds (OtuPreFecSd = active(1), or OtuPreFecSf = active(1)), but a clear sets every flag back to inactive(0), with Severity = cleared(1). The consequence: an SD clear and an SF clear are byte-identical on the wire apart from the Description (.9) and Instance (.8) strings. A collector cannot machine-correlate a clear back to the specific raise it resolves without parsing that text. nl6 does not paper over this. Setting the condition flag on a clear would make the varbinds contradict each other, asserting the condition is simultaneously active(1) and cleared(1), and a rule built against that invention would misfire against real hardware. That is the false pass this device type exists to prevent, so the faithful shape is kept and the awkwardness is documented here instead. If you need machine-correlatable clears, the syslog surface is the better target: those messages carry structured data naming the condition (condition=OtuPreFecSd, state=inactive), because syslog has no wire format to be faithful to.
documents.s: A clear names its condition only in text

documents.t: Aspect Real Waveserver nl6 Why Statistics precision decimal-3-dig (3 dp) 2 fraction digits The served surface is OpenConfig, whose stats groupings mandate 2. Emitting 3 would fail strict schema validation. Pre-FEC BER representation string-sci (scientific notation string) decimal64, 18 fraction digits Same reason: OpenConfig types govern the surface nl6 serves. DGD integer picoseconds polarization-mode-dispersion, decimal64, 2 dp First-order PMD is DGD; OpenConfig names and types it this way. OSNR not in Ciena's modem PM served A real WL5 modem reports electrical SNR. OpenConfig defines OSNR and collectors expect it, so it is served, with esnr alongside so the divergence narrows rather than widens.
documents.s: Divergences you can observe on the wire

documents.t: Layer Status OpenConfig schema Pinned: terminal-device 2026-01-14, platform-transceiver 2026-03-25, platform 2025-07-15. Served paths were traced against these. Waveserver native schema Verified leaf by leaf against the ONOS mirror of ciena-waveserver-{pm,xcvr-modem}, Waveserver Ai vintage, 2017 to 2018. Newer firmware may differ. Waveserver SNMP MIBs Publicly mirrored (kcsinclair/mibs), traced module by module for the notification content. The mirror is unversioned, but the modules are dated: CIENA-WS-NOTIFICATION-MIB LAST-UPDATED "201611140000Z" and CIENA-WS-MIB 201612140000Z, "Release 1.3". That is Waveserver Ai 1.x, matching the YANG vintage above. Waveserver values Not public. The Command Reference with real operating values is portal-gated, so no shipped value is derived from documented hardware output. Path validation is by an in-repo manifest, not by compiling the YANG. The test pins served paths against a hand-transcribed table in both directions, so it catches drift and invented paths, but it does not prove the table itself matches the models. A true schema check would need the YANG vendored plus ygot.

Stated so the limitations above are read in proportion, not as a disclaimer on everything: Paths, types and encodings come from the pinned models, not from invention. A path whose existence could not be confirmed was omitted. The cascade is physically coherent. OSNR to Q to pre-FEC BER to uncorrectable blocks, with the erfc tail's real shallowness at the SD-FEC threshold rather than a convenient decade-scale cliff. The two-dial model reproduces the real diagnostic split. Attenuation moves power without moving OSNR; ASE accumulation moves OSNR without moving power. Both quadrants are reachable, and off-spine leaves stay flat under a receive-side fault. fec-uncorrectable-blocks is monotonic across any sequence of degradations and reverts, which is the property a collector actually depends on. Cross-surface agreement. Every surface reads one dispatcher, so two reads at the same instant agree. See docs/reference/optical-telemetry.md for the served surface and a per-use-case validation walkthrough.

nl6 simulates a Ciena Waveserver 5 (WaveLogic 5 Extreme) coherent DWDM transport platform and serves its optical state over gNMI, using the pinned OpenConfig model. This page is the working reference: what is served, what the values mean, how to drive a channel across the FEC threshold, and how to validate a monitoring use case end to end. Two companion documents matter as much as this one: Waveserver 5 limitations states where the simulation stops. Read it before building anything you intend to deploy against real hardware. gNMI reference covers the transport, TLS, subscribe modes and encodings shared with the packet surface.

Not "synthetic-looking values". The false pass: you build a rule against nl6, it works, you deploy against a real Waveserver, and it does not. Every design decision below is ordered by that risk, which is why exact paths, types and negative states are treated as more important than exact values. Concretely, that is why post-fec-ber is not served even though OpenConfig defines it. Ciena removed it from their model, so a collector rule keyed on it could never fire against real hardware. A test asserts its absence.
documents.s: The failure mode this device type is designed against
