The workflow for verifying a profile fix is: edit the file, POST /resources/reload, then POST /devices for the type. A profile that fails to load after the edit is answered by that create with the usual 400 (see resource_file failures); a rejection is never cached, so fixing the file and creating again needs no second reload. Status When 200 Evicted. evicted lists the keys as <slug>.json, sorted; with nothing cached it is []. 400 Malformed JSON, an unknown field, an explicitly empty resource_file (omit the field to mean "all"), a resource_file that is not a device-type slug, or one naming a type that is not shipped (no directory or file under resources/). 404 resource_file names a type that is shipped but not cached, because no device of it has been created since startup or since the last reload. Not a silent no-op: the body names the key and says the next creation reads from disk regardless. 409 A device-creation batch, or another reload, holds the gate. Same Retry-After: 5 and body as the create endpoint's 409. 413 The body exceeds 4 KiB. A reload is refused during a batch, because evicting while a load is in flight could republish the old file. While a reload holds the gate, GET /api/v1/status reports resource_reload_in_progress: true; poll it as for the create endpoint's 409. There is no file watcher. Reload is explicit.

curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices/export -o devices.csv The CSV columns are, in order: Device ID, IP Address, Interface, SNMP Port, SSH Port, Status, Resource File. Devices without a known resource file emit N/A in that column, matching the Interface convention. A re-import tool must translate N/A to an omitted resource_file field; POST rejects "N/A".

curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices/routes -o add_routes.sh The generated script adds Linux kernel routes for every device IP. Use it when running the simulator inside a VM and testing from the host.
# Single device curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices/{device-id} # All devices curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices

Report the running simulator's version. The value is set at build time from the Makefile's APP_VERSION (resolution order: APP_VERSION env > git describe --tags > dev). It never changes for the lifetime of the process, so the endpoint sets Cache-Control: private, max-age=3600. Release binaries report the clean tag (e.g., vX.Y.Z). A make build from a HEAD ahead of the last tag reports the commit-distance form (e.g., vX.Y.Z-11-g0356c42). curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/version {"version": "vX.Y.Z"} A build without tags, or one made by go build directly, reports dev. -version prints the same string without starting the server: ./nl6 -version # → vX.Y.Z
The flow, trap and syslog status and fire endpoints are documented on each protocol's reference page, linked from the endpoint catalog.

The control-plane only manages devices. Once a device is up, you interact with it via its own IP on port 22 (SSH), 161 (SNMP), and, for storage devices, 8443 (HTTPS). # SSH (VT100 terminal emulation) ssh simadmin@192.168.100.1 # password: simadmin # SNMP v2c snmpget -v2c -c public 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0 snmpwalk -v2c -c public 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1 # SNMP v3 (when enabled). RFC 3414 USM, verified against net-snmp. # A CLI-started fleet uses simadmin for the user and for both passwords, and # defaults to -snmpv3-auth md5 with privacy off, so the level you can poll # follows the flags the simulator was started with. snmpget -v3 -l noAuthNoPriv -u simadmin 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0 # started with -snmpv3-auth md5 (the default) snmpget -v3 -l authNoPriv -u simadmin -a MD5 -A simadmin \ 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0 # started with -snmpv3-auth sha1 -snmpv3-priv aes128 snmpget -v3 -l authPriv -u simadmin -a SHA -A simadmin -x AES -X simadmin \ 192.168.100.1 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0 See SNMP reference for the OID coverage, including the dynamic HC interface counters on ifXTable.

Storage devices expose vendor-shaped REST APIs on port 8443 with shared TLS certificates generated at simulator startup. # Pure Storage FlashArray curl -k https://192.168.100.1:8443/api/2.14/volumes curl -k https://192.168.100.1:8443/api/2.14/arrays curl -k https://192.168.100.1:8443/api/2.14/arrays/space # NetApp ONTAP curl -k https://192.168.100.1:8443/api/cluster curl -k https://192.168.100.1:8443/api/storage/volumes curl -k https://192.168.100.1:8443/api/storage/aggregates # AWS S3 curl -k https://192.168.100.1:8443/ # list buckets curl -k https://192.168.100.1:8443/my-bucket # bucket contents

A huawei_ne8000 device can stream interface telemetry to a collector as YANG-Push over UDP-notif. It models Huawei VRP R025C00. The transport is RFC 9187 (UDP-notif version 1, JSON). The subscriptions follow RFC 8641. Opt in per device. Devices of other types never stream. NetGauze v0.13.0 is the collector nl6 is checked against. The collector learns the schema by logging in to the device over NETCONF, so NETCONF must be on too. device ── UDP-notif (JSON, segmented) ──▶ collector device ◀── NETCONF over SSH (YANG library, get-schema, get) ── collector

NETCONF needs -netconf-enable. A collector such as NetGauze logs in with a key, so also pass an authorized_keys file. sudo ./nl6 -netconf-enable -netconf-authorized-keys ~/.ssh/authorized_keys -netconf-authorized-keys lets those keys log in as simadmin on every NETCONF SSH listener and on call home. The password login stays. Key options in the file are ignored. nl6 reads the file at startup even without -netconf-enable. See NETCONF for the flags. A yang_push block sent while -netconf-enable is off is accepted, with one warning in the log per process. The collector then cannot fetch the YANG library or the modules. A collector must be an IPv4 address or a hostname. An IPv6 literal gets 400, the same as -yang-push-collector. Then opt devices in. curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/devices \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "start_ip": "10.42.0.1", "device_count": 3, "resource_file": "huawei_ne8000.json", "yang_push": { "collector": "10.254.0.1:10000" } }' Field Type Default Description collector string required UDP target as host:port. segment_size int 1436 Maximum UDP-notif segment size in bytes, 512 to 65507. It counts the whole UDP payload including the 16-byte header. A request whose devices cannot stream is rejected with 400. A mixed round-robin batch is accepted, and the other types are skipped with one log line per profile per process. The auto-start batch takes the seed flag -yang-push-collector host:port. It applies only with -auto-start-ip. See CLI flags. Each device sends from a UDP socket connected to the collector and bound to the device IP. A failed bind fails the opt-in for that device, with no fallback to another source address. The connection lets the device see ICMP port-unreachable when no collector listens.

Three subscriptions start when the device starts. ID Mode Subtree Filter reference 8 periodic, 60 s /ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface/statistics STATEINTERFACE2 9 periodic, 60 s /ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface STATSINTERFACE2 10 on-change, dampening 0, sync on start oper-status and admin-status of every interface ONCHANGEINTERFACE The periodic subscriptions anchor at 2025-01-01T00:00:30Z. Subscription 9 sends three seconds after subscription 8. Every device fires at the same wall-clock second. A large fleet therefore produces one synchronized burst a minute on the host and on the collector. nl6 gives every device the same anchor, so the whole fleet bursts together. A real fleet does only if every device is configured with one anchor. Subscription 10 sends a push-update once at start with name, admin-status and oper-status of every interface. Its point-in-time is initial-state. After that it sends a push-change-update for each oper-status or admin-status change, with point-in-time state-changed. Subscriptions 8 and 9 use current-accounting. Take an interface down with the interface state API and the change arrives within a second. The start of each subscription sends a subscription-started notification first. Message IDs and the envelope sequence-number count per subscription and start at 0 on subscription-started. Every message is JSON in the VRP envelope ietf-yp-notification:envelope. It carries event-time, hostname (the device sysName), sequence-number and contents. A statistics push for a whole device is larger than one datagram. nl6 splits it at segment_size using the UDP-notif segment option, and the last segment has the low bit set. The first segment of a message is 9 bytes shorter than the rest, as on a real NE8000. The device IPv4 address as a big-endian unsigned integer is both the header observation domain ID and the message-publisher-id in the payload. 10.42.0.1 is 170524673.

NETCONF over SSH on -netconf-port serves the VRP dialect. A collector can read the YANG library with yang-library-content-id, the module list, and the modules with get-schema. Only IETF and IANA modules ship. The library lists augmented-by entries so NetGauze can load the envelope, observation, distributed-notification, push-revision and UDP-notif transport modules. ietf-netconf-monitoring is served because the device lists it. The library lists each implemented module's features, in both yang-library and modules-state. The content-id is the FNV-32a hash of the module list and the features, as a decimal string. get returns the three subscriptions and their filters. The filters are answered by reference. The dialect serves only get, get-schema, close-session and kill-session. A get on one subscription by ID also returns its receiver-instances. An unknown ID returns an empty <data/>, and NetGauze reports that as a parse error.

GET /api/v1/yangpush/status: { "subsystem_active": true, "devices_exporting": 3, "collectors": [ { "collector": "10.254.0.1:10000", "devices": 3, "messages_sent": 27, "segments_sent": 61, "send_failures": 0, "state_events_dropped": 0, "fidelity_suppressed": 0 } ] } Field Meaning messages_sent UDP-notif messages, each one a notification. segments_sent Datagrams. It is above messages_sent when anything was segmented. send_failures Datagrams the socket refused. state_events_dropped Interface events lost because the exporter fell behind. Its queue drops the oldest, so the latest transition still goes out. fidelity_suppressed Messages muted by -fidelity. The same drops also count in state_events_dropped of GET /api/v1/gnmi/status, which gNMI and NETCONF share.

-fidelity mutes all three subscriptions. The subscription-started notification waits for the first unmuted activity. The subscriptions do not join a load-test scenario window. That participation is not implemented.

nl6 follows a real NE8000 on VRP R025C00. These differences are deliberate. Subscription 10 is not verified against a real device. The NE8000 advertises on-change; nl6 builds the subscription from RFC 8641 and the same envelope. Every interface appears in subscription 8. The real device sent statistics for a subset. The ietf-udp-client module revision 2025-05-14 is a guess. The device library lists none. ietf-yang-push-revision is served at revision 2025-08-29, the copy NetGauze bundles. The NE library does not list the module. Its payload keys module-version by name, which only 2025-08-29 defines (2024-12-17 used module-name). Two augmented-by rows under ietf-subscribed-notifications (ietf-yang-push-revision and ietf-udp-notif-transport) follow a Huawei MA5800T, not the NE8000. Features follow the NE8000. nl6 adds encode-json under ietf-subscribed-notifications and yang-push-revision-supported under ietf-yang-push-revision, because the payloads it sends sit behind them. The NE lists only ietf-notification-capabilities as augmenting ietf-system-capabilities. nl6 also lists ietf-yang-push-revision, ietf-yp-notification and ietf-yp-observation, because their YANG text augments /sysc:system-capabilities. A get on a subscription by ID returns receiver-instances, which strict subtree filtering would not. Hostnames, addresses and interface names are synthetic. See the limitations for the full list.

make test-interop-yangpush runs three devices against a real NetGauze v0.13.0 and Redpanda in Docker, on a Linux host. NetGauze v0.13.0 validates the messages with libyang and finds none invalid. It checks the YANG library fetch, the Kafka output for subscriptions 8, 9 and 10, segmentation, and an interface going down. The stack is in examples/netgauze/.
